concepts/adaptive-agent-frameworks.title: Adaptive Agent Frameworks
concepts/adaptive-agent-frameworks.content:
Adaptive Agent Frameworks
Shiva Kasiviswanathan’s three research directions from Toward Adaptive Agent Frameworks for
making agents adaptive enough for mission-critical deployment.
Direction 1 — budget-aware adaptive execution, formalized as a constrained MDP. Today’s agents
mostly use a fixed execution policy set by a prompt or local heuristic. The proposed fix: have the
agent learn its execution policy (what to do next — retrieve information, use a tool, verify
results, update memory) to maximize expected utility subject to an explicit computational budget
(latency, cost, tokens, or similar) — formalized as a constrained Markov Decision Process. Reported
results: learned adaptive policies outperformed a commonly-used fixed heuristic (“scalarized
reward”) and were substantially more sample-efficient, reaching the same competence level with
fewer iterations. This connects to the recurring “route to the cheapest sufficient mechanism”
pattern already in Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — both treat cost-aware execution as
something learned and dynamic, not a static rule.
Direction 2 — parallel reasoning, learned during training rather than assembled at inference.
Today’s models mostly follow a single reasoning path per query. The proposed alternative: train
models to explore multiple reasoning paths in parallel, with the parallelism itself and the
coordination down to a single final answer both learned during training, not a post-hoc
inference-time sampling trick. Reported results: consistent improvements over strong baselines on
math and coding benchmarks, notably strong even at pass@1. This connects to
the parallel-tool-calling finding elsewhere in the wiki — both treat
parallelism as a trained, learned property of agent behavior rather than an engineering bolt-on.
Direction 3 — continual model/agent adaptation, mentioned briefly as ongoing work: principled
post-training schemes that let a model or agent adapt to new tasks without catastrophically
forgetting what it already knew. A third independent voice, alongside
Intelligence vs. Expertise and Long-Horizon Agents, converging on continual learning as a
critical, still-open problem for agent capability.
Where it shows up

Toward Adaptive Agent Frameworks — the talk this framing comes from.
Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — the same cost-aware, dynamic-routing theme.
Entropy Collapse — parallelism as a trained behavior, from a different talk.
Intelligence vs. Expertise and Long-Horizon Agents — two other voices converging on
continual learning as a critical open problem.

concepts/agent-2.0.title: Agent 2.0
concepts/agent-2.0.content:
Agent 2.0
From OpenSage: an explicit analogy to feature engineering vs. deep learning, applied to agent
construction. Today’s dominant paradigm (“Agent 1.0”) pre-specifies an agent’s topology and
toolset before running it — the same way pre-deep-learning ML required hand-engineered features.
The limitation: pre-specifying structure constrains generalizability, especially for complex,
long-horizon jobs where an agent might discover mid-execution that its toolset is insufficient or a
different sub-agent structure is needed — a rigid system can’t adapt on the fly.
The proposed alternative: provide only a minimal scaffold and let the agent build its own
agent — spawning sub-agents, designing its own workflow topology, writing its own tools, and
designing its own memory structure, all during execution. The framing directly echoes the lesson
deep learning already taught the field once: drop the hand-engineered inductive bias and let the
system search a larger space itself, rather than constraining it upfront. This is a more extreme,
general version of Architect Agents: Nio’s architect agent builds harnesses for specific,
human-chosen use cases; OpenSage’s ambition is fully self-directed construction with no
pre-specified structure at all.
The concrete framework: OpenSage redesigns the underlying agent-development kit itself to
support self-directed topology, tool, and memory construction, positioned against existing frontier
agent-development kits. At release, it reportedly outperformed Claude Code and Codex on coding and
security benchmarks — a specific, time-bound competitive claim, kept brief here.
A striking real-world validation, self-reported and worth treating as a single-event result
rather than independently verified: an unmodified agent, run in a parallel non-interactive track,
against DEF CON qualifier challenges — one of the hardest offensive-security competitions in the
world, normally requiring teams of professional hackers working 42-48 hours. Against 15
non-interactive challenges, it solved 7 outright and was reportedly close on 4 more, retrieving 8
flags total and placing in the top 5 of all-time participating teams — notably beating teams of
human hackers using little or no AI. The run took 5-6 hours of continuous autonomous operation,
spawning thousands of sub-agents — a real demonstration of self-directed topology-scaling working
at genuine scale on a hard task, not a synthetic benchmark.
A candid, forward-looking limitation: current models haven’t fully learned how to build their
own agents — when running the framework with the latest available models, a model sometimes wants
to spawn a sub-agent but fails to do so correctly. This motivates the claim that the model itself,
not just the scaffolding framework, needs to co-evolve: models need explicit training to better
spawn agents and write tools, and even the inference stack needs rethinking, since agent
trajectories differ structurally from plain QA-style inference. A grounded counterweight to the
broader thesis — self-directed agent construction isn’t just a scaffolding problem, it also
requires model- and inference-level capability that doesn’t yet fully exist.
Where it shows up

OpenSage — the talk this framing comes from.
Architect Agents — a more scoped, human-directed version of the same underlying idea.
Three-Level Runtime Control — a complementary emphasis: efficiently reusing a precomputed
bank of workflows, rather than building or discovering structure from scratch each time.

concepts/agent-delegation-as-runtime-cho.title: Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice
concepts/agent-delegation-as-runtime-cho.content:
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice
Daniel Homola’s (Lead AI Engineer, BMW Research) reframe from
From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration: multi-agent orchestration isn’t really
about patterns — handoff, agents-as-tools, routing/classifier-dispatch get different names at
every enterprise but all reduce to the same underlying problem. The core question is who should
handle this piece of work, answered reliably and repeatedly at runtime, under constantly shifting
context. Patterns are just the connective tissue between agents; the delegation decision is what
actually matters. Grounded in an in-car voice assistant example: navigation, car-control (windows,
seats, climate), and a GUI/computer-use agent, coordinated by an orchestrator above them.
Two sharp, separable reasons agent delegation isn’t ordinary tool selection:


The ground truth is multi-valued, not single-label. Tool selection is typically scored
against one correct answer. Agent delegation isn’t — multiple agents can validly solve the same
task, and which is actually best depends on context: cost, latency, user experience. Example:
“play some jazz” — if the screen is empty, the media-API agent is the right call; if a playlist
is already showing, tapping through the GUI agent is equally valid. A reliable system shouldn’t
force one canonical label; it should accept multiple acceptable choices and adapt to runtime
context.


Tool calls are bounded; agent delegation is unbounded. Even when implemented syntactically
as a tool call, delegating to an agent can start an autonomous loop — the sub-agent may reason,
ask for clarification, get stuck, resume later, or never cleanly return. Orchestration therefore
isn’t just about selecting the right capability; it’s also deciding when it’s safe and useful to
hand over effectively unbounded control to another loop. Delegation-as-tool-call syntax masks a
fundamentally different risk profile than an actual bounded tool invocation looks like on the
surface.


Consequences for evaluation: since ground truth is multi-valued and delegation carries
unbounded-loop risk, scoring final-task-success alone isn’t enough — evaluation also needs to
weigh the reasonableness of the chosen path, cost, latency, and user experience, which requires
datasets carrying full runtime context rather than simple input/output pairs, with metrics chosen
per what’s actually being optimized (sometimes latency, sometimes human-machine collaboration
quality).
A suggested organizational pattern for building these benchmarks at enterprise scale: each team
owning an agent builds its own benchmark for that agent; teams then combine benchmarks into a
shared one that also captures cross-agent collaboration and coordination, not just individual
agent quality in isolation.
Closing framing — the three questions that actually matter: who handles this work? What path
should they take together? How do we know it was good?
Where it shows up

From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration — the talk this reframe comes from.
Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — the general orchestrator-delegates-to-specialists
pattern this page sharpens with two specific findings: multi-valued ground truth, and the
bounded/unbounded distinction neither that page nor the other orchestrator-pattern pages in this
wiki name explicitly.
Grounded Capability Delegation — a different axis of delegation from an unrelated talk:
delegating from an LLM’s own reasoning to a grounded, deterministic tool, rather than choosing
among multiple valid agents for the same task.
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability — the same “measure the path, not just the final answer”
principle, applied here specifically to which agent got delegated to and how, rather than to a
single agent’s internal trajectory.
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks — a concrete, validated production instance of hierarchical
delegation (a “frontman” root delegating through a middle tier to leaf agents), with real
deployment numbers: ~200 leaf agents, ~30% reduction in ticket volume.

concepts/agent-harness.title: Agent Harness
concepts/agent-harness.content:
Agent Harness
The infrastructure, context, and constraints wrapped around a raw model that convert its
probabilistic capability into safe, reliable, goal-directed action — the shared thread across two
consecutive talks in the same session: Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI (Jonathan Cohen,
NVIDIA) and Harness Engineering (Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI/Google).
Cohen’s framing: “An agent isn’t just a large language model. It’s a large language model
surrounded by infrastructure” — data marshalling, type checking, rule-based policy enforcement.
Another word for everything surrounding the LLM, in his words, “is computer science.” An agent is
the combination of the LLM’s probabilistic, non-deterministic intelligence with the deterministic
power of decades of software engineering. Concretely, his group’s “NeMo Object-Oriented Agents”
treats an agent as a literal, self-modifying Python object, passing state by reference rather than
compacting it into a string context — reported as a large lift over the raw model (same score at
half the tokens; among the strongest CyberGym scores).
Lopopolo’s framing: harness engineering exists because of a capability overhang — models are
more capable and intelligent than they’re safely permitted to “side-effect into the world,” because
they lack the organizational context to know what local and global good looks like to their
operators. The human’s job is to give the agent tools, context, guardrails, coaching, and trust.
His method: recursively “double-click” into a task until reaching something the current model can
actually do, then reassemble upward — each pass permanently accrues capability into the harness,
not just the model. He frames harness design as bounded by two scarce resources: human time
(ruthlessly eliminate repetitive interventions — reviewing code, rejecting “slop,” going
back-and-forth on a plan — since removing them is what lets agent autonomy expand) and context
window / attention, for both human and model (a rule of thumb: needing more than three
interventions on one agent run usually means the harness, not the model, needs fixing). His closing
analogy: harness engineering is onboarding a generally capable new hire who doesn’t yet know what
“good” looks like for you.
Where the two talks converge: both treat the model itself as close to a commodity —
Lopopolo says implementation (code) is “free to produce now” — and locate the real engineering
effort, and the real capability gain, in the harness surrounding the model rather than in the model
itself.
Dawn Song’s defenses in Securing Agentic AI — privilege separation, dynamic context-based
least-privilege guardrails — are concrete instantiations of the “guardrails” both Cohen and
Lopopolo gesture at here without much detail.
An open question against this whole concept: in Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities,
Weizhu Chen describes a framework where the model designs and builds its own agent components on
the fly, rather than a human hand-engineering them — which raises whether harness engineering stays
a human discipline at all as models get better at it, or whether the harness itself becomes
something models increasingly write for themselves. Oriol Vinyals gives this the same idea a
rigorous name in Recursive Self-Improvement: harness-level self-improvement, distinct from
model-weight-level self-improvement — code, compaction, and tool access as one axis a system can
modify, the model itself as another.
A harder version of the same open question: Backprop Beats Scaffolding argues today’s
harness-level techniques (/goal, plan mode, sub-agents) aren’t trained end-to-end, and that
whatever ML can eventually backpropagate through tends to displace what it can’t — a direct
tension with treating the harness as the durable locus of engineering effort, rather than a
transitional phase.
A reconciliation of the two views above, from Chen’s own dedicated talk,
Continuous Model Improvement: harnesses do get absorbed into the model over time as models
improve — what needs hand-built scaffolding today gets simpler as capability grows, agreeing with
Tworek’s prediction — but people keep inventing more ambitious scenarios that need new harnesses
just as fast, so the harness layer never actually disappears. It’s not either/or; it’s a moving
frontier between what’s currently trained-in and what still needs scaffolding.
The clearest measured confirmation of the whole concept: Harness Matters More Than Model
puts numbers on it — swapping a model’s harness changed measured benchmark performance and cost by
double-digit percentages in multiple cases, with the winning model-harness pairing often
unpredictable in advance.
A concrete, working answer to Chen’s open question: Architect Agents describes a system
where an agent — not a human — builds the reasoning-graph harness for each new use case, with no
custom code, and gets measurably better at that meta-skill over time.
A large-scale enterprise confirmation of “build the harness first, not last”: HubSpot (Duncan
Lennox, Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary) found off-the-shelf co-pilots couldn’t work at their
scale (~1M builds/day, 10,000+ microservices) because they didn’t understand a decade of custom
internal tooling. Rather than wait for tooling vendors to catch up, they built their own agent
execution platform/harness plus MCP integrations, deliberately without mandating adoption —
winning over reliability-worried engineers with data showing reliability stayed neutral, then
improved. Documented over three stages as harness and context quality matured: 80% engineer
adoption / 51% productivity gain (early rollout) → 96% adoption / 60% gain (after fixing context
quality specifically — noting an “overfitting” failure mode where too much low-specificity context
hurts results as much as too little) → 100% adoption / 73% more code / 90% less time-to-first-PR-
feedback (shared platform, every team’s agent improving every other team’s context). Their own
closing framing matches this page’s title almost exactly: harness investment “compounds,” and
skipping it causes results to plateau.
Where it shows up

Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI — Cohen’s definition and the NeMo Object-Oriented
Agents harness design.
Harness Engineering — Lopopolo’s capability-overhang framing and the two scarce resources.
Towards Building Safe and Secure Agentic AI — concrete guardrail/privilege-control
techniques that fill in this concept’s “constraints” side.
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities — Chen’s open question about whether harnesses stay
human-built.
Recursive Self-Improvement — Vinyals’ harness-vs-model-weights split as a formal name for
that same question.
Backprop Beats Scaffolding — Tworek’s tension: harnesses as a stopgap, not a destination.
Continuous Model Improvement — Chen’s reconciliation: harnesses get absorbed over time, but
the frontier of what needs one keeps moving too.
Harness Matters More Than Model — a measured, empirical confirmation of this whole concept.
Architect Agents — a concrete, working system where an agent builds the harness itself.
An Agent Is a Stack — the same “don’t let any one layer become closed” argument, generalized
from model vs. harness to the entire stack (harness, tools, environment, guardrails, RL system,
eval infra, compute).
End-to-End AI Research — the same open question (permanent architecture vs. transitional
stopgap), from a research-agent’s harness rather than a general-purpose one.
Zero Ops — “models are not the moat” — the same claim that durable value
sits in the harness/context around a model, not the model itself.
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel — Jianfeng Gao’s independent version of
Chen’s reconciliation above: harness capability gets deliberately distilled into the model
through training, generation over generation, rather than merely “getting absorbed” as a side
effect of general model improvement.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — a reliability-engineering counterpoint to harness-
as-durable-infrastructure: Dan Klein frames “models checking models” (an external harness) as a
step forward but a stopgap — added latency, cost, and fragility that built-in, model-native
verification would avoid.
Meta-Harness Architecture — a concrete, production system (Databricks’s Omnigent) that
extends this concept with an explicit multi-harness orchestration layer, treating harness choice
itself as pluggable and swappable rather than something to pick once or absorb into the model.
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs — a pragmatic, engineering-driven (not theoretical)
confirmation of Chen’s reconciliation: NVIDIA moved a training-optimization agent to a
lightweight harness specifically to keep benefiting from general coding agents absorbing
capability over time, purely for maintenance-cost reasons.

concepts/agent-memory-lifecycle.title: Agent Memory Lifecycle
concepts/agent-memory-lifecycle.content:
Agent Memory Lifecycle
From Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks (Microsoft
Fabric AI): the human-vs-agent memory contrast that motivates the architecture. Humans have storage
constraints, which forces us to get good at distilling memories — watching endless fields pass by
on a train, we don’t remember every blade of grass, just what’s interesting. Agents don’t have this
constraint — they can log everything cheaply — and the common approach (capture, retrieve,
summarize, keep the summary) produces “summaries of summaries of summaries” that work fine generally
but break down specifically when you need something very particular that got compressed away.
The five-stage memory lifecycle, as a feedback loop:

Ingestion — pull in raw data from the observability substrate.
Consolidation — deduplicate and merge memories into stable candidates, analogized to human
sleep-driven consolidation. An important nuance: consolidation cadence is domain-dependent,
not necessarily temporal. A Formula 1 telemetry agent needs a completely different
consolidation rhythm during a race versus an off-week versus across a season — “consolidate
daily” is the wrong default; the right cadence has to be chosen per domain and processed in
batches, not assumed to follow a fixed clock.
Forgetting — apply decay and interference to consolidated candidates, aiming to retain what
matters and let unimportant material fade.
Retrieval — a hybrid of stable, graph-structured cold storage plus live streaming data, with
the agent determining which source is actually best to use at a given moment.
Maturation / reconsolidation — resolve conflicts between newly-arriving information and
already-stabilized memory: update an existing entity, add a new one for genuinely new
information, or discard incoming live data if it turns out to be erroneous. This exists
specifically to avoid a memory graph that just keeps growing and becomes hard to retrieve from.

The summary thesis, in the speaker’s own words: “logs are not memories.” For long-running
agents, raw traces alone aren’t sufficient — the volume has to be actively distilled into something
that stays efficient and useful over time, the way the five-stage lifecycle above does.
A closing design principle: domain structure (graph schema and ontology) needs to be
predeclared, not fully inferred at runtime, and materially affects both efficiency and accuracy
beyond just lifecycle-stage tuning. This connects to
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — both converge on graph-based, domain-structured
representation as important infrastructure for agent knowledge and memory.
The complementary weight-level pole, missing from the lifecycle above: this whole framework is
in-context memory — retrieval via tokens and text. Igor Babuschkin (River AI, Agentic AI Summit
2026 Sunday Plenary) argues personal AI specifically needs the other pole too: weight-level
updates. In-context memory handles explicit facts well (a phone number, a past conversation) but
struggles with implicit knowledge like a user’s stylistic preferences; weight-level updates handle
implicit style well but struggle to store precise discrete facts cheaply. His claim: personal AI
needs both, not one instead of the other. River AI’s own multi-tenant LoRA system is built to
make the weight-level side cheap in practice — updating only a small per-user adapter rather than
a full trillion-parameter model, opening the door to one custom fine-tuned model per user.
Where it shows up

Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks — the talk this
framing comes from.
Memory Evaluation Framework — the evaluation methodology for this architecture, from the same
talk.
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — the same graph-based, domain-structured
representation theme, from a different application.
Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning — an independently-arrived-at, near-identical
distillation analogy (the same train-window “blade of grass” image) from a separate Microsoft
team, applied to task-specific test-time learning rather than general long-horizon memory.
Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops — the same active-decay-not-accumulation principle
as this page’s “forgetting” stage, in a different domain: AWS’s hardware-optimization knowledge
bases need periodic pruning as the underlying model’s general training catches up and starts
conflicting with curated domain knowledge.

concepts/agent-security-taxonomy.title: Agent Security Taxonomy
concepts/agent-security-taxonomy.content:
Agent Security Taxonomy
Bo Li’s framing from Securing AI Agents: three buckets that organize the space of agent
security work.

Risk assessment / red teaming — a “pentest for AI,” stress-testing agentic systems with
varied skill sets, autonomous environments, and attack strategies to discover vulnerabilities
before deciding how to protect against them.
Protection, itself two-way:

Fundamental / model-level — train the model to have genuine policy-following reasoning
(e.g., actually following the EU AI Act or sector regulations) rather than relying on a system
prompt, which carries real uncertainty about whether the agent complies.
Plug-and-play — a “firewall for AI,” guardrails applied at the prompt level, the MCP
level, the tool-call level, and the tool-call-trajectory level, as an end-to-end closed loop
covering intent, in-flight behavior, and output.


Certification / self-improvement — formal guarantees about behavior, not just probabilistic
filtering. Her group’s “ShieldAgent” extracts rules from regulatory and policy frameworks,
represents allowed/disallowed behavior as an “action graph,” and uses that analysis to provide
runtime guardrails with a certification-level guarantee rather than black-box filtering alone.

Two principles for categorizing the risks themselves: regulatory/compliance-driven (organize by
existing frameworks — OWASP Top 10, NIST, MITRE, sector regulations, the EU AI Act) and use-case-
driven (organize by what actually happens — hallucination, data exfiltration, misuse). A third
dimension: organize by agent type or domain (computer-use vs. tool-use, etc.), since a universally
secure framework across every domain is infeasible — domain-specific analysis is more tractable.
This sharpens Securing Agentic AI’s existing three historical defense paradigms from a
different talk: reactive detection maps loosely onto plug-and-play guardrails here, and
security-by-construction maps onto fundamental protection plus certification — two independent
speakers converging on a similar three-way split of the same design space.
Where it shows up

Securing AI Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming — the concrete red-teaming platform from the same talk.
Securing Agentic AI — an independent, similarly-shaped three-way taxonomy from a different
speaker.

concepts/agent-suspend-resume-pattern.title: Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern
concepts/agent-suspend-resume-pattern.content:
Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern
The architectural response Tim Hockin describes in
Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? to the mismatch documented in
Agent Workload Shape. Instead of treating an idle agent as a running-but-unused process (the
naive approach) or building a bespoke scheduler to manage that waste manually (the DIY approach),
stop running it at all while it’s idle:

Snapshot the agent’s state the moment it goes idle (a “golden snapshot” for a freshly-created
agent, an actual runtime snapshot thereafter) and shuffle it off to storage.
Multiplex many suspended agents onto a shared pool of pre-warmed workers, rather than
reserving a dedicated worker per agent for its entire (mostly idle) lifetime.
Resume from the snapshot on the next incoming message, driving the idle-to-active wake cost
down from the tens-of-seconds-to-tens-of-minutes range naive pod lifecycles produce to
low-hundreds-of-milliseconds.

The concrete implementation Hockin describes (Google’s open-sourced “Agent Substrate” project, with
its own vocabulary of actors/templates/workers) is one instantiation of this; the durable part is
the pattern itself — decouple “idle” from “resource-consuming” via snapshot + suspend/resume +
shared warm-pool multiplexing — which should generalize to any platform running large numbers of
bursty, single-tenant, sandboxed agents, not just Kubernetes.
Where it shows up

Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? — the talk this framing comes
from.
Agent Workload Shape — the mismatch this pattern is a response to.
Dynamic KV-Cache Management — the same suspend/resume idea at a much finer grain: KV cache
specifically, rather than a whole agent process.

concepts/agent-workload-shape.title: Agent Workload Shape
concepts/agent-workload-shape.content:
Agent Workload Shape
Tim Hockin’s argument from Is Kubernetes Good for Agents?: agent
workloads have a resource profile that’s structurally at odds with what general-purpose
orchestration platforms (Kubernetes, but the point generalizes) are built to run efficiently. Three
properties, taken together:

Bursty. Agents work in short spurts, then go idle for minutes, hours, days, or weeks.
Untrusted and single-tenant. Agent code has to run sandboxed, and sandboxes can’t be shared —
which forecloses the overhead-amortization that makes horizontal scaling of traditional
applications cheap.
Latency-sensitive despite being bursty. A human is usually waiting on the other end of each
turn, so perceived responsiveness still matters even though the workload itself is idle most of
the time.

Kubernetes (and most general-purpose orchestrators) were designed for the opposite profile:
long-running, horizontally-scalable, cost-amortizable processes. Running agents naively on top of
that model means paying for large amounts of idle-but-reserved capacity — the mismatch, not any
specific missing feature, is the actual problem. See Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern for the
architectural response to this mismatch.
Where it shows up

Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? — the talk this framing comes
from.
Diffusion Language Models — the same latency-sensitivity-despite-burstiness point, from a
different domain (model decoding speed, not orchestration).
The Bazaar Era of AI — this page and
Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? are a concrete,
orchestration-layer instance of Raskar’s broader “X for agents” reframing.
An Open Compute Layer — a complementary infra concern one layer up: cross-cluster
orchestration, rather than single-cluster agent lifecycle.
Durable Execution — the same burstiness observation from a different angle: execution-model
design (serverless-style crash recovery) rather than deployment lifecycle.

concepts/agent-native-data-infrastructur.title: Agent-Native Data Infrastructure
concepts/agent-native-data-infrastructur.content:
Agent-Native Data Infrastructure
James Zou’s point from
Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science: existing scientific databases
(proteins, molecules, gene expression, and similar) were designed to be consumed by humans, or by
pre-AI algorithms — and are “too brittle and too limited” for AI agents to use efficiently through
the interfaces built for those consumers (traditional APIs, or giving a model MCP access to the
database as-is).
His fix (“PaperClip”): convert existing databases into agent-native virtual file systems —
restructuring the same underlying data (millions of proteins, molecules, gene-expression records,
and full-text papers) into a representation built for how an agent actually needs to synthesize and
aggregate information across sources. Measured results: meaningfully better accuracy than giving a
model the same data through a frontier lab’s own science-specific tooling, and roughly an order of
magnitude faster and cheaper than traditional MCP/API access to the same underlying databases.
The general point: the bottleneck isn’t necessarily the data itself or the model — it’s the
representation layer between them. This is a data-layer complement to Data for Agents, though a
distinct specific claim: Roth’s point is about access and planning (retrieval isn’t as simple as
it looks, ordering and conflicting sources matter); Zou’s point is about representation format
(a virtual file system built for agents beats an API built for humans). Both converge on the same
underlying idea — the data layer that works for human consumers isn’t the one agents need.
Where it shows up

Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science — the talk this framing comes
from.
Data for Agents — a related but distinct claim about the same underlying gap (access/planning
vs. representation format).

concepts/agent-native-payment-rails.title: Agent-Native Payment Rails
concepts/agent-native-payment-rails.content:
Agent-Native Payment Rails
Nikhil Chandhok’s (Circle) argument from Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy:
agents becoming outward-facing endpoints on the internet — his framing, “much like websites are
endpoints on the internet” — need a fundamentally different payment substrate than the one built
for humans, for three specific structural reasons, not just a general “crypto is faster” pitch.
1. Programmability. Every existing payment rail (credit card, bank account) assumes a human is
one step away, present to authorize. That assumption breaks the moment an agent spawns 100
sub-agents, each spawning 100 more, where every one of them needs to transact value under its own
governance rules. Stablecoins solve this by making money itself programmable: every sub-agent gets
its own on-chain wallet with rules attached to it, fully trackable, without requiring a bank account
or credit card of its own.
2. Finality. A credit-card swipe has only probabilistic finality — the merchant is paid only
once the issuer bank clears funds, later. That’s tolerable at human transaction volume. At agent
scale — potentially more transacting agents than humans, the way there are already more web pages
than people — probabilistic finality compounds risk across an enormous number of small
transactions. On-chain settlement gives absolute finality by construction, which agent-scale
commerce specifically needs.
3. Privacy vs. auditability. A fully public ledger is excellent for auditability but corrosive
to real economic activity if every agent’s wallet balance leaks to anyone watching. “Trust at the
application layer” is a viable compromise for a handful of human-run accounts; it doesn’t obviously
scale to agent-scale transaction volume, and this tension isn’t resolved in the talk, just named.
The framing device: designing payment rails for agents the way full self-driving could be
designed if you assumed you could rebuild the entire highway system, rather than assuming the roads
(existing financial rails) stay fixed and agents have to adapt around them.
The proposed fix: open architecture. Agents transact across open systems, paying in whichever
stablecoin is available in the market rather than being locked to one issuer — deliberately
mirroring how the web grew from a handful of FTP/HTTP servers in the early 90s into an unbounded
number of independent sites. Concrete instantiation: agentscircle.com, a marketplace/CLI for
agent-to-agent task commerce with micropayments as small as a millionth of a cent per task.
A parallel to draw, not stated in the talk itself: this is the same “an army of agents” future
Surapaneni’s identity/governance framework assumes internally
within an enterprise — Chandhok’s talk is the same problem’s external, cross-organizational
counterpart: once agents transact with other agents outside any single company’s IAM boundary,
identity and governance (Surapaneni’s problem) and value transfer (this page’s problem) become two
halves of the same infrastructure gap.
Where it shows up

Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy — the talk this argument comes from.
Enterprise AI - Agent Governance — the internal/enterprise counterpart to this talk’s
external/cross-organizational agent-to-agent problem.

concepts/agentic-ai-full-stack.title: Agentic AI Full Stack
concepts/agentic-ai-full-stack.content:
Agentic AI Full Stack
A layered framework for what it takes to run agentic AI at scale, presented by Saurabh Tiwary
in From Models to Agents to Discovery using Google’s stack as the example. Bottom to top:

AI hypercomputer — the hardware layer (GPUs/TPUs).
Frontier models — trained on that hardware.
Data — needed for models/agents to do anything meaningful.
Agentic security & defense — as agents start doing meaningful things, they become a
meaningful attack surface.
Platform — lets people reuse the lower layers cheaply and effectively. Broken into four
problems: build (model access, dev kits), scale (single instance → millions of
agents), govern (agent identity separate from the user’s own identity, since agents can act
beyond what the user can do directly), optimize (tracing, simulation, evaluation,
observability).
End-to-end agentic task force — the agents that actually do things for you.

The talk’s claim is that these layers need to be co-optimized together to extract value, not
built independently — the same conclusion Peter DeSantis reaches from Amazon’s side; see
Model-Hardware Co-Design.
Where it shows up

From Models to Agents to Discovery — the talk this framework comes from.

concepts/agentifying-the-web's-long-tail.title: Agentifying the Web's Long Tail
concepts/agentifying-the-web's-long-tail.content:
Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail
Dhruv Batra’s argument from
Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs, targeting a specific, widely-repeated
three-step narrative: (1) AI agents will become the web’s primary actors, not humans — right; (2)
so the web will be “agentified” — right; (3) via a proliferation of API standards agents call
through — wrong. His counter-claim: computer-use agents, which operate a browser visually the
way a human does, will agentify the web’s long tail — not APIs. (The common counter-demo, an agent
clicking through a flight-search site, is misleading precisely because flight search already has
structured API aggregators — it was never representative of the actual long tail.)
Argument 1 — the long tail won’t get APIs, for economic reasons, not lack of ambition.
Generalize past flight search to something with no aggregator — “does this specific restaurant have
gluten-free items?” Real small-business websites range from readable text, to unstructured PDFs, to
unOCR’d scanned menu photos, maintained by hundreds of thousands of small business owners (his
example: roughly 200,000 in one European country) who will never build or maintain a clean API for
their own site. Any one site has limited value; the tail cumulatively matters enormously; and this
kind of infrastructure changes very slowly. The API-ification “cavalry” isn’t coming.
Argument 2 — reading raw HTML doesn’t substitute for rendering; this is a technical fact, not a
current limitation. Checking whether a product is in stock: a human sees a dropdown with some
options visibly grayed out. The raw HTML’s selector elements contain no quantity data at all — that
data arrives via a separate API call at page-load time, and a distinct piece of client-side
JavaScript decides how to render availability, entirely at runtime. For a large class of real
queries, the ground truth only exists after JavaScript executes — it isn’t present in the static
markup at all. A browser is fundamentally a rendering engine (his analogy: like a video-game engine
— assets plus code produce pixels) — so reading source code, however capable the reading agent, is
not equivalent to actually rendering and observing the page.
The resulting framing: “the bitter lesson for web agents” — a deliberate echo of Sutton’s
Bitter Lesson. The web was built for human eyeballs, so machines need vision to reach its long
tail; anything short of that becomes brittle, hand-engineered scraping logic that doesn’t
generalize. Batra’s group builds a model (“Navigator”) that takes a screenshot as input and
predicts human-like browser actions (click, type, scroll) as output. A sharper example of where no
API will ever exist, by design rather than neglect: checking whether a promo code works at
checkout — merchants will never expose that as an API, since it would let anyone enumerate valid
codes; the only way to check is to actually run the flow and observe whether the price changes.
“There is your API of the web.”
One nuance — vision-grounded doesn’t mean human-paced. In a form-filling example, the model
doesn’t click field-by-field like a human; it writes and executes custom JavaScript directly to
fill multiple fields at once — an action space beyond literal button-clicking, made possible
precisely because the model can see and reason about the page, not because it’s imitating human
interaction speed.
Closing framing: the future “API of the web” won’t be a formal protocol at all — it will be a
large population of agents operating browsers in the background, able to answer any natural-language
question about any website by actually visiting and interacting with it.
Where it shows up

Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs — the talk this framing comes from.

concepts/agents'-last-exam.title: Agents' Last Exam
concepts/agents'-last-exam.content:
Agents’ Last Exam
Eson’s argument from Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation:
as frontier labs increasingly frame agents as assistants for professional work rather than
question-answering systems, the evaluation bar needs to rise correspondingly — a benchmark should
test completed workflows and the quality of the resulting artifacts, not isolated Q&A.
A sharp, quantified critique of existing benchmark coverage: agent benchmarks concentrate
almost entirely on programming and mathematical domains, which represent only about 7% of actual US
employment. Huge swaths of real professional work — management, finance, law, engineering — remain
essentially untested. What gets measured is what gets optimized, so this coverage gap isn’t
neutral; it shapes where the whole field’s effort goes.
A methodologically serious fix for building representative coverage. Start from an authoritative
external map of real work — the US Standard Occupation Classification (867 detailed occupations) —
screen roughly 10,000 O*NET entries for computer-centered workflows, consolidate into about 100
SOC-based codes, and group those into 55 fields, with expert review of borderline cases. Starting
from an authoritative taxonomy of real-world work, rather than from what’s easy to benchmark, is
the durable, reusable part of this approach.
Design choices that distinguish Agents’ Last Exam (ALE) from prior benchmarks:

Authentic scope — 300+ practitioners contributed real workflows; the initial snapshot
contains 760 workflows and 1,500 task instances across 55 fields, sourced from experts’ own
already-completed past projects (with necessary sanitization of sensitive details), not
synthetic prompts.
Outcome-only measurement, agnostic to interface — the benchmark doesn’t care whether a task
is completed via CLI or GUI, only the final outcome, better simulating realistic human work
environments.
Deliverable- and milestone-based evaluation against a hidden reference, with light reliance
on LLM judges — outputs and intermediate states are checked against held-out references rather
than another model’s fallible judgment.
A different unit of work: professional deliverables spanning hours to weeks of real expert
effort, not short, isolated operational patches.

Construction pipeline: tasks are filtered from real completed expert submissions on three axes
— representativeness, complexity (expert-level tasks take days, not minutes), and verifiability.
Each submission specifies the task ask, input files, expected deliverables, and evaluation
criteria; engineers make the package executable, and domain experts do repeatable execution and
scoring.
Current results: even the best models pass only a low single-digit percentage of the hardest
tier — though that’s up from zero passing tasks just three months prior, showing rapid capability
movement even at low absolute readiness. On an easier tier, per-task best-agent pass rates reach
roughly 60%. No single agent wins everywhere — different models have different domain-specific
weaknesses (e.g., life sciences, certain visual/media domains), and some decline sensitive-seeming
tasks outright, which itself affects their measured score. This echoes the “no universal winner”
theme already recurring in the wiki: Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity,
Spectrum of Agency, Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability.
The double meaning of “Last Exam”: a full pass signals genuine readiness to sustain
economically valuable work in that profession, and the benchmark is deliberately placed at the
boundary of what today’s models can reliably accomplish — both an aspirational finish line and a
genuinely hard test.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation — the talk this
framing comes from.
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity, Spectrum of Agency,
Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability — the same “no universal winner” theme, from
unrelated domains.

concepts/an-agent-is-a-stack.title: An Agent Is a Stack
concepts/an-agent-is-a-stack.content:
An Agent Is a Stack
Matt White’s framing from Open Source Agentic RL Environment: AI capability is rising fast
just as openness comes under genuine political pressure. Restricting or banning open-weight models
— via chip controls, compute controls, distillation restrictions, mandatory safety testing, or
release-process rules — is being actively debated for real, legitimate safety and national-security
reasons. But the risk on the other side is equally real: blunt restrictions concentrate capability,
infrastructure, and decision-making into a small number of institutions, turning AI from a broadly
accessible, general-purpose technology into something the rest of society can only rent from a few
labs.
A precise clarification worth keeping distinct: openness doesn’t mean ungoverned. It means
systems can be inspected, evaluated, adapted, and improved, with interoperable interfaces and no
single organization controlling every layer — not a free-for-all. Openness is itself a component of
safety, not opposed to it: it enables reproducible evaluation, transparent interfaces, independent
scrutiny, and shared security tooling, letting many people find and fix problems rather than
depending on one vendor to do so.
The sharpest, most quotable line: “an agent is not simply a model. An agent is a stack.” It
includes the model, the harness, the tools it invokes, the environment it acts in, guardrails, the
reinforcement learning system it improves through, the evaluation infrastructure that measures it,
and the compute it runs on — often crossing organizational, cloud, and geographic boundaries within
a single task. If any one layer of that stack becomes closed and vertically controlled, the whole
ecosystem becomes less portable, less competitive, and more fragile. Open models alone are
insufficient; the argument extends the same logic to every layer — open environments, open
reinforcement-learning frameworks, open compute layers, and open standards connecting all of it.
This generalizes what Agent Harness and Punk Software already argue at narrower scope
(model vs. harness; individual tooling) to the entire stack at once, and gives the argument its
most quotable single line.
Where it shows up

Open Source Agentic RL Environment — the talk this framing comes from.
Agent Harness and Punk Software — the same “don’t let any one layer become closed”
argument, at narrower scope.
RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer — the concrete case for one specific layer of
this stack (environments) from the same talk.

concepts/an-open-compute-layer.title: An Open Compute Layer
concepts/an-open-compute-layer.content:
An Open Compute Layer
Romil Bhardwaj’s argument from AI Needs an Open Compute Layer: AI organizations need a layer
that manages across their fragmented compute, not a better single-cluster scheduler.
Fragmentation is a structural inevitability, not a mistake. A typical AI org accumulates a
NeoCloud reservation, on-demand hyperscaler capacity, on-prem clusters (regulatory or data-
residency reasons), regional clusters (serving customers in specific geographies), and separate CPU
clusters for running sandboxes and environments. Each decision made sense in isolation; the
cumulative result is a heterogeneous collection of clusters someone now has to manage as one whole.
Even the most capitalized AI companies hit this: escalating, sequential multi-billion-dollar
compute deals with different providers show that securing enough compute in a single cluster is
hard at any scale.
RL workloads make scheduling qualitatively harder, because “one RL job” is really several
sub-workloads with very different resource profiles bundled together: the trainer needs relatively
few but very high-VRAM GPUs; the rollout server generating trajectories needs many GPUs but less
VRAM each; sandboxes (e.g. for code-generation RL) need huge parallel CPU counts and fast I/O.
Treating RL as one monolithic scheduling unit misses this internal heterogeneity.
Why Slurm and Kubernetes don’t solve this, despite each being excellent at what they do.
Slurm: a 20-year-old HPC scheduler, superb at quota and priority management, but not designed for
container-based isolation and built for batch jobs rather than serving. Kubernetes: excellent for
elastic, cloud-native microservices, but has a steep learning curve for researchers and lacks
native AI-specific primitives like gang scheduling (bolted on via schedulers like Volcano). The
real point: both are fundamentally single-cluster managers — however good either one is, neither
solves the problem of managing many different clusters and platforms at once.
The proposed fix: a layer that bridges workloads and fragmented clusters, without replacing any
of them. The explicit design principle is not to replace Kubernetes or Slurm — they’re good at
what they do — but to build a layer that sits between workloads and whatever mix of Slurm,
Kubernetes, and cloud-VM clusters actually exists, so workloads don’t need to know what’s
underneath. SkyPilot, Bhardwaj’s own open-source project (originating at UC Berkeley’s Sky
Computing Lab), is the concrete instantiation: bring your own framework (Ray, PyTorch, Unsloth, and
similar), declare the resources a job needs, and SkyPilot orchestrates across whatever’s available
— including a “job groups” abstraction for declaring heterogeneous resource requirements across a
single workload’s sub-components (e.g., a rollout server on one GPU type, a trainer on another),
with automatic restart-on-failure for individual sub-jobs rather than failing an entire run. The
layer itself never brokers or sells compute — organizations bring their own, from their own
providers.
An emergent benefit of unifying the layer: dynamic reallocation between training and serving.
With both workload types running through one layer over the same GPU pool, the system can preempt
training when inference demand spikes (checkpointing prevents data loss), then scale training back
up once the spike subsides. This kind of cross-workload elasticity is impossible when training and
serving sit on siloed infrastructure — unifying the scheduling layer is what unlocks it.
This completes an infra trio now in the wiki, each addressing a different layer of the same
underlying strain on AI infrastructure:
Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? (single-cluster agent lifecycle and
suspend/resume), Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity (inference-serving hardware
diversity), and this page (cross-cluster orchestration).
Where it shows up

AI Needs an Open Compute Layer — the talk this framing comes from.
Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? — a complementary infra concern
(single-cluster agent lifecycle) rather than a redundant one (cross-cluster orchestration).
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity — a third complementary infra concern
(inference-serving hardware diversity).
Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance — a different lever on the same GPU-scarcity problem,
at the training-algorithm level rather than infrastructure orchestration.
Punk Software — a similar provider-agnostic design (Manager), motivated by avoiding platform
lock-in rather than GPU scarcity.

concepts/architect-agents.title: Architect Agents
concepts/architect-agents.content:
Architect Agents
The sharpest point in
Agent Learning Requires Compressing Information into an Executable Reasoning Structure: a
reasoning graph for a new use case isn’t hand-coded — it’s built by an agent.
An “architect agent,” trained specifically to work well with this harness type, constructs the
graph for each new use case — choosing the wiring between agents, their instructions, which model
each node uses, and memory setup — with no human-written custom code anywhere in the process.
This is a concrete, working answer to an open question already in the wiki. Agent Harness
records Weizhu Chen’s open question — does harness engineering stay a human discipline as models
get better at it, or does the harness become something models increasingly build for themselves?
Here, empirically: an agent builds it, launching new use cases in about a week instead of requiring
bespoke human engineering each time.
“Compounding intelligence”: every new use case the architect agent handles makes it better at
the meta-skill of building reasoning graphs, not just better at any one graph instance. This is a
form of harness-level self-improvement in Oriol Vinyals’ vocabulary from
Recursive Self-Improvement — but one level up from what that page describes: it’s the skill of
building harnesses that compounds, not any single harness improving itself.
Illustrated with a compressed case study: matching invoices to purchase orders is long-horizon,
exception-heavy (currency, units, tax, and one memorable ad hoc rule — a liquid invoice can be up to
5% short in summer because some of it evaporates), and needs both high consistency and
explainability. A general-purpose harness on a strong model got well under half of cases right; an
architect-built reasoning graph for this exact process reached near-total accuracy, correctly
explained its decisions in the large majority of cases, and launched within about a week with no
custom code — cost per invoice processed falling sharply across successive iterations. The
generalizable claim, independent of the specific numbers: an agent-built reasoning graph tailored
automatically to a long-horizon, exception-heavy process can dramatically outperform a
general-purpose harness on that exact process, without bespoke human engineering.
Where it shows up

Agent Learning Requires Compressing Information into an Executable Reasoning Structure — the
talk this framing comes from.
Agent Harness — the open question this talk gives a concrete, working answer to.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the harness-level self-improvement vocabulary this is one level
up from: the skill of building harnesses compounding, not one harness improving itself.
Agent 2.0 — a more extreme, general version of the same idea: fully self-directed agent
construction with no pre-specified structure at all, rather than a scoped, human-chosen use case.
Three-Level Runtime Control — a complementary emphasis: efficiently reusing a precomputed
bank of workflows, rather than building or discovering structure from scratch each time.
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks — a close cousin via a different mechanism: multi-agent
systems generating other multi-agent systems’ JSON/HOCON configs as disposable “perishable
thoughts,” rather than one agent constructing a single reasoning graph.

concepts/assistive,-collaborative,-semi-.title: Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents
concepts/assistive,-collaborative,-semi-.content:
Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents
Venkat Bhat’s “cornerstone” framing from
Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration:
a human-in-the-loop maturity taxonomy for mental-health agents, developed several years before this
talk. Three tiers, each with a different role for the human clinician: assistive (the AI scribe
is the clearest, most widely-adopted example, already in clinical use), collaborative (agents
working alongside a clinician within a shared task), and semi-autonomous (agents doing more of
the work independently, still within human oversight). A third independent autonomy-tier taxonomy
now in the wiki, alongside Spectrum of Agency and Zero Ops’s maturity
model — three domain-specific instances of the same underlying design question: how much autonomy
should an agent actually have, and who stays in the loop at each level.
The sharpest epistemic point: sandbox/simulation success is not evidence of real-world
efficacy. As a clinical trialist, Bhat’s standard workflow is: identify an automatable clinical
workflow, build single- or multi-agent automation, validate in simulation with a bot playing the
end-user role — and then run actual multi-year clinical trials to see whether something that works
in simulation works in real care. A related point: even an agent that’s non-inferior to a human at
a specific task isn’t automatically worth adopting — real deployment requires change management,
service redesign, and explicit cost-benefit analysis, not just task-level parity.
A disciplined scoping practice, illustrated with a DSM-based diagnostic-interviewing system
(one agent asks questions, another enforces the diagnostic kit’s skip logic, an orchestrator ties
it together, validated against a bot patient across various DSM diagnoses): the system is
deliberately scoped to mild-to-moderate symptoms only, with an explicit acknowledgment that someone
with severe psychosis, depression, or Alzheimer’s is not a safe user for it. Declaring a system’s
appropriate range, rather than overclaiming generality, is itself the durable practice worth
preserving.
A closing, sobering statistic: despite enormous interest, there was only one (soon two) actual
randomized controlled trial of GenAI-based mental-health tools at the time of this talk — a stark
gap between hype and rigorous clinical validation. Bhat’s own honest framing: “most of these things
are not going to work… but the few things which would work will have a transformative effect.”
Where it shows up

Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration
— the talk this framing comes from.
Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity — the sharper technical finding from the same talk.
Spectrum of Agency and Zero Ops — two other domain-specific autonomy-
tier taxonomies, from unrelated fields.

concepts/asynchronous-rl-and-staleness-t.title: Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance
concepts/asynchronous-rl-and-staleness-t.content:
Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance
Silas Alberti’s systems-level finding from Scaling RL for Coding Agents: decouple the trainer
from rollout generation. Rollout workers continuously feed trajectory batches into a shared data
buffer; the trainer consumes from that buffer whenever it’s ready and periodically pushes weight
updates back out to the rollout workers. This means the rollout (“inference”) policy generating
trajectories at any given moment may lag the trainer’s current policy by some number of steps — this
lag is called staleness.
The key finding: the more stable your training algorithm, the more staleness it can tolerate
without breaking — and tolerating more staleness is what lets you keep inference/rollout engines
fully utilized, rather than idling while waiting for synchronized updates. Stability and compute
utilization turn out to be linked through staleness tolerance, not independent engineering
concerns: an unstable algorithm forces tight synchronization (and therefore idle rollout capacity),
while a more stable one can let training and rollout drift further apart and still converge
correctly.
A striking practical payoff: intercontinental training. Large, contiguous GPU clusters are hard
to secure on demand — often requiring booking roughly a year in advance — while smaller, scattered
slices of compute are comparatively easy to find. Because RL’s cross-cluster traffic (token batches,
periodic weight updates) is relatively low-bandwidth compared to tightly-coupled synchronous
training, sufficient staleness tolerance made it practical to run a single training job with one
training cluster and multiple rollout clusters spread across four countries on three continents,
communicating over the open internet rather than a single datacenter’s interconnect. The general
point: algorithmic staleness tolerance converts a compute-acquisition constraint (no single big
cluster available) into a solvable engineering problem (federate many small clusters globally) — a
genuinely different lever on the GPU-scarcity problem than An Open Compute Layer’s
cross-scheduler orchestration, operating at the algorithm level rather than the
infrastructure-management level.
Where it shows up

Scaling RL for Coding Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Entropy Collapse — the training-science counterpart from the same talk.
An Open Compute Layer — a different lever on the same underlying GPU-scarcity problem, at the
infrastructure-orchestration level rather than the training-algorithm level.
Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts — a smaller-scale, fully-synchronous case study
(Qwen3-8B on 8 H100s) that this page’s async/staleness-tolerant approach is built to move beyond.
Train-Inference Mismatch — a related but distinct source of train/rollout divergence, from
Miles (SGLang’s RL framework): unintentional numerical mismatch between engines, rather than
this page’s intentional staleness traded for throughput.

concepts/autonomous-research-agents.title: Autonomous Research Agents
concepts/autonomous-research-agents.content:
Autonomous Research Agents
Agents that run an open-ended research loop with no human instruction in the middle: generate
approaches, pursue them, evaluate the results, preserve what was learned, and use that record to
choose the next attempt. Two complementary cases make the pattern clearer. The empirical case in
A Lab Notebook for Agents shows the infrastructure that keeps many experiments reproducible
and coordinated; The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt shows the search policy that can be
written into a single theorem-proving prompt. Chuan Li’s term for the broader pattern is
“auto-research.”
Li’s talk argues that what makes the empirical version work isn’t model intelligence alone but
forcing the agent to keep lab notes the way a human scientist would: a notebook (note-taking API),
a whiteboard (leaderboard to query past results), sticky notes (inter-agent messages), and a signup
sheet (job queue) — standardized so the agent does bookkeeping the same correct way every time,
instead of the inconsistent way humans do it by hand. Two properties this requires that a naive
single-shot agent loop doesn’t have:

Reproducibility: every idea gets committed to its own git branch with its code and settings,
so a run can be reproduced and, since results are noisy run-to-run, averaged rather than trusted
on a single lucky or unlucky score.
Self-application: the tooling can be pointed at itself — in the talk, the same experiment
tracker was used to cut its own per-experiment cost ~10x by analyzing its own API traces.

The theorem-proving counterpart replaces experimental infrastructure with an explicit cognitive
protocol. In The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt, the agent is told to maintain a diversified
portfolio of proof strategies, work them independently before allowing cross-pollination, keep a
registry of lemmas and failure modes, build reusable intermediate artifacts, attack candidate
arguments adversarially, and continue until it has a novel proof or a precise account of what
blocks one. The prompt therefore encodes the shape of a research program, not merely the desired
answer.
The two implementations have nearly isomorphic primitives:

The Lab’s job queue becomes a portfolio of named proof programs.
Its branches and commits become an explicit registry of lemmas, dependencies, and discarded
approaches.
Its leaderboard becomes hard evaluation gates: correctness, closure of dependencies, and
genuine novelty.
Its messages and shared notes become delayed cross-pollination between initially independent
lines of attack.

Together they suggest a practical discipline for auto-research: make the objective testable;
preserve enough state to resume and compare attempts; diversify before converging; isolate early
search to prevent one seductive idea from collapsing the portfolio; share only useful artifacts;
stress-test promising results; and distinguish persistence from repetition by requiring each new
attempt to be conditioned on the accumulated record.
Also where Reward Hacking shows up as a hazard: an unsupervised loop that’s free to pursue any
avenue toward the score will find the ones you didn’t intend to allow.
Oriol Vinyals independently names Li’s talk as a worked example of what he calls plain
self-improvement. The Tetris and Crouzeix cases are both better described as autonomous
research or SI than as RSI: each improves an external target, not
the researcher doing the improving. By Ian Fischer’s stricter test in
An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement, the bridge to RSI requires two
additional facts: the target must be a component of the optimizing system, and gains from one
round must improve the next round’s optimizer rather than merely accumulate in a notebook.
Self-Optimizing Optimizers is a concrete example of that stronger shape.
A revised counterweight: Backprop Beats Scaffolding records Jerry Tworek’s observation that
the common pattern across auto-research rollouts was real progress followed by a stall. The
Crouzeix case is a direct update to the incident-level claim that no rollout had yet crossed into
a complete research result. It does not settle Tworek’s architectural argument: the successful
run depended on extensive prompt-level scaffolding for decomposing and governing a long-horizon
search. A hand-designed research process can occasionally bridge short-horizon model cognition
into a long result; whether that process will remain outside the trained model is a separate
question.
A sibling pattern at a different granularity: Paper Agents describes no-human-in-the-loop
research emerging not from one lab’s experimentation loop but from autonomous synthesis across the
existing published corpus — unrelated papers’ agents recognizing on their own that they should
collaborate.
The reproducibility scaffolding here — git branch per idea, so runs can be re-executed and compared
— is specifically what physical science lacks: there’s no
checkpoint or log for a bench experiment the way there is for a training run, which Mengdi Wang
argues is why physical science can’t yet scale verification the way it’s scaling hypothesis
generation.
Where it shows up

A Lab Notebook for Agents — the talk this framing and its “the Lab” tooling come from.
The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt — a theorem-proving instance that makes the research search
policy explicit inside the prompt rather than mainly in external infrastructure.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the theoretical framing this is a worked example of.
Backprop Beats Scaffolding — the distinction between a now-superseded no-success-yet
observation and the still-open claim that trained policies will displace research scaffolding.
Paper Agents — a sibling no-human-in-the-loop pattern at cross-corpus granularity.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — why this page’s reproducibility scaffolding doesn’t
transfer to physical science, and what trying to build an equivalent for it looks like.
An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement — the stricter SI-vs-RSI test this
loop fails to clear.
Decentralized Science Swarms — the same complete-record instinct, applied at field scale to
fix publication bias rather than single-lab reproducibility.

concepts/backprop-beats-scaffolding.title: Backprop Beats Scaffolding
concepts/backprop-beats-scaffolding.content:
Backprop Beats Scaffolding
Jerry Tworek’s sharper, more contrarian claim in
Opportunities and Challenges for Long-Horizon Agents, stated as a near-law drawn from the
history of machine learning: “whatever we can backpropagate through wins over what we cannot.”
Most of today’s apparent long-horizon agent capability — see Long-Horizon Agents for why
training genuinely long trajectories is economically brutal — actually comes from harness-level
scaffolding glued on top of models that are really only good at short-horizon work: /goal in
Codex/Claude Code (fix a goal, let the model run as long as it can, have it revisit and continue),
plan mode, sub-agents. None of this is trained end-to-end or backpropagated through. Tworek’s
prediction: this is a stopgap. Whatever ML has been able to move from hand-engineered scaffolding
into something trained end-to-end has historically won out, and he expects the same here — native,
trained long-horizon capability eventually displacing today’s harness-level glue.
The sharpest illustration he gives: the common pattern across “auto-research” rollouts is real
progress early on, then a stall — he hasn’t seen a genuinely successful one yet with today’s
models, because research is inherently serial and long-horizon, and current models can’t glue
small-horizon thinking into large research projects the way harnesses glue short tasks into longer
ones elsewhere. That’s a direct counterweight to Autonomous Research Agents’s success story
(Chuan Li’s Tetris/Lab talk) — not a contradiction, since Li’s own results plateaued repeatedly and
needed constant human-designed intervention to keep climbing, but a reminder that the pattern
generalizes and doesn’t obviously get easier with scale alone.
Where this complicates Agent Harness: that concept treats the harness — the
infrastructure/context/constraints wrapped around a model — as the durable locus of engineering
effort. Tworek’s claim is a direct tension with that: if backprop reliably wins, today’s
harness-level techniques (including the self-modifying-harness ideas in
Recursive Self-Improvement) may be a transitional phase rather than the long-term architecture,
with capability migrating back into the trained model itself over time.
A reconciliation, not just a tension: Weizhu Chen, independently, agrees with the direction
of this claim — harnesses do get absorbed into the model over time — but argues in
Continuous Model Improvement that the harness layer never fully disappears, because people keep
inventing more ambitious scenarios needing new scaffolding just as fast as old scaffolding gets
trained away. Both can be true at once: backprop wins each individual race, but the finish line
keeps moving.
Two updates separate the empirical observation from the architectural claim. Milad Nasr’s
talk demonstrates a genuinely novel, publishable cryptanalysis
improvement, but only after a harness generated and tested thousands of throwaway ideas and humans
supplied heavy verification. The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt is a stronger counterexample to
the claim that auto-research had not yet produced a complete research result: one prompted
GPT-5.6 Sol run produced the first public proof preprint for the conjecture it was assigned. That
supersedes “haven’t seen a genuinely successful one yet” as a current empirical generalization.
At the same time, both cases reinforce the deeper scaffolding caveat. Their success came from
carefully constructed search processes — a high-throughput experimental harness in one case, and
a prompt encoding portfolio management, memory, artifact construction, and adversarial review in
the other. They show that scaffolding can already bridge some long research horizons; they do not
show whether trained, end-to-end research policies will eventually displace that scaffolding.
Where it shows up

Opportunities and Challenges for Long-Horizon Agents — the talk this claim comes from.
Agent Harness — a durable tension with that concept’s premise.
Autonomous Research Agents — the auto-research-stalls-past-early-progress illustration.
Continuous Model Improvement — Chen’s reconciliation: true in each instance, but the target
keeps moving.
End-to-End AI Research — a real end-to-end research success that nuances, rather than
cleanly refutes, the auto-research-stalls pattern.
The Crouzeix Autoresearch Prompt — a stronger counterexample to the historical no-success-yet
observation, while still depending on explicit process scaffolding.

concepts/builder-breaker-discovery.title: Builder-Breaker Discovery
concepts/builder-breaker-discovery.content:
Builder-Breaker Discovery
Markus Buehler’s argument from Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery: real scientific
discovery requires “breaking the world model” — an AI system has to be able to actually change what
a scientist believes to be correct, not just interpolate within an existing framework or sample
from an existing data distribution.
A three-stage historical arc, for context: simple regression-style machine learning models
(decades ago) → generative AI (recent years — sampling and learning from an existing data
landscape) → the current “discovery era,” where systems don’t just generate candidate ideas but
also generate new training data, test it, and validate it themselves.
The concrete mechanism — an adversarial builder/breaker loop:

A builder agent proposes an explicit, externalized world model that explains observed data,
optimized to maximize coverage while penalizing complexity (an MDL/Occam’s-razor-style
simplicity gate) — the goal is a model that explains the world as simply and completely as
possible, not a black box.
A breaker agent actively tries to falsify that model by collecting new evidence — running new
experiments, mining the literature for contradicting cases.
As the breaker succeeds in finding evidence the current model can’t explain, the data the builder
must account for gets more complex, forcing further refinement. This produces a genuinely
adversarial, iterative discovery loop, rather than a single-shot model fit.

Applied concretely (unpublished/in-review work at the time of the talk): the loop produced a
simple, interpretable scaling theory predicting a specific protein property, and separately
discovered new metamaterial resonator designs in a previously unexplored region of design space —
notably identifying where the most impactful research could even be done, not just answering a
posed question.
This is a strong complement to Verification as Science’s Bottleneck: where Mengdi Wang
diagnoses verification as science’s bottleneck, Buehler offers one candidate mechanism for
addressing it — folding falsification directly into the discovery loop itself as the thing driving
progress, rather than treating verification as a separate downstream step performed after ideas are
generated.
Where it shows up

Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery — the talk this framing comes from.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — the problem this mechanism is one candidate answer to.
Interpretability as Scientific Discovery — a third, distinct discovery mechanism: reading
knowledge already implicit inside a model, rather than an adversarial hypothesis-generation loop.
Verifiable Substrate — a related but distinct discovery mechanism: ELO-tournament evaluation
and a precise three-part definition of verifiability, rather than an adversarial builder/breaker
pair.
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — a different strategic response to the same
bottleneck: rather than folding falsification into the loop, sidestep the need for an external
verifier during evolution entirely, using intrinsic model signals as fitness.

concepts/causal-evaluation-from-producti.title: Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic
concepts/causal-evaluation-from-producti.content:
Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic
Anastasios Angelopoulos’s (Co-Founder & CEO, LMArena) methodology from
Agent Arena - Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World: a philosophy and mechanism for
evaluating agents from real usage rather than static benchmarks.
The philosophy: “there’s only one judge that matters and that’s reality.” Static benchmarks
have two structural flaws — they can be overfit, and there’s typically a distribution shift
between what a benchmark’s dataset captures and what actually happens in production. Measuring
post-deployment impact directly sidesteps both: doing well in reality requires actually completing
real people’s real jobs, which is much harder to game than a fixed test set.
The incentive design that makes free, high-quality feedback at scale possible: “the act of
providing feedback should be value back to the user.” In the classic pairwise-battle mechanism,
a user who votes for their preferred response gets to continue the conversation with that
response — so voting your true preference is the rational move, not an act of altruism. This is
what lets Arena collect millions of feedback signals without paying anyone. Beyond simple
pairwise votes, “trace mining” extracts far richer signals from long multi-turn agentic sessions
(days or weeks, hundreds of tool calls): explicit task-completion clicks, hallucination rate
(strip every factual claim, verify or refute it against the internet), steerability (did the model
correctly land a fix after a complaint, or did the user keep struggling), bash-error recovery, and
user frustration/praise ratio — roughly 25 distinct signals.
The genuinely novel move: causal inference on live traffic, not just aggregated preference
scores. Users never see which specific orchestrator or tool-model is running underneath a given
agentic session — Arena randomizes that assignment, a true experimental intervention, and measures
the treatment effect of using one orchestrator versus another (versus a randomized-average
baseline). This is, in effect, a continuously running, large multi-factor A/B test over real
users’ real tasks, not a fixed leaderboard run once against a static set. All ~25 signals get
combined into one leaderboard via a weighted average of treatment effects, with confidence
intervals — a genuinely different aggregation than simple win-rate scoring, and one that lets new
signals be added without redesigning the whole benchmark.
Why this sidesteps rather than fixes the standardization problem:
Triple-A Benchmark Standardization argues most fixed benchmarks can’t even properly measure a
model paired with a different harness. Causal evaluation from production traffic avoids that problem
structurally, rather than patching it — there’s no fixed benchmark to measure a harness against; the
harness (and everything about the deployment) is simply part of what gets randomized and measured
directly in the live distribution.
Where it shows up

Agent Arena - Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World — the talk this methodology
comes from.
Triple-A Benchmark Standardization — a related but structurally different approach to the
same underlying problem (benchmarks not reflecting real deployment conditions): this page
measures in the live distribution directly rather than trying to standardize a fixed one.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — an implicit tension worth naming: that page’s whole
framework is about building better curated benchmarks; this page rejects curated benchmarks
in favor of measuring reality directly. Neither talk engages the other’s position, but they’re
two genuinely different bets on how agent evaluation should work going forward.

concepts/clinical-multi-agent-orchestrat.title: Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration
concepts/clinical-multi-agent-orchestrat.content:
Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration
Krishnaram Kenthapadi’s architecture from
Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned
(Oracle Health).
Query routing across heterogeneous data types. Given a clinical query (“show me recent labs,”
“what are the side effects of her current medications,” “best course of action given her history
