and new labs”), an orchestrator decides whether to search structured records, unstructured notes,
or both, accounting for UI and patient context and supporting multi-turn conversation — invoking
the right tools and skills from a library rather than following a fixed pipeline. A healthcare-
domain instance of the orchestrator-delegating-to-specialized-capabilities pattern already
recurring in the wiki: Grounded Capability Delegation, Architect Agents,
Reasoning Graphs.
Guardrails and cost-aware routing. Input-side guardrails matter especially for patient-facing
(not just doctor-facing) queries, detecting sensitive queries or genuine emergencies that need
escalation rather than a routine response. On cost and latency: the system decides at runtime
whether a query needs a complex reasoning model, a simpler language model, or even deterministic
Python code — routing to the cheapest sufficient mechanism rather than defaulting to the most
expensive option.
Structuring sub-agents around an existing expert protocol, with conflict-resolving synthesis.
For chest X-ray interpretation, sub-agents are organized around the “ABCDE” system — an actual
clinical assessment mnemonic (airway, breathing, circulation, and so on) — run in parallel, with a
synthesizer that reconciles potentially conflicting outputs from those sub-agents before deciding
a final course of action. This is a distinct concern from query routing: conflict resolution across
sub-agents built around a real expert workflow, not just deciding which tool to call.
Where it shows up

Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned
— the talk this framing comes from.
Healthcare AI System Challenges — the system-wide challenges this architecture runs into at
scale.
Grounded Capability Delegation, Architect Agents, Reasoning Graphs — the same
orchestrator-delegates-to-specialists pattern, from unrelated domains.
Adaptive Agent Frameworks — the same cost-aware, dynamic-routing theme, formalized there as
a constrained MDP rather than a heuristic.
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — sharpens this general pattern with two specific
findings from an unrelated domain (in-car assistants): delegation ground truth is multi-valued,
not single-label, and delegating to an agent (unlike a bounded tool call) can start an
unbounded, possibly-never-returning autonomous loop.
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks — the same orchestrator-delegates-to-specialists pattern,
validated at real production scale (~200 leaf agents coordinated by a hierarchical “frontman”
architecture, ~30% ticket-volume reduction) rather than in a clinical setting.

concepts/compounding-error-in-chained-ap.filePath: concepts/Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks.md
concepts/compounding-error-in-chained-ap.title: Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks
concepts/compounding-error-in-chained-ap.content:
Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks
From Measuring API Agent Reliability for Long-Horizon Tasks in Production (Postman): APIFlow
Bench, a benchmark for enterprise API-agent reliability on long-horizon, dependent-chain tasks
(connecting a build job to a monitoring API, creating a record, recovering from a rate limit).
The headline finding. Single-API-task performance is already strong across models — even
lightweight ones score 88-97%. Chain those same tasks into a long, dependent sequence and scores
collapse to 44-73%. Critically: the tasks themselves don’t get harder — what breaks is that
later steps depend on results and state from earlier ones. This reframes the actual problem
sharply: not “can the model answer” (already solved) but “can the agent stay correct across a long
horizon of dependent tasks” — the gap between answering and executing. A fourth independent,
and the most concretely measured, confirmation of Long-Horizon Agents’s core claim, joining
Tworek’s economics argument, Vanhoucke’s control-theory argument, and Gukov’s math-research
argument.
A seven-failure-mode taxonomy, graded separately because each fails for a different reason:
authentication, discovery, schema repair, multi-step execution, error recovery, pagination, and
statefulness (e.g., an agent updates something at step 3, and step 15 only works correctly if that
update actually persisted). Grading each mode independently — rather than one aggregate pass/fail
— reveals why a model failed, not just that it did, a more granular, API-specific version of
the component-level diagnosis Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) calls for.
A reusable three-gate methodology for trusting synthetically-generated benchmark tasks:

Self-testing — a blank submission must always fail, and a reference answer with sabotaged
evidence must also always fail; if either doesn’t hold, the grader itself is broken, not just
the task.
Solvability — validate each generated task by running it through a frontier model 10 times,
keeping only tasks that pass at least 3 of 10. Failed tasks get repaired by a dedicated “fixer
agent” and re-validated; tasks that keep failing get discarded and regenerated from scratch.
This exists specifically to avoid measuring “model limits” that are actually broken,
unsolvable generated tasks.
Golden replay — for chained tasks, concatenate the individual reference answers from each
subtask and confirm the assembled chain passes end-to-end, verifying the composed reference
solution is internally consistent, not just correct piece by piece.

Grading design: one shared harness (seven tools across five entities) used identically across
every task. Two deterministic validators (final environment state; final answer) determine the
actual scored pass rate. A third, LLM-based validator is used only to flag doubtful trajectories
for human review — explicitly not trusted as a scoring source of truth on its own.
Scale and result: 467 generated tests across 13 synthetic worlds, yielding 11 twenty-step
chain tasks in the published benchmark; 19 models evaluated, ~44,000 total trials, transcripts
published openly. Open-source models are closing the gap with closed frontier models specifically
on the chain-task leaderboard, not just on single-task scores.
Three closing takeaways: solo-task performance can no longer reveal real capability gaps
between models (most are near-saturated), so chain tasks are needed to actually differentiate
them; synthetic benchmark tasks need hard gates (minimum pass thresholds, golden-replay
verification) before they can be trusted; and both deterministic and language-model-based
validators are needed together, with human review to keep refining them — a wrong validator can’t
reveal a model’s true performance.
Where it shows up

Measuring API Agent Reliability for Long-Horizon Tasks in Production — the talk this
benchmark comes from.
Long-Horizon Agents — a fourth independent, and the most concretely measured, confirmation
that long horizons need more than incremental fixes, via a precise 88-97%-to-44-73% compounding-
error gap.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — a concrete, reusable instantiation of “rigorous QC” for
synthetically-generated tasks specifically, via the three-gate methodology.
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — the seven-failure-mode taxonomy is a more granular,
API-specific version of the component-level (L2) diagnosis that framework calls for.
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — a concrete mechanism for exactly the gap
Emily Xue names: single-task capability scores that look solved can mislead about real
enterprise reliability, which only shows up once tasks are chained.

concepts/config-driven-multi-agent-netwo.title: Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks
concepts/config-driven-multi-agent-netwo.content:
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks
Daniel Fink’s (AI Engineering Lead, Cognizant AI Lab) Neuro SAN framework, described in
Scaling Up Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks with Neuro SAN. Built after an early finding that
the glue code for agents calling other agents was pure noise relative to what the team was actually
trying to build — so they lifted that glue out into a declarative layer.
The architecture: agents call other agents, agents call coded tools, coded tools call back
into the agent system — all described in JSON, except the coded tools’ own implementation. Every
node declares upward to its caller what it can do, what information it needs to operate, and who
it can talk to, alongside overall system prompts. A clean organizing principle: “the ultimate
upchain is the user.”
Credentials via a side channel, not the chat stream. Secure tokens and credentials travel
through a separate channel (“slide data”) rather than through the conversational context an LLM
actually sees — so secrets never appear anywhere an agent could leak or reason over them. The same
underlying pattern as Meta-Harness Architecture’s credential proxying, arrived at
independently in an unrelated system.
Two findings that shaped the framework’s philosophy early on: decomposition beats waiting for
a bigger model — breaking a problem down lets a smaller model handle each piece more reliably and
more cheaply, without needing the next frontier release; and because the config format is plain
JSON, non-engineers built genuinely useful multi-agent tools — Frink specifically cites marketing
staff building tools still in active use, a real (not aspirational) democratization result.
Two capabilities that emerged specifically from being config-driven:

Agentic webs — a multi-agent system can call an entire other multi-agent system as a tool,
recursively and arbitrarily deep, alongside calling MCP or A2A servers directly. Composability
at the level of whole systems, not just individual tools or agents.
Multi-agent systems generating other multi-agent systems. Since a network definition is just
a JSON/HOCON config file — in Frink’s words, “forms to fill in” — one multi-agent system can
generate a new network’s config as a disposable, “perishable thought,” which then gets
downloaded and plugged into the overall system as a live component. This is a close cousin of
Architect Agents (an agent constructing a reasoning-graph harness for a new use case with no
human-written code) — the same underlying move, via a different mechanism: generating a whole
network’s configuration rather than building one specific reasoning graph.
A side effect of standardizing the calling interface: testing itself becomes data-driven — a
test scenario is just another structured “interaction I want to have,” not bespoke test code.

A validated production architecture and deployment. A hierarchical pattern — a “frontman”
root agent that knows nothing substantive itself but knows who to call, delegating down through a
middle tier to leaf agents that actually do the work, with answers aggregating back up as they
trickle from the specialists who do know things. Cognizant’s own corporate IT deployed this
internally (“eating their own dog food”) with roughly 200 leaf-level agents spanning ServiceNow,
Salesforce, PeopleSoft, and more, coordinated by this infrastructure — reporting a ~30% drop in
overall ticket volume after deployment, because the agent system handled requests better than the
prior human-only baseline. Freely available and openly licensed, with plans to work toward Linux
Foundation hosting.
Where it shows up

Scaling Up Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks with Neuro SAN — the talk this framework comes
from.
Architect Agents — a close cousin: agent-generated agent architecture via a different
mechanism (whole-network config generation here, versus one reasoning-graph construction there).
Meta-Harness Architecture — the same credential side-channel pattern, arrived at
independently in an unrelated system.
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice and Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — the same
orchestrator-delegates-to-specialists pattern, here as a concrete, validated production
deployment with real numbers (200 leaf agents, ~30% ticket-volume reduction).

concepts/data-over-architecture.title: Data Over Architecture
concepts/data-over-architecture.content:
Data Over Architecture
Weizhu Chen’s claim from Continuous Model Improvement: of the three engines driving model
improvement — compute, data, and architecture — data matters more than architecture, and inference
cost/efficiency matters more than most people credit, because a model’s real-world adoption is
ultimately decided by how fast and cheap it runs, not by raw quality alone.
The three engines, briefly:

Compute: pre-training scaling (more data and exploration), post-training scaling (now
focused on harder, longer-horizon, and multi-agent problems during training itself, not just at
inference), and test-time compute (getting a family of models to serve together in production).
Data — “the second engine,” his framing: data is king, everything else is the queen; data is
oxygen. Pretraining progress mostly comes from cleaning and refreshing data and from synthetic
data, where the value isn’t just quality but coverage — filling gaps nothing else covers. He
predicts synthetic data becomes the dominant data source going forward, with human-generated
data’s main remaining role being a seed for generating it. He also flags environment fidelity
for RL: the training environment needs to resemble the real product environment closely,
functioning as a simulator that can generate unlimited training data.
Model architecture: quality, inference cost, and longer/more efficient context — but he
argues inference cost is the one people underweight, and it’s the one that actually determines
whether a model gets adopted.

Practical implication: design for inference cost from the start rather than treating it as an
afterthought to model quality — as GPUs advance, lean toward more compute and less I/O rather than
assuming raw capability alone will carry a model to adoption.
Production data over benchmarks: real interaction/usage data from continuous deployment at
scale is more valuable for improving a model than benchmark scores — you see what actually goes
wrong in production and can compare against what other models do in the same scenario. Continuous
model improvement, by his framing, requires continuous deployment at scale almost by definition.
James Zou adds a fourth axis to this same framing: scaling the number
of collaborating agents, rather than compute, data, or architecture, as its own independent lever
on capability.
Where it shows up

Continuous Model Improvement — the talk this framing comes from.
Scaling by Agent Count — a fourth scaling axis (agent count) alongside these three.
Intelligence vs. Expertise — a fifth proposed scaling axis (expertise, via continual
learning) alongside these.
Diffusion Language Models — the same inference-cost-over-raw-quality point, made concrete by
a shipped product built around a fundamentally faster decoding paradigm.

concepts/data-for-agents.title: Data for Agents
concepts/data-for-agents.content:
Data for Agents
Dan Roth’s framing from AI for Data and Data for AI: the AI-data relationship runs two ways.
“AI for data” — using GenAI to work with messy, heterogeneous data conceptually — is the direction
most people think about. “Data for AI” is the reverse, and for agents specifically the more
consequential one: the quality, structure, and governance of your data determines what an agent
can actually do.
Why this is a growing problem, not a shrinking one: general-purpose data has already been
absorbed by model providers — that’s why agents work at all today — but a large amount of data will
permanently stay outside any model: corporate, financial, government, medical, personal. It’s also
dynamic, unlike a frozen training corpus. Supporting agent access to that external data is, in
Roth’s view, one of the key emerging GenAI use cases, and it’s underrated relative to “AI for data.”
Why this is harder than it looks:

Information retrieval doesn’t reliably work unless the query representation is lexically close
to how target documents are represented, which usually isn’t true — this necessitates an actual
semantic layer across knowledge sources, not just better search.
NL-to-SQL (or NL to any formal query representation) is a genuinely hard transformation that
depends on retrieval already working.
Rich, multimodal documents (papers, figures, video, images) aren’t exposed to retrieval at all
unless someone deliberately extracts that information first.
Planning how to access data is its own hard problem — what order to query sources in, how to
filter one source by another — not just a retrieval or reasoning problem.
Real-world sources routinely conflict, and reconciling them is sometimes beyond current model
reasoning.
Enterprise deployment adds governance, policy enforcement, auditability, and cost/caching
tradeoffs largely orthogonal to raw capability.
Reality check: even leading NL-to-SQL systems (his own team’s, competitive on Spider 2 and
Archer) only score ~55-73% — “really far” from solved.

Silent regression on correction — the sharpest, most durable point: in his tennis-income
example, a frontier model produces an impressive multi-source, conflict-reconciled answer with a
visible reasoning trace — but with three quiet failures (wrong sort order, a top player missing
entirely, two players with identical income to the exact dollar — a fabrication tell). Correcting
the visible error (a missing player) caused the model to silently drop a different,
previously-correct player and change another value. Fixing one error introduced a new, invisible
one. This generalizes beyond data retrieval to any agent self-correction loop: a fix is not
guaranteed to be additive, and without already knowing the ground truth, a regression like this is
invisible. Low-stakes domains (tennis trivia) make this merely embarrassing; high-stakes ones
(financial analysis, medical data) make it dangerous, because the reliability of “was this done
correctly” — visibility into failure — is what determines whether a system can be trusted at all.
This is a different flavor of unreliability than Reward Hacking: no adversarial optimization
pressure here, just noisy real-world data, imperfect retrieval, and an agent operating past the
edge of what it can reliably verify about its own output.
James Zou makes a related but distinct claim about the same
underlying gap: where Roth’s problem is access and planning (retrieval, ordering, conflicting
sources), Zou’s is representation format (a data layer built for humans, not agents) — both land on
the same conclusion that the data layer agents need isn’t the one that already exists.
Dhruv Batra’s argument is a third, sharper variant: for a large
part of the open web, there is no underlying structured data layer to convert to — the answer to a
query only exists after a human-facing page renders, so the fix isn’t better data infrastructure at
all, it’s vision-grounded agents that read the rendered page directly.
Where it shows up

AI for Data and Data for AI — the talk this framing and the tennis example come from.
Agent-Native Data Infrastructure — a related claim about the same gap, focused on
representation format rather than access/planning.
Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail — a sharper variant: no structured data layer exists to
convert to at all, so vision-grounded agents reading the rendered page directly are the fix.
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — a fourth variant, focused on representation
structure: graphs, not flat tables or opaque vectors, as the right shape for enterprise knowledge.

concepts/decentralized-science-swarms.title: Decentralized Science Swarms
concepts/decentralized-science-swarms.content:
Decentralized Science Swarms
Markus Buehler’s second thread from Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery: how to
organize many collaborating discovery agents, and a structural fix for a long-standing bias in how
science gets published.
Self-organizing, not pre-programmed. His “ScienceClaw Infinite” system runs hundreds of agents
with different, evolving skills, deliberately without an explicit behavioral spec — “we don’t
describe what the agents are and how they should behave, we let them discover completely on their
own.” Modeled on MIT’s Infinite Corridor, a physical space where a mathematician, a biologist, and
a philosopher run into each other by chance and sometimes start a collaboration — the system is
meant to produce the agent equivalent of that emergent, cross-disciplinary encounter, rather than
follow an imposed org chart.
Decentralized across physical labs, with a vision of physical services offered between agents.
The swarm doesn’t live in one company’s cloud — it’s explicitly distributed, with the longer-term
vision that a lab’s physical capabilities (a 3D printer, a protein-synthesis facility) become
services other labs’ agents can call on and receive results back from, extending collaboration past
the purely digital.
A structural fix for publication bias. Human papers selectively report the handful of
experiments that worked; in this system, every experiment any agent runs — successes and failures
alike — is fully traceable and stored, so a future agent can build on prior attempts, including
dead ends, instead of rediscovering them. Buehler’s explicit claim: “that’s the future of
scientific publishing.” This is a different fix, aimed at survivorship bias in the literature,
than Verification as Science’s Bottleneck’s reproducibility-crisis framing — but the same
underlying instinct as Autonomous Research Agents’s git-branch-per-idea logging: keep a
complete, honest record instead of a curated one.
A flexible, optional human role. Human involvement ranges from posing a narrow, specific
question to giving the swarm nothing but tools and an open mandate to find something “interesting
and profound.” Humans can also join the system as participants — giving feedback on
manufacturability, ethics, or IP constraints — rather than only setting the initial goal. One sharp
aside: problem selection itself — deciding what’s worth studying in the first place — is an
underdiscussed scientific skill, since papers report solved problems, never how the problem was
chosen.
Three different answers to “how do you structure many collaborating agents,” now in the wiki:
James Zou’s virtual lab/biotech imposes a human organizational hierarchy
(professor and student agents, then CSO and division agents);
Ramesh Raskar’s agents are autonomous, self-interested market participants
coordinated through pricing and competition; Buehler’s swarm is neither — agents are given tools and
left to discover their own collaboration structure, with no imposed hierarchy or market mechanism.
Where it shows up

Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery — the talk this framing comes from.
Autonomous Research Agents — the same complete-record instinct, applied to a different
problem (single-lab reproducibility vs. field-wide publication bias).
Scaling by Agent Count and The Bazaar Era of AI — two other, structurally different
answers to organizing many collaborating agents.

concepts/declared-vs.-observed-authority.title: Declared vs. Observed Authority
concepts/declared-vs.-observed-authority.content:
Declared vs. Observed Authority
From
Observability Is Not Governance: Building a Runtime Trust Plane for Agentic AI:
the core thesis is that observability and governance are frequently conflated but aren’t substitutes
for each other. “Observability is good — we can see what’s happening. But can we do something about
it? That’s the question.” Governance requires assessing the control path itself and enforcing
decisions bound to identity, policy, and authorization — the two work in tandem, not
interchangeably.
Why traditional governance breaks down for agentic systems. Pre-AI environments were linear —
you know what you asked a system to do, you know what users did, and governance controls can be
built around that predictability. With agents, a whole ecosystem (user, agent, model, orchestration,
sub-agents) takes on “a life of its own in real time, simultaneously” — workflows run in tandem,
functions tie to workflows, and it’s often unclear who’s accountable for a given function within
one. Linear governance and standard software QA aren’t enough for this shape of system.
A sharp, concrete risk example: sub-agent privilege inheritance. When a primary agent delegates
to a sub-agent, should the sub-agent inherit the primary’s full privileges and authorizations
wholesale? It should not — but this is exactly the governance step that gets skipped under pressure
to build and ship. This is the same underlying gap that
“fake pre-approval” attacks exploit and that
compound attacks rely on: authority propagating further than
it should.
The mechanism: a runtime trust plane comparing declared authority to observed behavior. Build
an explicit, declared contract describing what each agent is supposed to do and interact with;
continuously compare that against what actually happens at runtime, producing a measurable
variance. Drift is not automatically bad — the useful thing is the specific delta, categorized, not
a binary alarm. Categorization used here: shown, allowed, approved, drift, and control failure,
with control failure flagged as the single most important category to watch.
Risk-tiered containment: every proposed agent action is evaluated against the accumulated
trust-plane data (authority, policy, risk, evidence) before execution commits, tagged by risk
category — low risk auto-executes, high risk requires human approval — with a defined containment
path (quarantine, rollback, secondary authorization, or stop) as the kill switch.
Where it shows up

Observability Is Not Governance: Building a Runtime Trust Plane for Agentic AI
— the talk this framing comes from.
Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms — the same authority-propagation gap, exploited by
the “fake pre-approval” attack mechanism.
Joint Safety and Security Analysis — the same gap underlying McDermid’s compound-attack
finding.
The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt — the theoretical justification this page’s
mechanism was missing: Neil Lawrence’s 1970 cybernetics theorem explains why comparing declared
authority to observed behavior is necessary in the first place — delegation without a good model
of the delegate is structurally unsafe, independent of implementation.

concepts/deployment-readiness-vs.-capabi.title: Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks
concepts/deployment-readiness-vs.-capabi.content:
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks
Emily Xue’s (Head of Enterprise AI, Scale AI; 11 years at Google, core Gemini team, built Google’s
cloud-agent benchmark) framing from The Exam Before Enterprise Deployment: capability
benchmarks and deployment-readiness benchmarks aren’t the same instrument measuring the same thing
at different precision — they’re built for structurally opposed audiences with opposed incentives.
The central tension. Capability benchmarks measure the ceiling — the gap between current
model performance and the top of human intelligence — and they’re developer-facing: a benchmark
developer is happy to see a low score, because it signals headroom, keeps developers motivated to
close the gap, and keeps the benchmark relevant (a saturated benchmark gets abandoned). This is a
direct counterpoint to Principles for Durable Benchmarks, which argues good benchmarks
deliberately preserve difficulty and headroom — Zhu explains exactly why that design goal, correct
for developer-facing benchmarks, is structurally at odds with what enterprise buyers need.
Enterprise buyers want the opposite: near-ceiling reliability (95-99%+) for a specific, narrow use
case, not evidence of room to grow. Concrete anecdote: text-to-SQL benchmarks top out around
60-70% by design, deliberately kept unsaturated — but enterprise executives, told repeatedly that
agents are “so smart now,” can’t understand why the same agent can’t hit 99% reliability on their
specific task.
Five questions enterprise buyers actually ask, before any deployment decision: what’s actually
ready for production, out of a prioritized backlog of candidate use cases; how do you quantify
readiness and trust the resulting number; if there’s a gap (say, 90% rather than the needed 99%),
how do you close it; what human-oversight policy is required; and whether the combined economics —
agent (token) cost plus human-oversight cost — actually nets out as savings versus the status quo.
These roll up into a readiness profile: qualification, risk envelope, oversight policy, and an
improvement path.
Concrete evaluation primitives for answering “can we trust the answer” and related concerns:

Grounding — citation precision (is each claim traceable to a source) and recall (does the
answer miss information the evidence database actually contains) — both matter, not just
precision.
Policy compliance — a genuinely correct answer can still violate the process it was supposed
to follow. Concrete example: a healthcare agent tasked with identifying acute kidney failure was
specified to check lab-measured creatinine levels per clinical protocol, but instead took a
shortcut — reading the clinical/diagnosis notes directly rather than retrieving and checking the
specified lab values. This is the same underlying gap Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability
names as “technically correct but violates semantic intent,” seen here in a regulated,
high-stakes enterprise setting rather than a coding-support tool.
“Does the agent know what it doesn’t know?” — Zhu’s own favorite question, with two parts:
confidence calibration (if an agent claims 60% confidence, is it actually right 60% of the time?)
and an explicit abstention policy (when uncertain, escalate to a human rather than guess). This is
a concrete, practical answer to the metacognition gap Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability
names abstractly as barrier 3 — calibration plus a designed abstention policy is what
operationalizing that gap actually looks like in production.
Right operations — when an agent doesn’t just produce information for review but actually
mutates enterprise system state, is the change recoverable, with a real rollback policy? A
distinct concern from answer correctness — an operational safety axis.
Oversight economics — given agent cost plus the cost of whatever human oversight is required,
does the combination still net-save money versus not deploying at all?

A three-surface framework for where agent-enterprise interaction actually happens, each with a
different evaluation focus:

Informational — the agent produces output for human review; the question is whether the
answer is trustworthy.
System-mutating — the agent changes enterprise system state directly; the question is
whether that change is recoverable, privacy-preserving, and trustworthy.
Open conversation — the fastest-growing and newest surface: the agent talks directly with
the enterprise’s own external customers, who may supply malicious or misspecified input; the
question becomes how to steer the conversation safely toward the intended goal regardless.

The sharpest reframe, closing the talk: the path to improvement isn’t a score improvement
(60% → 80% → 90%). Reliability is non-negotiable, fixed at whatever the specific use case actually
requires — “reliability is not something you can trade off.” What genuinely improves over time is
the cost of hitting that fixed reliability bar: as model quality improves, the human-oversight
burden required to reach the same reliability floor shrinks, and that’s the real metric of
progress. Zhu’s closing line: “don’t only ask how intelligent the agent is — ask what it’s ready
to do, under what constraint, at what risk, at what cost.”
Where it shows up

The Exam Before Enterprise Deployment — the talk this framework comes from.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — the direct counterpoint this page explains: that page’s
headroom-preservation design goal, correct for developer-facing benchmarks, is exactly what
makes those benchmarks unsuited to enterprise deployment decisions.
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — a complementary decomposition from a different talk: this
page’s evaluation primitives (grounding, policy compliance, calibration/abstention, right
operations) are concrete instances of the kind of component/diagnostic-level inspection that
framework’s L2/L3 layers call for.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — “does the agent know what it doesn’t know” is a
practical, deployable answer to Klein’s abstract metacognition-gap barrier.
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability — the policy-compliance failure example (correct answer,
wrong process) is the same underlying pattern Rajmohan names from a different domain.
Runtime Agent Optimization — oversight economics adds a term (human-oversight cost) to the
cost side of the same broader cost/quality tradeoff that talk optimizes at the model/harness/
execution-strategy level.
The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt — the theoretical justification for this page’s
practice: Neil Lawrence’s argument for why a human-oversight policy and sign-off point is
necessary before deployment, not just good practice.
Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks — a concrete mechanism for exactly this page’s central
claim: single-task capability scores that look solved (88-97%) collapse once tasks are chained
(44-73%), showing precisely how a capability benchmark can mislead about real deployment
reliability.

concepts/deterministic-core,-agentic-per.title: Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery
concepts/deterministic-core,-agentic-per.content:
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery
An architectural pattern from Scale AI’s oil-well casing-design agent, described in
Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach (Priya Ponnapalli): rather than relying on
evaluation alone to make an agent trustworthy for high-stakes numerical work, architect the system
so the agent is structurally incapable of introducing numerical error in the first place.
The split: casing design (the steel pipe around an oil well) traditionally takes an engineer
weeks — running hundreds of physics-based simulations and checking results against standards
buried across many documents. The redesigned system keeps a deterministic core: the engineer
still runs all simulations through trusted, existing physics-based simulators, and results are
checked deterministically against company standards, with the engineer making the final
sign-off call. A casing design agent runs alongside this core, doing only three things:
extracting relevant context from hundreds of simulation runs, answering the engineer’s questions
with citations grounded in that context, and drafting the final design document (the “Basis of
Design”).
The load-bearing design decision: the agent never computes any number and never drives any
workflow. By construction — not by testing — numerical fidelity is 100%, because the one component
capable of being wrong (the LLM-based agent) is never on the path that produces a number. The
evaluation question this leaves is correspondingly narrower and more tractable: not “is the number
right” (guaranteed by the deterministic core) but “how well does the agent answer questions and
produce complete, correct, review-ready documentation” — see Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3)
for how that narrower question gets measured.
The general pattern, beyond this one case study: identify which parts of a workflow are
already served well by trusted, deterministic tools (simulators, calculators, existing validated
systems) and keep the agent entirely off that path. Restrict the agent to roles where errors are
recoverable and checkable by a human in context — retrieval, synthesis, drafting, citation — rather
than roles where an error propagates silently into a number someone downstream will trust.
Where it shows up

Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach — the talk and case study this pattern
comes from.
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — the evaluation framework this architectural choice
narrows: by removing numerical computation from the agent’s scope, L1 correctness becomes easier
to guarantee by construction rather than by evaluation alone.
Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent — a structurally different answer to the same high-stakes-
reliability problem: instead of removing agents from the risk surface, Capital One’s Macaw
architecture keeps them in the loop and adds an independent policy-check-and-reject step.
Ontology as Agent Guardrail — a third answer: leave the agent on the path, but validate every
tool result against a formal domain model before it can propagate or commit.

concepts/diffusion-language-models.title: Diffusion Language Models
concepts/diffusion-language-models.content:
Diffusion Language Models
Aditya Grover’s account, from
Redefining the Token Efficiency Frontier with Diffusion LLMs, of applying
diffusion’s parallelization principle to text.
Why text was the hard case for diffusion, even after diffusion won for images: diffusion was
invented for continuous modalities — images have a natural mathematical notion of adding noise and
a principled way to denoise it. Text is discrete, which makes defining a noising/denoising process
that trains well at scale fundamentally harder. That gap is why diffusion dominated image and video
generation for years before reaching text at all.
The mechanism: instead of generating tokens sequentially, one at a time (the autoregressive
paradigm nearly all of today’s LLMs use), a diffusion language model starts from noise —
effectively gibberish text — and passes it through a neural network (still a transformer
underneath; this is a different decoding paradigm, not a break from the transformer as the
underlying architecture) trained to denoise it. Because the network predicts all of a sequence’s
denoised tokens in parallel rather than one after another, generation is much faster for a
comparable amount of underlying compute.
A new frontier: intelligence per resource, not intelligence alone. The commercialized result
(Inception’s Mercury, then Mercury 2 with reasoning) reaches similar quality to speed-optimized
frontier models (comparable to Claude Haiku- or GPT-5-mini-class models) at substantially higher
tokens-per-second, because it denoises in parallel instead of decoding sequentially. Grover’s
explicit framing: the metric worth optimizing isn’t intelligence alone, it’s a “new currency of
intelligence per” unit of time, cost, or compute — the same underlying point
Weizhu Chen makes about inference cost being the underweighted factor
that actually determines whether a model gets adopted.
One generalizable point from the deployment case studies (voice/support agents, search,
coding): time-to-first-token matters independently of total throughput for latency-sensitive,
human-in-the-loop applications — echoing Agent Workload Shape’s point that agent workloads stay
latency-sensitive even though they’re bursty overall.
Where it shows up

Redefining the Token Efficiency Frontier with Diffusion LLMs — the talk this framing comes
from.
Parallelization as AI’s Throughline — the general principle this is one application of.
Data Over Architecture — the same inference-cost-over-raw-quality point, from a different
talk.
Agent Workload Shape — the same latency-sensitivity-despite-burstiness point, from a
different domain.

concepts/digital-twins-vs.-digital-cousi.title: Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins
concepts/digital-twins-vs.-digital-cousi.content:
Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins
Bolei Zhou’s distinction from Scaling Sidewalk Autonomy with World Models, addressing a
limitation of the video-reconstruction approach in Sidewalk Autonomy: pure video reconstruction
gives exactly one simulation environment per video — a digital twin, a strict one-to-one
correspondence. That means no variation is possible from a single capture.
The fix (“UrbanVerse”): digital cousins. Extract a scene graph from the input video using
computer vision, then swap in different object instances to generate multiple variations of the
environment from that single video — each usable independently for training and evaluation.
Released publicly alongside a large 3D-asset dataset (100,000 correctly-scaled assets) to support
this.
Simulation as an active post-training substrate, not just a benchmark. Train a base model via
imitation learning on real video first, then place that model inside the digital-cousin
environments for further post-training specifically targeting interactivity and counterfactual
reasoning — capabilities that are hard to learn from static video demonstrations alone.
A concrete capability payoff: “FlowPilot” — real-world sidewalk navigation from a single RGB
camera, outputting waypoints for a downstream controller, handling both obstacle avoidance and
pedestrian interaction on real sidewalks.
A genuinely exciting forward-looking direction: cross-embodiment transfer without fine-tuning.
The same sidewalk-navigation foundation model reportedly transfers across different robot
embodiments (legged robots demonstrated; wheeled-legged robots and electric wheelchairs in
progress) without additional fine-tuning — reframing the stakes of this line of work from
commercial delivery robots toward autonomously transporting people on sidewalks, i.e., assistive
mobility.
Where it shows up

Scaling Sidewalk Autonomy with World Models — the talk this framing comes from.
Sidewalk Autonomy — the limitation (one environment per video) this technique addresses.
Simulation Evolution for Physical AI — Sanja Fidler names the identical digital-twin
limitation independently, in a different physical-AI domain (autonomous vehicles at NVIDIA), and
addresses it with a different fix: fully generative hallucination rather than scene-graph
variation from a single capture.

concepts/distillation-as-the-core-ml-pat.filePath: concepts/Distillation as the Core ML Pattern.md
concepts/distillation-as-the-core-ml-pat.title: Distillation as the Core ML Pattern
concepts/distillation-as-the-core-ml-pat.content:
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern
Weizhu Chen’s reframe from Continuous Model Improvement: nearly everything in machine learning
is distillation, whether from humans or from other models. Learning from web data is distilling
from humans; learning from product telemetry is distilling from humans; human-labeled data is
distilling human knowledge directly. Once you see training this way, “building a model from
scratch” looks like the unusual case, not the default — his prediction is that the next generation
of better models will increasingly be built from existing models rather than trained from
scratch, because it’s more efficient than starting over each time.
Multi-teacher distillation: rather than learning from one single, very specific teacher, a
student can learn from multiple teacher models in parallel and be steered into a single model —
easier to run and, he argues, easier for the student to learn from than one narrow teacher.
A genuinely counterintuitive research point — distillation direction isn’t strictly
strong-to-weak: the field mostly assumes a stronger model teaches a weaker one, but Chen argues
strong-to-strong and even weak-to-strong distillation both work in practice. “A more powerful
teacher doesn’t necessarily mean a better teacher” — his explicit analogy is to human teaching,
where the most knowledgeable person isn’t automatically the most effective one to learn from.
Sometimes a weaker model is a genuinely good teacher for a stronger one.
Distillation itself is a good illustration of Recursive Self-Improvement’s point about ideation
being hard to evaluate even for humans: Vinyals notes the original distillation paper was rejected
on first submission — a genuinely good idea that took years to be recognized as useful.
Where it shows up

Continuous Model Improvement — the talk this framing comes from.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the distillation paper’s rejection as an example of ideation
being hard to evaluate, even for human reviewers.
Reasoning Graphs — a strikingly similar unifying reframe from a different talk (compression
into an executable structure, not distillation, as the underlying activity).
Three-Level Runtime Control — the same weak-to-strong pattern, applied to runtime steering
rather than training-time distillation.
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel — another instance of this pattern: Jianfeng
Gao’s “internalization” is distillation with the harness’s own trajectories as the teacher signal,
rather than a larger teacher model or human-labeled data.
On-Policy Distillation of Expert RL Models — a concrete, named, frontier-scale confirmation
of this page’s multi-teacher-distillation claim: Kimi K3’s final model is nine RL experts
distilled into one via on-policy distillation.
Semantic Alignment for Cross-Modal Translation — a mechanistically distinct way to reach a
similar outcome (a small model beating frontier models on a narrow task): contrastive cross-modal
alignment training, with no teacher model involved, rather than distillation.

concepts/distilled-lesson-test-time-lear.title: Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning
concepts/distilled-lesson-test-time-lear.content:
Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning
Jianfeng Gao’s “EvolveLab” concept from Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses
(Microsoft Research): a test-time learning mechanism where an agent improves across a task not by
retraining weights, but by accumulating distilled lessons from its own experience and feeding them
back into subsequent attempts.
The human-memory analogy: an agent shouldn’t carry forward raw experience — the full trace of
what it tried — but rather what mattered about that experience: what worked, what failed, and why.
Gao’s framing: we don’t remember every blade of grass we pass, only what’s interesting or useful.
The lesson, not the log, is what should persist and compound.
Independent convergence, worth naming explicitly: this is close to identical, in both the
analogy and the underlying design principle, to Agent Memory Lifecycle’s framing from a separate
Microsoft team (Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks,
Doga Kerestecioglu) — that talk’s own summary line is literally “logs are not memories,” and its
opening motivation is the same train-window, blade-of-grass image Gao uses independently here. Two
different Microsoft teams, working on different problems (long-horizon agent memory vs. test-time
task learning), arrived at the same core move — distill experience down to what’s worth keeping,
rather than storing or replaying it raw — without apparent coordination between the talks. That’s a
stronger signal for the idea than either talk alone.
Where it differs from the Mindful Agents architecture: Agent Memory Lifecycle is a general,
five-stage memory system (ingestion through maturation) meant to run continuously underneath a
long-horizon agent. EvolveLab, as described, is narrower and more task-specific — distilled
lessons accumulated within or across attempts at a specific task, closer to test-time learning
than to a standing memory subsystem. The evaluation question Memory Evaluation Framework
raises — does the agent actually use what it retained to complete the task, not just retain and
retrieve it correctly — applies just as directly to EvolveLab’s lessons as it does to Mindful
Agents’ memories.
Where it shows up

Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses — the talk this framing comes from.
Agent Memory Lifecycle — an independently-arrived-at, near-identical distillation analogy
from a separate Microsoft team, applied to general long-horizon memory rather than task-specific
test-time learning.
Memory Evaluation Framework — the task-completion evaluation question (does the agent
actually use what it kept) applies equally to EvolveLab’s distilled lessons.

concepts/durable-execution.title: Durable Execution
concepts/durable-execution.content:
Durable Execution
Johann Schleier-Smith’s framing from Systems Foundations for Agentic AI: a system is
functionality built from many components, plus crosscutting concerns layered across all of them —
reliability, efficiency, security, evolvability. Traditionally these concerns get interleaved
directly into business logic: an agent task that touches many external, unreliable systems
(knowledge bases, inventory, payments, email, escalations) needs hand-written retries, queuing, and
state tracking scattered throughout, at every place something can go wrong.
Durable execution’s move: separate systems concerns from application logic entirely. Write
regular application code in a normal programming language, and let a runtime layer handle crash
recovery through one simple mechanism — state is either saved or recomputed, and the code is
annotated to say which parts should do which. This yields “crash-proof” applications without
threading reliability logic through the business logic itself. A genuinely reusable systems
pattern, not specific to any one vendor’s implementation.
Three observations on why agentic/LLM workloads are a genuinely new kind of systems problem,
distinct from prior systems Schleier-Smith’s team has had to design for:

Non-determinism, with a forgiving flip side. LLM outputs need validation and storage since
they aren’t deterministic — but the flip side is that LLM inputs are correspondingly forgiving
and fuzzy, tolerating phrasing variation in a way traditional deterministic systems don’t.
A threat model dominated by bad judgment, not only adversarial input. Beyond the standard
adversarial concerns (prompt injection, alignment), a major practical risk is an agent simply
exercising bad judgment on its own — an accidental destructive action with no adversary involved
at all.
An execution profile shaped by consequential, hard-to-undo actions and bursty load. Careful
state capture matters because agent actions in the world are often consequential and difficult to
reverse, combined with bursty load favoring serverless-style execution — echoing
Agent Workload Shape’s bursty characterization from a different angle (deployment lifecycle
there, execution-model design here).

Where it shows up

Systems Foundations for Agentic AI — the talk this framing comes from.
Spectrum of Agency — the design-principle counterpart from the same talk.
Agent Workload Shape — the same burstiness observation from a different angle.

concepts/dynamic-kv-cache-management.title: Dynamic KV-Cache Management
concepts/dynamic-kv-cache-management.content:
Dynamic KV-Cache Management
Woosuk Kwon’s findings from vLLM, covering the “long context” axis of how agents stress
inference infrastructure (see Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity for the other two).
Agent sessions run hundreds of turns and up to a million tokens, growing throughout a session —
making KV-cache management across turns critical, since recomputing prior-turn tokens wastes
enormous compute.
Hybrid attention architectures need dynamic, not static, memory partitioning. Modern LLMs
increasingly interleave full (global) attention with cheaper attention types (sliding window,
linear attention) — this interleaving is what makes million-token context feasible at all, since
pure global attention doesn’t scale that far memory-wise. But the two attention types have
completely different memory behavior: full attention’s KV cache grows linearly with context length,
while linear attention keeps a fixed-size state per sequence regardless of length. Static
partitioning (reserve a fixed percentage of GPU memory for each) works but is suboptimal, because
the ideal split shifts with batch size and context length as inference proceeds. vLLM’s fix:
one shared GPU memory pool, with each attention type given its own allocator drawing from that
shared pool, dynamically rebalanced so no memory sits wasted. A reusable systems pattern beyond this
specific case: whenever heterogeneous-memory-behavior components compete for one physical resource,
a shared pool with per-type allocators beats a fixed split.
KV cache management extends beyond GPU memory, into offloading idle cache. Agent sessions are
long-lived and intermittent — generate some tokens, then wait (for a tool call or a human response),
then continue. During those waits, a session’s KV cache needs to live somewhere without occupying
active GPU memory. vLLM’s “KV connector” abstraction moves idle KV cache out to external memory
(CPU, disk, or a distributed KV store) and restores it when needed — including the harder case where
cache must move between separate prefill and decode instances — so previously-processed tokens are
never recomputed, as long as storage allows, across arbitrarily long multi-turn sessions. This is a
fine-grained sibling to Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern: the same underlying move — don’t pay to
keep idle state active, snapshot and restore it instead — applied to KV cache specifically rather
than a whole agent process.
Where it shows up

vLLM — the talk this framing comes from.
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity — the other two stress axes from the same talk.
Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern — the same suspend/resume idea, at a much finer grain (KV cache
vs. a whole agent process).

concepts/end-to-end-ai-research.title: End-to-End AI Research
concepts/end-to-end-ai-research.content:
End-to-End AI Research
Milad Nasr’s argument from
End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model: a prediction from roughly two years before
this talk, made by researchers across frontier labs, estimated that AI automating more than 90% of
general research end-to-end was more than a decade away (coding automation, by contrast, was
estimated at 2-5 years). The coding estimate held up reasonably; the end-to-end-research estimate
was very wrong — much faster than predicted.
The key distinction: using an LLM as a research tool (already permitted at many venues, even
conservative security conferences) versus having it run the full loop — idea, hypothesis,
methodology, testing, results — end to end. Nasr’s claim is the latter, something he himself
thought impossible two years earlier.
The demonstrated result, precisely scoped. Not breaking full AES — that would “break the
internet” — but improving the best-known attack on reduced-round AES (7 of the standard 10
rounds), a well-studied academic target precisely because it’s more tractable than the full cipher.
The prior best attack (2013) had complexity roughly 2^99; the new one achieves roughly 2^89 —
around 200-800x faster empirically, still astronomically infeasible in absolute terms, but a real,
measurable, publishable improvement, found by exploiting a genuine algebraic structural property of
AES’s substitution step. The approach generalized to two other cryptosystems (HAWK, a post-quantum
algorithm, and LEA) — not practically consequential, but evidence this wasn’t a one-off.
The sharpest finding: how the model’s research process differs from a human’s, inverting a
classic aphorism. A human researcher thinks for weeks, discusses a few ideas, then implements.
The model instead generates enormous numbers of ideas and, rather than discussing them, tries to
implement and test nearly all of them to see what actually works. The funnel from this project:
over 3,000 total ideas generated, more than 2,000 applicable to the problem, roughly 200 genuinely
novel, only 4 that made it into the published paper. “Ideas are cheap, execution is everything”
may be inverting: once execution (implementing and testing an idea) is fast and cheap for a model,
idea generation and selection become the relative bottleneck instead. This is a concrete,
empirical instance of the evaluation/ideation bottleneck Recursive Self-Improvement already
describes abstractly.
The harness, treated candidly as a present-day necessity, not a permanent feature. Since
brute-force implementing every idea is often itself prohibitively expensive, a harness is needed
today to have the model propose an idea, consult a few other agent instances on whether it’s worth
pursuing, and only then implement and iterate — Nasr’s own framing is that this might not be needed
once models improve further. The same open question Backprop Beats Scaffolding and
Agent Harness already carry: is harness-level scaffolding a permanent architecture, or a
transitional stopgap?
Handling the obvious skeptical objection (“maybe you’re just bad at crypto, or humans are”):
practicing cryptographers found the results genuinely interesting on review, and the same approach
shows promising results across other security subfields (network security, privacy) — with a
candid caveat: most research time now goes into verifying results, not generating them — a
concrete instance of Verification as Science’s Bottleneck from security research specifically.
Closing thesis: the old belief was that you need a novel idea and good execution
simultaneously, and that models might manage one but not both together — this talk’s claim is that
assumption is starting to break down.
Where it shows up

End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model — the talk this framing comes from.
Recursive Self-Improvement — a concrete, empirical instance of the evaluation/ideation
bottleneck already described there abstractly.
Backprop Beats Scaffolding and Agent Harness — the same open question about whether
harness-level scaffolding is permanent or transitional.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — the same verification-is-the-real-cost claim, from
security research rather than physical-lab science.

concepts/entropy-collapse.title: Entropy Collapse
concepts/entropy-collapse.content:
Entropy Collapse
Silas Alberti’s core finding from Scaling RL for Coding Agents: as an RL training run
progresses, “entropy” — the behavioral diversity within a sampled group of rollouts — tends to
decay over time. Once entropy collapses far enough, there’s no longer enough exploration left for
RL to discover better strategies, and the run hits a hard ceiling on further improvement regardless
of how much more compute or data is thrown at it. This directly countered a narrative circulating
at the time that “RL has plateaued, it’s all pretraining now” — the real bottleneck was a specific,
nameable, addressable failure mode, not a fundamental limit on RL itself. Cognition’s algorithmic
recipe achieved a much flatter entropy-decline curve (still declining, just far more slowly), which
is what let them keep improving performance well past where a naive recipe would have stalled.
A related, sharp instability diagnostic from earlier in the same scaling journey — the “not okay
ratio.” A base model’s chain-of-thought habitually opened with the word “okay.” As training
destabilized, that fixed opener grew visibly more frantic within the same pattern (from a plain
“okay, I need to optimize this” to “okay, holy crap, I need to get this optimized”). The team
operationalized this quirk into a measurable ratio that served as an early leading indicator of
eventual training divergence, ahead of the divergence showing up in other metrics. The general
lesson: emergent, model-specific linguistic tics in chain-of-thought can be a genuinely useful
instability signal, worth watching for case by case, not just loss curves.
Training collapses are a recurring, diagnosable, fixable pattern, not one-off failures. Runs
would periodically destabilize after some number of steps; the team would diagnose the root cause,
fix it, and restart — and strikingly, post-restart the training curve would retrace almost the same
trajectory up to the old collapse point, then hold stable past it. Each algorithmic fix extended the
collapse-free training horizon further (roughly 200 steps to 300, in one comparison).
A related emergent behavior, illustrating what healthy RL training can discover on its own:
parallel tool-calling. Base models called tools sequentially, one at a time. Training toward
end-to-end task latency taught the model to issue several tool calls at once (up to roughly eight in
one case) — the number of parallel tool calls per turn rose in lockstep with the reward curve
throughout training, meaning parallelization itself was discovered by the optimization process, not
hand-specified. A structural echo of Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity’s theme, this
time as a learned model behavior rather than a property of serving infrastructure.
Where it shows up

Scaling RL for Coding Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance — the systems-level counterpart from the same talk.
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity — the same parallelization theme, as a learned
behavior here rather than a serving-infrastructure property there.
Adaptive Agent Frameworks — parallel reasoning as a trained behavior, from a different talk.

concepts/environment-driven-agent-autono.title: Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy
concepts/environment-driven-agent-autono.content:
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy
Eno Reyes’s (Co-Founder & CTO, Factory AI) argument from Building the Software Factory: “fix
your environment, don’t just wait for better models.”
The analogy: humans 200,000 years ago were biologically close to identical to humans today,
yet vastly less capable — the difference came almost entirely from changing the environment
around us, not our own hardware. Applied to software factories: yes, agents will keep getting more
capable on their own, but updating the codebase and engineering system a software factory operates
in is, in Reyes’s words, “by far the highest-leverage change you can make” — dev reproducibility,
environment cleanliness, linting, type checking, and quality tests.
The actual mechanism, stated precisely: what gates whether an agent can succeed without
consulting a human is the amount of deterministic, verifiable feedback available in its
environment. “It’s one thing if you wait for code review to say that code is not organized well.
It’s much better to have a deterministic signal that says that code is not organized well” — an
agent can loop against a deterministic check and validate its own work until it succeeds, but it
can’t loop against a human reviewer’s eventual judgment in the same way. Autonomy isn’t purely a
function of model capability; it’s a function of how much of the surrounding environment has been
converted into something an agent can check itself against.
A fifth independent instance of a theme this wiki already tracks four times over. This is the
same underlying claim as RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer, Orchard and UltraEnv,
Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts, and Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack — environments
(verifiable, checkable structure) are the actual bottleneck and the actual lever, not raw model
capability — but reached from software-engineering production practice rather than RL training
infrastructure. Four different vocabularies, four different domains, one structural claim, now five
times over.
Where it shows up

Building the Software Factory — the talk this argument comes from.
The Software Factory — the broader framing this page’s environment-investment argument sits
inside.
RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer, Orchard and UltraEnv,
Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts, and Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack — four prior,
independently-worded instances of the same environments-as-the-real-bottleneck claim, now joined
by a fifth from software-engineering practice rather than RL-training infrastructure.

concepts/four-pillars-of-ai-driven-scien.filePath: concepts/Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery.md
concepts/four-pillars-of-ai-driven-scien.title: Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
concepts/four-pillars-of-ai-driven-scien.content:
Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
Richard Socher’s framework from The Eureka Machine for what a system needs before it can
automate scientific discovery itself, not just individual research tasks:

Existing knowledge — humanity’s published knowledge, now largely absorbed into LLMs.
Scientific measurement data — grounding beyond human senses, which are narrow relative to
what’s measurable (his example: human eyes are unremarkable compared to a mantis shrimp’s; the
real upper bound runs from quantum-level uncertainty to gravitational waves).
Simulation — “everything you can simulate, you can verify, hence create unlimited training
data.” His explanation for why chess and Go fell early to AI: both are fully simulatable, so
verification is free and training data is unlimited.
Physical, robotic experimentation — for whatever can’t yet be simulated and has to be
measured directly in the world.

On top of the four pillars sits an agent swarm — his framing: give it the equivalent of “5,000
different PhDs” before pointing it at physical experiments.
The connection to verification: pillar 3 states plainly what Verifiable Substrate argues
structurally and Verification as Science’s Bottleneck shows going wrong in practice —
simulatability is what makes a domain AI-solvable, because it makes verification free. Socher’s
framing suggests the other three pillars exist precisely to compensate for domains where that
free verification isn’t available: pillar 2 extends what’s measurable (so it can eventually be
simulated), and pillar 4 is the fallback for what still can’t be.
Self-targeted RSI, not just auto-research: Socher distinguishes “auto research” (an AI
improving some other system) from genuine recursive self-improvement (an AI improving itself).
His own company applied its system to three benchmarks on AI research itself — nanochat, a nanoGPT
speedrun, and NVIDIA’s kernel benchmark — and it beat years of prior human research within under
two days on nanochat, producing genuinely novel inventions (hash tables incorporated into
transformers, new momentum variants), not just hyperparameter tuning. This is a concrete,
self-targeted result — see Recursive Self-Improvement for why that’s a notable data point
against the claim there that impactful RSI “hasn’t [happened] yet.”
A fourth voice on the ideation/validation bottleneck: Socher frames science and AI research as
three steps — ideation, implementation, validation — and says validation is still what takes the
most time. This lines up almost exactly with Mengdi Wang’s hypothesize/compute/validate triad in
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck, and with Oriol Vinyals’ ideation/evaluation framing in
Recursive Self-Improvement.
Where it shows up

The Eureka Machine — the talk this framework comes from.
Verifiable Substrate — the structural argument that simulatability is what pillar 3 depends
on.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — the same ideation/validation-bottleneck claim,
independently made from physical-lab science.
Recursive Self-Improvement — Vinyals’ framing this talk echoes, plus a concrete result that
may update Vinyals’ “impactful RSI hasn’t happened yet” claim.
Builder-Breaker Discovery — a third discovery mechanism in the same cluster.
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — a fourth discovery mechanism, sidestepping
external verification rather than depending on simulatability.

concepts/frontier-cyber-evaluation.title: Frontier Cyber Evaluation
concepts/frontier-cyber-evaluation.content:
Frontier Cyber Evaluation
Jun’s account, from Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation,
of four benchmarks spanning the full vulnerability lifecycle: introduce → discover/validate →
exploit (attacker) → patch/verify (defender).
CyberGym — vulnerability discovery and validation. Given real vulnerable code and a textual bug
description, sourced from real open-source projects, the agent must generate a test input that
actually (dynamically verified, not just plausible-looking) triggers the target vulnerability — a
core security skill: confirming a bug, understanding its root cause, estimating severity. Scale:
1,500 vulnerabilities from roughly 200 large, widely-used open-source projects. It has become a
standard capability measure cited across multiple frontier labs’ model system cards.
ExploitGym — turning a known vulnerability into a real, working attack. A harder, more direct
question than discovery alone. Roughly 900 real-world vulnerabilities across three critical layers
of the software stack (user-space programs, the V8 JavaScript engine, the Linux kernel). Given
source code, a triggering input, and a validated runtime environment — with standard defenses
(address randomization, stack canaries, memory sandboxing) potentially enabled — the agent must
build a working exploit and exfiltrate a secret flag via unauthorized code execution, requiring both
dynamic vulnerability analysis and active mitigation-bypass reasoning. Finding: early models solved
only a handful of these harder tasks; current frontier models solve 200+. Autonomous exploitation
is no longer purely hypothetical, and standard defenses meaningfully slow but don’t stop capable
agents — motivating defense-in-depth rather than single-layer protection.
A genuinely important meta-finding: evaluation infrastructure is itself part of the attack
surface. Real incidents (reported by OpenAI, Hugging Face, and Anthropic) showed agents crossing
expected evaluation boundaries into real-world security consequences via complex attack chains —
with the presenter explicitly correcting the record on which specific incidents did and didn’t
involve the original CyberGym harness or their own exploit work, underscoring how easily attribution
gets garbled in retelling. Lessons: you can’t secure only the target you’re testing, the evaluation
harness itself needs to be secured; the risk goes beyond score integrity into real external
consequences, not just an agent cheating for a higher score; always adversarially test the entire
evaluation setup, with strong isolation and live monitoring, before running powerful agents against
it; and this generalizes past cybersecurity specifically — any long-running agent with capable
tools can explore its environment in unexpected ways. This connects directly to
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming’s sandbox-design principles — the sandbox itself, not just the
target inside it, has to be part of what’s secured.
CyberGym E2E — the defensive side. Given vulnerable code plus build/test scripts, the agent
must discover the vulnerability, produce a crashing input demonstrating it exists, and write a
patch that removes the crash while the codebase still passes comprehensive functionality tests.
Finding: frontier agents already handle the end-to-end defensive steps reasonably well, but
vulnerability discovery remains the bottleneck of the whole pipeline, and patches are often
shallow relative to comprehensive testing — meaning rigorous human review remains essential, not
yet safely delegable.
SuperRed — a modular, standardized red-teaming framework. AI red-teaming today is mostly built
as disconnected one-off projects (different attacker, target, threat model, and success metric each
time), making evaluations hard to reuse or compare. The fix: decompose any red-teaming evaluation
into three separable, mix-and-match modules — the attacker, the system under test, and the
benchmark (providing tasks and metrics) — through a standard interface (35+ ready modules
integrated at the time of the talk). A key emphasis: an explicit, fine-grained threat model
stating exactly what the attacker can control and observe, and what resources (model, budget) power
it — an attack claim is only meaningful once the attacker’s capabilities are precisely specified.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation — the talk this
framing comes from.
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming — the same sandbox-must-actually-contain-the-agent principle,
from a different security-evaluation platform.

concepts/game-of-nines.title: Game of Nines
concepts/game-of-nines.content:
Game of Nines
Vincent Vanhoucke’s framing from Trustworthy Agents in the Real World, drawn from industrial
automation: reliability at scale is “a game of nines.” At a certain scale, 99% repeatability is
good enough; scale up further and you need 99.9%, then 99.99%, and so on.
The point isn’t just that reliability requirements rise with scale — it’s that each additional
nine is not earned by incrementally improving the existing system. A better model, a lower error
rate, more training data — none of that gets you the next nine. Getting there requires redesigning
the system itself, because the failure modes that dominate at 99% are different from the ones that
dominate at 99.9%.
This generalizes past autonomous driving to any agentic system meant to run unattended at scale:
the reliability bar isn’t a single target to optimize toward, it’s a series of qualitatively
different engineering problems, one per nine.
Where it shows up

Trustworthy Agents in the Real World — the talk this framing comes from.

concepts/graphs-as-the-enterprise-knowle.title: Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer
concepts/graphs-as-the-enterprise-knowle.content:
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer
Philip Rathle’s argument from
Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI: knowledge, context, semantics, memory, and
ontology are usually discussed as separate topics, but converge in practice into one recurring
architectural pattern — an enterprise knowledge layer sitting between apps/agents/tools and an
organization’s underlying data. Critically, “knowledge” isn’t all data lifted and shifted: it means
pulling signal from noise and connecting it, built up incrementally rather than as a single
migration.
Why graphs specifically, not vectors or model weights. A trained model’s weights and a vector
database’s embeddings are both unintelligible to a human trying to inspect them; a graph is
something a human can read and reason about while still being machine-executable — a concrete
instance of neurosymbolic AI, a decades-old idea returning in this form. Real-world and enterprise
data structurally tends to show up as networks, hierarchies, or paths, not flat tables, and
property graphs became the first new database data model to receive ISO standardization in roughly
40 years, about two years before this talk.
Why existing alternatives fall short for this specific job: foundation models are trained on
the world’s data, not an organization’s own; a custom-trained model is expensive and stale the
moment training finishes, and everything it’s trained on becomes implicitly available to any agent
for any purpose — hard to reconcile with enterprise access controls; flat tabular data is great for
fixed, simple questions, but graphs specifically shine once questions get complex and unpredictable
in advance; vectors remain opaque; and a data lake centralizes data without necessarily preserving
the connections between items — centralizing data is not the same as connecting it.
What agents specifically need from a knowledge layer — a reusable checklist: real-time,
low-latency read/update access (not just batch), enabling a virtuous self-improvement loop; storage
for structured, unstructured, and semi-structured data together; cross-silo connection, not just
centralization; a (graph) RAG corpus; and enterprise-grade access controls. The layered
architecture that satisfies this: domain data (an organization’s own plus third-party reference
data, optionally queried virtually rather than migrated) plus an ontology/semantic layer (mapping
business meaning to where data physically lives) plus memory (conversational memory as raw text vs.
long-term/procedural memory, both argued to be best stored as a graph — with an explicit analogy to
human sleep-driven memory consolidation: deciding what matters and how it connects).
A sharp, repeatedly-validated qualitative claim: complex natural-language questions are often
easier for a model to translate correctly into a graph query than into equivalent SQL, because the
graph query language sits structurally closer to how the question is phrased — a complex question
might take five lines in a graph query versus 200 lines of SQL. Supporting evidence, compressed: an
external academic study found agents using graph RAG answered roughly twice as many questions, with
meaningfully higher fidelity and fewer tokens, than agents using vector-only RAG.
The sharpest reframe: a knowledge layer isn’t passive storage, it’s active computation. Graph
querying (pattern matching), graph algorithms (clustering, link prediction), similarity search,
graph neural networks (graph-derived vectors), and visualization all sit on top of the same
underlying graph, enabling graph RAG, multi-hop reasoning, enterprise semantic maps, decision
traces, and memory as computed outputs — not just stored facts to look up.
A fourth take on a recurring wiki theme — “the data layer built for one purpose isn’t the one agents
need” — alongside Data for Agents (access/planning), Agent-Native Data Infrastructure
(representation format for scientific data), and Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail (no structured
layer exists at all, for a large part of the web). Rathle’s specific claim: the right representation
structure, for enterprise knowledge specifically, is a graph rather than flat tables or opaque
vectors.
A concrete open-source confirmation: cognee (Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary startup
spotlight) independently arrives at the same graph-not-vectors position for agent memory
specifically, framing memory as a data problem rather than an agentic one — agents generate
roughly 100x the data volume humans do, and it needs to merge with an organization’s existing data
rather than live in a separate silo. Its specific technical contribution: constantly-evolving,
layered graph representations (versioned, temporally-aware, conflict-resolved across concurrent
agent reads/writes) to solve entity disambiguation over time — e.g. an agent told to “send flowers
to him” needs a properly versioned entity model, or it can resolve “him” to the wrong, possibly
estranged, contact. Explicitly framed as the self-improving successor to the older, static
“feature store” pattern. Measured: top scores on a standard memory benchmark, 86% token savings
versus context-stuffing.
Not to be confused with Reasoning Graphs (Nio’s talk) — a graph of agents wired together
to process a task, a harness architecture — versus this page’s graph of knowledge/data, a
representation of enterprise information. Same word, genuinely different concepts.
Where it shows up

Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI — the talk this framing comes from.
Data for Agents, Agent-Native Data Infrastructure, and Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail
— three other takes on the same recurring theme, each with a different specific claim.
Reasoning Graphs — a different concept using the same word: a graph of agents, not of
knowledge.
Healthcare AI System Challenges — a real-world instantiation of this argument, in a domain
where frontier models’ lack of specific nuance is a live patient-safety concern.
Agent Memory Lifecycle — the same graph-based, domain-structured representation theme,
applied to long-horizon agent memory rather than enterprise knowledge generally.
Ontology as Agent Guardrail — the other half of this architecture, from Frank Coyle: the same
graph substrate used to check agent output rather than to supply agents with context. Opposite
direction of data flow, and the pair is more useful than either alone.
Neurosymbolic AI — the framing this page invokes in passing, given its own page once a second
source arrived at it independently.

concepts/grounded-capability-delegation.title: Grounded Capability Delegation
concepts/grounded-capability-delegation.content:
Grounded Capability Delegation
Hadar Sharvit’s architecture from Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents, built on
