Market Models: delegate high-stakes quantitative decisions to grounded,
purpose-built tools rather than an LLM’s own reasoning, and let the LLM handle orchestration
instead.
The forecaster-plus-optimizer decomposition. Most business decisions reduce to pairing a
forecaster (predicting how demand or market dynamics will move — as a point estimate or a full
probabilistic distribution, e.g. quantile forecasts, when uncertainty matters) with an optimizer
(given that forecast, a reward like revenue, and a feasible action set, search for the best action
subject to hard and soft constraints — price bounds, limits on consecutive-price variation, sane
orderings between related products).
Why naive LLM agents structurally fail at this class of task. Real business questions are
open-ended (“are our prices for this product still sensible given current demand?”). A
general-purpose coding agent generally has neither a forecaster that generalizes to genuinely
out-of-distribution market conditions, nor a reliable constrained-optimization process — this isn’t
a prompting gap, it’s a missing capability that no amount of reasoning skill substitutes for.
The architecture: LLM orchestrates, grounded tools carry the guarantees. Market-dynamics
prediction and constrained optimization are wrapped as callable tools. A top-level orchestrating
agent delegates to specialized sub-agents — one for market dynamics, one for pricing-policy
optimization, and a QA/evaluation sub-agent that checks whether predictions and recommendations
are actually sensible, with its own tool for flagging high forecast uncertainty. This QA role is a
reusable pattern in its own right: a dedicated evaluator, distinct from the specialists producing
the primary output, that can trigger targeted rework on just the uncertain subset rather than
shipping every recommendation with uniform, unwarranted confidence.
The core payoff — a sharp comparison experiment. Two agents, identical real (anonymized) data,
identical open-ended question (“is the price right?”): a vanilla coding-agent harness (full
reasoning, web access, writes and runs its own analysis) versus the capability-grounded agent.
They reached opposite recommendations. The vanilla agent’s own analysis confused correlation
with causation — comparing markets and products that shouldn’t have been treated as correlated —
and concluded demand was inelastic, so raising prices carried “near zero” risk. The grounded agent
instead ran a genuine counterfactual analysis through the market model — holding the product and
market fixed, varying price — and correctly identified that demand was actually elastic at that
price point (a given percentage price cut yields a larger percentage demand increase, more than
offsetting the lower unit price), recommending a price decrease toward the point of maximum
revenue, adjusted for a holiday-driven demand shift the QA process caught. In simulated terms, the
vanilla agent’s call would have produced a meaningful negative revenue impact; the grounded
agent’s call produced a meaningful positive uplift. A concrete case of a genuinely wrong causal
inference from an otherwise capable general-purpose agent, avoided entirely by delegating the
actual causal reasoning to a purpose-built tool rather than the LLM’s own analysis.
Closing thesis: there’s real power in combining LLM orchestration and harness development with
knowing when and how to delegate to capabilities you can actually trust — the LLM orchestrates, but
the grounded capabilities carry the guarantees.
Where it shows up

Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Market Models — the underlying model class this architecture delegates
to.
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — a different axis of delegation from an unrelated talk:
choosing among multiple valid agents for the same task at runtime, rather than delegating from
LLM reasoning to a grounded, deterministic tool.

concepts/guardrail-degradation-under-com.title: Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity
concepts/guardrail-degradation-under-com.content:
Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity
Venkat Bhat’s finding from
Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration:
an agent’s safety guardrails are not complexity-invariant — they degrade as task complexity rises.
Forcing an agent to perform an actual therapeutic technique (motivational interviewing) works up to
a point; beyond a complexity threshold, the agent both fails at the technique itself and its safety
guardrails degrade alongside it.
A related measured finding: the strength of an agent’s safety guardrails materially affects how
it’s perceived when delivering therapy independently — comparing low-safety-guardrail against
high-safety-guardrail configurations showed a significant difference in how the agent was received.
This is a genuinely distinct failure mode from the wiki’s existing security-cluster material — the
“attacker” here is task complexity itself, not an adversary crafting an exploit. It’s a durable
caution for any domain considering semi-autonomous or autonomous agent deployment in a
safety-critical setting: guardrails validated at a modest complexity level may not hold as the
system is asked to do more.
Where it shows up

Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration
— the talk this framing comes from.
Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents — the methodological caution from the same
talk.

concepts/hallucination-squatting.title: Hallucination-Squatting
concepts/hallucination-squatting.content:
Hallucination-Squatting
Mohamed Nabeel’s argument from
Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks:
LLM hallucination is itself a supply-chain attack surface. Because LLMs are snapshot learners with
no live grounding of what currently exists, attackers can register and weaponize the exact
fictitious artifact names an LLM confidently recommends — prior research documented this for PyPI
and npm packages and for domain names; this talk extends it to browser extensions, motivated by “the
browser as the new operating system”: extensions hold session tokens and cookies, so a compromised
one is a front-row seat into a victim’s accounts.
Three structural reasons a namespace becomes a “hallucination-prone zone,” generalizable beyond
browser extensions:

Explosive growth outpacing recency. Tens of thousands of new browser extensions are created
monthly now, versus that many in an entire prior year. LLMs are poor at recency, so anything past
a training cutoff invites confident, plausible-sounding guessing rather than admitted ignorance.
Snapshot-learner blindness to deletions. Thousands of extensions are removed continuously too
— some specifically because they’re malware — but a model trained on an earlier snapshot has no
mechanism to know a once-real artifact no longer exists, and will recommend it anyway.
Uneven brand recognition. Not every legitimate extension has an established brand identity;
obscure-but-real, low-signal artifacts are exactly what a model is most likely to hallucinate a
plausible but wrong (or entirely fictitious) name for.

A related but distinct hallucination mechanism, worth noting as illustration: confident
analogical extrapolation from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one that actually inverts the
relevant underlying mechanism. Example: asked what color a Mars sunset would be, a model correctly
recognized Mars has a different atmosphere than Earth but extrapolated the wrong way — Earth’s red
sunsets result from long-wavelength light scattering less through its particular atmosphere; Mars’s
different atmospheric composition produces the opposite result, a blue sunset, not a more intense
red one.
Empirical confirmation: monitoring found real hallucinated extension recommendations in two
categories — actually-deleted extensions (some already flagged as malware) and never-claimed names
an LLM confidently asserts are installable. Tracking and rescoring these, the researchers found
roughly a dozen actually got registered and used for malicious activity during their study period —
a real, confirmed instance of the attack pattern in the wild, not just a theoretical risk.
The standing takeaway: hallucination is inherent to how LLMs work and won’t disappear with
better models alone, so independent verification before installing anything an AI recommends is a
permanent requirement, not a one-time fix.
Where it shows up

Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks
— the talk this framing comes from.

concepts/harness-diversity-as-data-augme.title: Harness Diversity as Data Augmentation
concepts/harness-diversity-as-data-augme.content:
Harness Diversity as Data Augmentation
From Workshop - Turning Chatbots into Agents (Daytona), describing a training choice made by
Kimi K3: rather than training against one fixed harness, use a config that randomly toggles
harness features — system prompts, sub-agents, memory, skills — on and off across training runs.
The harness itself becomes a data-augmentation axis: the model sees many permutations of what
scaffolding might or might not be present, and learns to be robust to whichever harness it’s
actually deployed into later (Kimi CLI, Claude Code, or anywhere else), including harness
configurations that didn’t exist yet at training time.
A direct, named contrast: Cursor’s Composer 2 model took the opposite bet — trained
specifically for Cursor’s own harness, optimizing for depth of fit to one known environment rather
than breadth of robustness across unknown ones. Two frontier labs making opposite choices on the
same axis, both presumably rational for their own product: Kimi ships into many third-party
harnesses it doesn’t control and needs generality; Cursor controls its own harness end-to-end and
can afford to specialize.
Why this belongs next to Harness Matters More Than Model: that page’s empirical finding is
that a model’s measured performance depends heavily on which harness it’s paired with, and the
winning pairing is often unpredictable without testing. Harness-diversity training is a direct
response to that finding at training time — instead of accepting that a model’s apparent
capability is harness-dependent, train the harness-dependence out by exposing the model to many
harnesses during training. Composer 2’s approach accepts and leans into harness-dependence instead
of training it away. Both are legitimate answers to the same underlying fact.
Where it shows up

Workshop - Turning Chatbots into Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Harness Matters More Than Model — the empirical finding (harness pairing affects measured
performance unpredictably) that this training strategy is a direct response to.
On-Policy Distillation of Expert RL Models — another piece of the same Kimi K3 training
recipe, from the same talk.

concepts/harness-matters-more-than-model.title: Harness Matters More Than Model
concepts/harness-matters-more-than-model.content:
Harness Matters More Than Model
Zach Mueller’s findings from
Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations (“the model is not
the agent”) — a measured, empirical version of the harness/model distinction already argued more
abstractly in Agent Harness.
The core finding: no harness is universally best, and the winning model-harness pairing is often
unpredictable in advance. Measured examples: Gemini 3 Pro dropped into a minimal, third-party
harness beat its own native Gemini CLI harness by 8% on the terminal-2 benchmark, and cost roughly
20 less to run. GPT-5.5 with Codex (OpenAI's own harness) was 5% better than alternatives but 4x
the cost — a deliberate "let the model run longer" design choice, a valid engineering tradeoff, not
an accident. Across 26 identical tasks with Kimi K3, its own native harness unsurprisingly won
(21/26, 0.54, ~300 seconds), but Claude Code scored nearly as well (~19) while costing 3x more —
attributed to Claude Code injecting a large system prompt into its harness regardless of which
model runs inside it, eating context and cost. Lesson: a model’s harness isn’t a neutral wrapper —
it materially changes measured performance and cost, sometimes by double digits, and you often
can’t know which pairing wins without testing it directly.
A clean definition of an agent “trace”: the full loop between a prompt (e.g. “implement this
function”) and the model’s eventual solution or human-escalation — reason about the next step, call
a tool, judge whether the task is fulfilled, repeat.
Building an open, license-clean agent-trace dataset — the concrete project this talk describes:
pick a standardized harness to generate traces in (Lambda chose Hermes Agent, an open-source
project — explicitly a judgment call, not an objectively “correct” choice); pick source models by
three criteria — permissively licensed (so resulting traces are freely reusable), too large for
most people to run at home, and genuinely capable (specifically citing “swarm” parallel tool-calling
within a single reasoning chain as a capability worth capturing, since it’s especially valuable for
smaller, faster models to learn). Scale: roughly 7,000 coding scenarios, run through the chosen
harness across ~184 H100s over about a week, yielding around 150 million traces per source model,
split into verified-success and failure buckets. Released openly; the community used the traces to
fine-tune small (1-27B parameter) models into more performant home-runnable coding assistants.
The real takeaway, made explicit by the speaker: not “go distill your own traces” — take a
model you already use daily and drop it into a different harness than the one it’s normally
paired with. A model’s apparent behavior and capability profile are partly artifacts of the harness
and system prompt it’s usually run in, not a fixed property of the model alone — so assuming a
model’s native harness is automatically the right choice is often wrong, and testing alternate
pairings is underrated.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations — the talk this
framing comes from.
Agent Harness — the abstract version of this same claim; this page is its clearest measured
confirmation so far.
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming — the same model-plus-harness-jointly-determines-the-outcome
point, applied to security rather than raw task performance.
Triple-A Benchmark Standardization — sharpens this claim further: most benchmarks can’t even
properly measure a different harness, not just that harness affects outcomes.
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel — a counterpoint on a different time
horizon: this page’s finding is a snapshot showing harness effects dominate today; Jianfeng Gao
argues that snapshot is moving, as differentiating harness capability gets trained into the
model itself generation over generation.
Harness Diversity as Data Augmentation — a direct training-time response to this page’s
finding: Kimi K3 trains against many randomized harness configurations to make the model robust
to harness choice, while Cursor’s Composer 2 makes the opposite bet and specializes to one.

concepts/healthcare-ai-system-challenges.title: Healthcare AI System Challenges
concepts/healthcare-ai-system-challenges.content:
Healthcare AI System Challenges
Krishnaram Kenthapadi’s account, from
Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned,
of what changes once a single clinical application scales into a multi-agent healthcare system
spanning multiple stakeholders (patients, doctors, administrative staff, payers) and systems (EHRs,
search, document summarization, medical coding).
Offline-online evaluation mismatch. An evaluation that looks good offline may not hold up
online, because assumptions no longer apply or the patient distribution has shifted — a
domain-specific instance of a general evaluation-validity problem.
Mapping business metrics to applied-science metrics. A disciplined translation is needed from
what the business actually cares about into something concretely measurable and iterable on — the
two aren’t automatically the same thing.
The sharpest, most domain-specific point: recall matters far more here than in typical search.
In a patient-summary context, missing one medically pertinent fact can directly cause a
patient-safety incident — a precision/recall tradeoff that inverts what’s usually acceptable in
general search or summarization, where a missed result is merely inconvenient.
Encoding domain knowledge via a semantic knowledge graph. Frontier models lack healthcare-
specific nuance by default, so domain and task-specific knowledge needs to be explicitly encoded —
here, via a semantic knowledge graph and semantic data layer. A direct, real-world instantiation of
Philip Rathle’s argument that graphs bridge human and
machine understanding in a way flat tables and opaque vectors don’t.
Closing methodological takeaways: understand the domain deeply, not just develop the model —
invest as much in data validation and evaluation methodology as in modeling itself; and iterate
directly with clinicians, shipping early versions and refining based on real feedback rather than
developing in isolation.
Where it shows up

Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned
— the talk this framing comes from.
Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — the architecture these challenges apply to.
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — a real-world healthcare instantiation of that
page’s general argument.

concepts/inference-engine-design-for-age.filePath: concepts/Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving.md
concepts/inference-engine-design-for-age.title: Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving
concepts/inference-engine-design-for-age.content:
Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving
From
Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent - A Case Study of SGLang and Miles:
agentic workloads change what an inference engine needs to optimize for, relative to single-turn
chat serving.
Cache reuse becomes the top priority. Agentic sessions are long, multi-turn, and heavy on tool
calls — the same context gets extended and re-processed repeatedly rather than each request
starting fresh, so how well an engine reuses previously-computed key-value cache dominates both
latency and cost. Two techniques cited: a unified radix cache designed to keep working smoothly
across newer hybrid model architectures, and hierarchical KV-cache placement — moving cache down
from HBM to DRAM to external storage as it cools, rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice
between fast memory and cache retention.
Scaling to trillion-parameter models pushes deployment topology, not just parallelism math.
Beyond standard 5D parallelism (data, tensor, context, pipeline, expert) and newer strategies,
deployments move from co-located serving toward prefill-decode disaggregation as scale and load
imbalance grow — separating the compute-bound prefill phase from the memory-bound decode phase
onto different resources. Vision-language models add a further disaggregation axis (splitting the
encoder out too), since encoding runs on a different resource profile than decoding.
1M-token context windows are described as already the norm, not a future target — driving
techniques like chunked prefill (processing a long prompt in pieces rather than all at once) and
sequence-level parallelism (splitting a sequence across GPUs) specifically to make very long
context practical rather than merely possible.
The underlying claim, generalized beyond this specific engine: serving infrastructure tuned
for single-turn chat doesn’t transfer cleanly to agentic workloads — the bottlenecks shift (from
raw throughput toward cache reuse and context length), and the fix is architectural (disaggregation,
hierarchical caching), not just more compute. The talk’s own concrete payoff from applying this: a
2.2x throughput improvement and up to 500 tokens/sec/user, measured on GLM 5.2.
Where it shows up

Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent - A Case Study of SGLang and Miles
— the talk this framing comes from.
Train-Inference Mismatch — a related concern from the same infrastructure stack: once an
inference engine like this is also used to generate RL rollouts, its numerical behavior has to
match the training backend, not just serve efficiently.

concepts/inference-parallelism-and-hardw.title: Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity
concepts/inference-parallelism-and-hardw.content:
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity
Woosuk Kwon’s findings from vLLM, covering two of the three axes along which agents stress
inference infrastructure (large models and exploding token demand — see
Dynamic KV-Cache Management for the third, long context).
No universal parallelism strategy exists. Serving trillion-parameter frontier models requires
model parallelism, and vLLM supports seven kinds (tensor, pipeline, data, expert, sequence, and two
kinds of context parallelism — including “decode context parallelism,” specific to the KV cache,
which has no equivalent in training). The finding: there is no default configuration that wins.
Concrete example — for a large mixture-of-experts model’s prefill workload, the “obvious” choice
(8-way tensor parallelism) was beaten by a far less obvious combination (2-way tensor × 8-way
pipeline × sequence × expert parallelism, across 16 GPUs), yielding much lower time-to-first-token
and much higher throughput per GPU. The right configuration depends on model architecture, cluster
setup, and workload shape simultaneously — getting it right requires a real performance model, not
a default.
Token economics have flipped, forcing hardware diversification. As models get smarter, the
value of a generated token now exceeds the cost of generating it — driving demand that’s effectively
unbounded and growing faster than GPU supply. Kwon’s framing of the resulting question: can all
available compute on Earth be used to generate tokens efficiently? vLLM’s answer is to support 10+
hardware backends (NVIDIA as the primary focus, but also Google TPU, AMD, and others) through a
plug-in architecture that shares vLLM’s core while letting each backend customize its specifics.
This is a concrete, software-side instance of Model-Hardware Co-Design’s claim that chip
diversity is inevitable — the same conclusion Peter DeSantis reaches from the chip-design side,
reached here from the inference-serving side instead.
Where it shows up

vLLM — the talk this framing comes from.
Dynamic KV-Cache Management — the third stress axis (long context) from the same talk.
Model-Hardware Co-Design — the same chip-diversity conclusion, reached independently from a
different part of the stack.
An Open Compute Layer — a complementary infra concern one layer up: cross-cluster
orchestration, rather than inference-serving hardware diversity.
Entropy Collapse — the same parallelization theme as a learned model behavior (discovered
through RL training) rather than a property of serving infrastructure.
Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability — the same “no universal winner, match the choice
to the workload” theme, from agent-communication protocol design rather than inference serving.
Agents’ Last Exam — the same “no universal winner” finding, this time across professional
domains rather than model/cluster/workload combinations.

concepts/infrastructure-for-long-running.title: Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents
concepts/infrastructure-for-long-running.content:
Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents
Ankit Goyal’s (Principal Staff Software Engineer, AI Platforms, LinkedIn) account from
Infrastructure for Long-Running Agents of re-architecting infrastructure for agents running
in production at scale.
Three production agents, one shared lifecycle. A model-migration agent moves LinkedIn’s 400+
production TensorFlow models to PyTorch, with the hard constraint that new models must match or
beat production models that were human-tuned by engineers over months or years. A performance-
optimization agent scans the cluster for low-utilization jobs, profiles and benchmarks them
against an accumulated team knowledge base, and opens review requests for the owning teams. An
autonomous research agent runs architectural sweeps or hyperparameter tuning against an
engineer-defined objective. All three share the same loop: hypothesis → code generation → GPU
execution → evaluation, running continuously and autonomously over hours or days without human
intervention.
Three infrastructure shifts driven by introducing agents at this scale:

UX. The prior focus was rich abstractions that made it easy for humans to write ML
pipelines, training loops, and data access. Now that code is LLM-generated, the abstraction
target moves up a level: users focus on designing agentic workflows and the guardrails that keep
agents from deviating from the original task, not on making raw code-writing easier.
Compute. Humans used to launch a limited number of long-running jobs, where a couple minutes
of launch delay was amortized over the run. Agents launch hundreds of jobs in a short window,
ranging from minutes to days — a fundamentally different, bursty load pattern that breaks
assumptions baked into infrastructure designed around the old one.
Trust. Human-written code is inherently trusted; agent-generated code is not, and runs in a
highly restricted environment: no network egress, no direct credential access, with all
communication routed through proxies using the agent’s own scoped identity rather than a
human’s or a shared service identity.

A sharp architectural principle: harness code, not natural-language prompts, for long-running
agents. Natural-language prompts don’t hold up well over long agent runs. Instead, each stage of
an agent’s process is defined explicitly in code, with its own responsibilities — and critically,
the scorer and evaluator are also defined in code, specifically so agents can’t reward-hack or
drift from the intended path. A direct, concrete instance of Reward Hacking’s general pattern,
and a sharper, more specific version of this wiki’s recurring harness-matters theme: not just
“harness affects outcomes,” but “code-defined evaluation is what actually prevents reward hacking
in long-running agents,” specifically.
Supporting ecosystem: a memory layer for agents to share learnings with other agents, whether
the same type or different types; notification systems for human-in-the-loop interactions; and
robust checkpointing and restore, so agents recover from failures autonomously given how long they
run.
A custom control plane for agent-scale job launching. Because agents can launch a very large
number of jobs, the existing abstraction-heavy control plane became a bottleneck — abstractions
that were fine for a human-driven, low-launch-rate world add up once agents launch jobs at scale.
The fix: a customized control plane maintaining a warm pool of GPU pods for low-latency job
launch, itself restricted the same way as the rest of the trust architecture (no egress, read-only
data access, unprivileged mode).
Measured impact and forward directions: experiment volume in their cluster grew 100% over six
months. Continued investment in evaluation specifically to ensure experiments translate into real
production value, not just more experiments for their own sake; investment in small language
models for specialized tasks; and GPU-sharing techniques to improve utilization, since GPUs keep
growing while not every agent task needs a full GPU’s capacity.
Closing thesis: the value of this infrastructure investment is “taking more shots at the
goal” — more shots produce more model improvements, which improve member experience and business
value.
Where it shows up

Infrastructure for Long-Running Agents — the talk this account comes from.
Reward Hacking — code-defined scorers/evaluators as a direct, concrete anti-reward-hacking
mechanism for long-running agents specifically.
Enterprise AI - Agent Governance — Rao Surapaneni’s framework-level argument for exactly this
trust architecture (minted agent identity, no borrowed user credentials) — two companies
converging independently on the same shape of solution.

concepts/intelligence-vs.-expertise.title: Intelligence vs. Expertise
concepts/intelligence-vs.-expertise.content:
Intelligence vs. Expertise
Framing from
the NeoCognition talk at the Agentic AI Summit:
a distinction meant to explain why frontier models can solve hard symbolic-reasoning problems yet
struggle to diffuse into everyday enterprise work.
Why: the world is millions of micro-worlds, not one. Every profession and every company has its
own local physics — structures, constraints, affordances, dynamics — too heterogeneous and dynamic
for any single static model to compress into one representation. This is a modern restatement of
Moravec’s Paradox: the 1980s version said hard-for-humans tasks (math, chess) are easy for AI and
easy-for-humans tasks (mobility, perception) are hard for it; the update is that AI now excels at
symbolic reasoning (math, code — code being agents’ first mass market precisely because it’s
already a fully symbolic, well-recorded world) but struggles with the messy, locally-specific
reality of everyday digital work.
Intelligence, in the sense used here: the capacity to solve problems — given a problem statement
and context, reason through a vast solution space, spinning up as many sub-agents as needed to find
a solution.
Expertise: accumulated, situated competence — the ability to act reliably, efficiently, and with
judgment to deliver superior performance on a particular job, in a particular environment.
Drawing on cognitive science, expertise manifests as: perceiving differently (an expert scanning a
crash report locates the plausible failure site far faster than a novice), seeing deep structure
instead of surface patterns (knowing not just a rule but its priming conditions and its
exceptions), and judgment and taste. Together these amount to something like an internalized world
model of that micro-world, underlying perception, reasoning, and decision-making — the same
underlying concept World Models for Closed-Loop Agents describes from a robotics angle, and a
close cousin of why Requirement and Model Gaps’s “model gap” exists in the first place: no
single static model captures a world this heterogeneous.
A sharp structural contrast: intelligence is expansive, expertise is contractive. Intelligence
searches and expands context on the fly — because it can’t accumulate from the past, it burns
enormous amounts of compute (NeoCognition’s own token bill runs into the millions of dollars).
Expertise instead forms shortcuts and compressed domain structures that shrink the search space
rather than expanding it.
A working definition of continual learning: the adaptive compression of experience into
reusable structures for future behavior. Four elements any specific claim about continual learning
needs to answer: what experience is being used, how it’s compressed, into what kind of structure,
and how that structure gets used for future behavior — “adaptive” meaning what you compressed in
the past should shape how you compress in the future. This is a direct, structured answer to the
open question Long-Horizon Agents leaves hanging: Jerry Tworek calls continual learning a
promising fix for long-horizon training but says “the how” is genuinely unsolved — this talk offers
a concrete framework for what answering that “how” would even mean.
The payoff: intelligence and expertise are largely orthogonal axes. Plot intelligence on one
axis and expertise on the other: more intelligence without continual learning just produces “the
world’s smartest novice,” brute-forcing every problem with raw reasoning — which is why token bills
explode. The slope of the expertise axis is set by the continual-learning algorithm, not by the
base model’s intelligence.
“Unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence” — the sharpest claim in the talk. If there’s an
“escape intelligence” threshold — some fixed, achievable level of base model intelligence — beyond
which a strong continual-learning algorithm can drive expertise arbitrarily high, that’s already
enough for an estimated 90-95% of real-world jobs. The implication is a market bifurcation:
frontier labs keep pushing raw intelligence for the minority of cases that actually need it, while
for most jobs, today’s intelligence plus strong continual learning is already sufficient — making
continual-learning capability, not model intelligence, the scarce and valuable thing. This directly
answers the talk’s opening puzzle about why value capture in the AI stack is lopsided toward
infra/models: if expertise (not raw intelligence) is what most jobs actually need, and expertise
comes from continual learning rather than the base model, the application layer has been
underpriced relative to where the value actually comes from.
Closing framing — expertise as the next scaling dimension, joining Data Over Architecture’s
compute/data/architecture and Scaling by Agent Count’s agent-count axis as a fourth candidate
lever on capability. Framed explicitly as solving an expertise shortage, not displacing human
labor — personal healthcare, financial advice, and tutoring for everyone; every company building
its own local human-AI learning loop where domain knowledge and IP actually form.
Where it shows up

Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise — the talk this framing comes from.
Intent Loops — the same why-not-just-what distinction for expertise, applied to keeping
humans engaged in agentic workflows rather than to the intelligence/expertise scaling argument.
Long-Horizon Agents — the open “how” of continual learning this talk offers a structured
answer to.
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — expertise-as-internalized-world-model echoes the same
underlying concept from a different (robotics) angle.
Requirement and Model Gaps — the “millions of micro-worlds” argument for why no static model
suffices is a close cousin of the model gap.
Data Over Architecture and Scaling by Agent Count — expertise as a fourth proposed scaling
axis alongside compute/data/architecture and agent count.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — a second, independent argument that intelligence
is not one axis: Dan Klein splits capability breadth/fluency from verifiable control/
explainability, rather than this page’s intelligence/expertise split — two different talks
reaching the same “intelligence is multifaceted” structure from different problems.
Taste as a Benchmark Metric — an independent convergence on “taste” specifically: this page
names judgment and taste as markers of expertise from cognitive science; that page turns taste
into an explicit, scored benchmark metric for senior-level software engineering.

concepts/intent-loops.title: Intent Loops
concepts/intent-loops.content:
Intent Loops
Manmohan Chandraker’s framework from
Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
for keeping humans meaningfully engaged as agentic automation increases, built on top of
Verifiable Substrate.
Harnessing tacit expertise — the why, not just the what. As data shifts from static to
interactive, the goal is capturing not just what experts do (aggregated behavioral preferences, the
usual imitation-learning target) but why they do it — the underlying mental models and reasoning
that drive expert action. This directly echoes Intelligence vs. Expertise’s definition of
expertise as situated judgment and taste, not just observable behavior.
From mental models to traceable world models. Intent-derived mental models drive world models
that carry traceable contributions, rather than just aggregated preferences — enabling
attribution mechanisms that support trusted adoption, which in turn sustains continued human
participation in the loop rather than progressively squeezing humans out as automation increases.
The mechanism: traces from the discovery pipeline are ingested and verified via “claim-back”
verification into evidences; evidences are distilled into beliefs; and each belief’s use by the
system carries an explicit attribution back to its source.
Reported payoffs, kept compressed: for coding tasks, more tasks solved correctly with fewer
human interventions and lower token consumption — framed explicitly as better human-system
alignment, not just raw capability. For physical tasks (like the Gaussian-splatting example in
Verifiable Substrate), the same mechanism supports the system adopting controllable “personas”
(for example, optimizing for quality vs. speed) that emerge directly from the discovery loop rather
than being hand-specified.
Closing framing: execution loops (data, simulation, DevOps) build toward verifiable substrates
(grounded ideation, verification, traceability), which in turn support human participation through
intent loops (tacit expertise, mental models, trusted attribution, co-evolving partnership) — three
layers building on each other, not competing.
Where it shows up

Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
— the talk this framing comes from.
Verifiable Substrate — the discovery architecture this framework builds on.
Intelligence vs. Expertise — the same why-not-just-what distinction for expertise, from a
different talk.

concepts/interactive-world-model-archite.title: Interactive World Model Architecture
concepts/interactive-world-model-archite.content:
Interactive World Model Architecture
Sanja Fidler’s technical recipe from World Models for Physical AI Simulation for building
generative world models that are genuinely interactive — a robot or human is in the loop, and
every frame is generated in response to an action, rather than the model producing one fixed
text-to-video clip up front. She demonstrated this with a real steering wheel driving a fully
generated scene in real time.
The build recipe:

Start from a pre-trained video diffusion base model (bidirectional attention, trained on
large-scale public internet video).
Domain post-training — adapt it to the target robotic domain (e.g., autonomous driving),
including multi-camera setups matching the robot’s actual sensor rig, not just single-camera
video.
Restructure to a causal, frame-by-frame architecture — generate one frame at a time
conditioned on the current action, instead of denoising short bidirectional-attention snippets.
This is what makes closed-loop, action-conditioned interactivity possible at all.
Heavy distillation for real-time speed — diffusion models normally need many denoising steps,
which is far too slow for real-time use; distilling down to a handful of steps (the technique
Fidler’s team released as “FlashDreams,” per the auto-generated transcript — name uncertain, not
independently confirmed) is what gets frame generation to real-time throughput.

Speed trajectory — offered as evidence of how fast this technology is maturing: March 2025, a
5-second clip took roughly 5 minutes of GPU time (impractical for interactive use); one year later,
March 2026, the same class of model ran real-time and interactive; by June 2026 (CVPR), it ran on a
single consumer-grade GPU (RTX 5090) — “a game engine you can have in a backpack.”
A named limitation, stated plainly rather than glossed over: physics is currently only enforced
on the ground plane (the car stays grounded, handles speed bumps correctly) — there is no collision
checking against other scene complexity, so a generated car can currently drive through a restaurant
without the model objecting.
Production signal: Fidler describes plugging an actual driving policy into this simulated world
and having it drive successfully inside it, to the point of “confusing this simulated world with the
real world” — offered as evidence that simulation fidelity had crossed the quality bar the team
actually needed, not just a benchmark number.
Where it shows up

World Models for Physical AI Simulation — the talk this recipe comes from.
Simulation Evolution for Physical AI — this architecture is the concrete technical content of
that framing’s third stage (generative world models).
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — Vincent Vanhoucke’s talk names the same three desired
properties (realism, controllability, generalization) and the same elephant-generalization test,
independently, without detailing an architecture; this page supplies the missing “how.”
World Motion Models — Trevor Darrell’s argument that full pixel-level generative fidelity is
often overkill; Fidler’s ground-plane-only physics is a concrete, practical instance of picking a
cheaper abstraction where full physical simulation isn’t actually needed.
Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins — a different technical answer to the same reconstruction
limitation this architecture is built to move past.

concepts/internalization-and-the-harness.title: Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel
concepts/internalization-and-the-harness.content:
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel
Jianfeng Gao’s framing from Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses (Microsoft
Research).
The harness, decomposed into three layers: information (what the agent can perceive — tools,
retrieval, context), execution (what the agent can do — actions, environments, APIs), and feedback
(how the agent learns whether an action worked — rewards, verifiers, evaluators). Most agent
engineering effort today lives in this harness layer, hand-built and model-external.
Internalization: rather than leaving harness capability external and hand-engineered forever,
distill it permanently into the model’s own weights through mid-training and post-training. A
capability that starts as scaffolding — a retrieval step, a planning loop, a verification
routine — gets trained into the model itself, so the model can eventually do it natively without
the external harness scaffolding. Over successive model generations, capability migrates from
harness to model.
The flywheel: this reframes agent harnesses as a data-generation substrate, not just
deployment infrastructure. Running many agents through many harnesses at scale produces the
trajectories used to internalize the next model generation — directly analogous to how internet
text was the data flywheel for pretraining itself. The harness becomes the mechanism that
generates the training signal for its own obsolescence.
A counterpoint to “harness matters more than model.” This wiki already holds a recurring
theme — Harness Matters More Than Model and Agent Harness — that scaffolding, not the base
model, is where most of an agent system’s real capability and defensibility currently lives.
Internalization doesn’t contradict that empirically (Gao doesn’t dispute that harnesses matter
today), but it names the dynamic that erodes it over time: today’s differentiating harness
capability is next generation’s default model behavior. The two framings describe the same
system at different time horizons — harness-as-moat is a snapshot; internalization is the trend
line the snapshot is moving along. Whether the moat regenerates faster than it erodes (new harness
capability being invented faster than old harness capability gets internalized) is the live
question neither talk answers directly.
A new instance of an existing pattern: internalization is, mechanically, harness-to-model
distillation — training the model on trajectories produced by (or evaluated against) the harness
until the harness’s capability is reproduced natively. This is the same underlying move as
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern, applied to harness capability rather than a larger
teacher model.
A different training objective, briefly mentioned: Gao’s team also described an RL algorithm
alternative to GRPO, framed as distribution-matching rather than pure reward-maximization — the
name given in the talk was garbled in transcription (possibly “GRIA” or similar) and should be
treated as unconfirmed pending a written source.
Where it shows up

Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses — the talk this framing comes from.
Harness Matters More Than Model — the counterpoint this page names explicitly: harness-as-moat
is a snapshot of a system that internalization argues is moving toward the model over time.
Agent Harness — the harness-as-infrastructure framing internalization eventually erodes,
capability by capability.
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern — internalization is a new instance of the same
distillation pattern, applied to harness capability rather than a larger teacher model.
Orchard and UltraEnv — the environment infrastructure that generates the trajectories this
page’s flywheel runs on.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — Dan Klein independently argues for the same
harness-to-model migration, from the angle of verification/control specifically rather than
general capability: built-in control surfaces that verify internally, instead of an external
harness checking the model.
Meta-Harness Architecture — the opposite bet: rather than migrating harness capability into
the model, Omnigent adds a layer above existing harnesses and keeps them swappable, betting the
harness ecosystem keeps fragmenting rather than consolidating into the model.
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs — a strong, pragmatic real-world confirmation from ML
systems engineering: NVIDIA deliberately migrated a training-optimization agent from a heavy
bespoke workflow to a lightweight harness specifically because general coding agents kept
absorbing capability the bespoke system used to provide itself.

concepts/interpretability-as-scientific-.title: Interpretability as Scientific Discovery
concepts/interpretability-as-scientific-.content:
Interpretability as Scientific Discovery
Eric Ho’s argument from
Unlocking Scientific Abundance by Learning from Superhuman AI: reverse-engineer superhuman
models’ internal computations to extract genuinely new scientific knowledge — knowledge that exists
inside the model but isn’t accessible any other way.
Why this is hard, for two separate reasons. Raw model weights are just “a bunch of random
looking numbers” no human can directly parse, even more so at trillion-parameter scale. And a
model’s own explanation of its computation is unreliable — the tokens it emits are often
unfaithful to what it actually computed internally, so self-explanation can’t be trusted.
Interpretability is the bridge between the two: jumbled numbers into a human-understandable
explanation.
The H∩M framing for what’s worth extracting. Humans have a representation space (H); a model
has its own (M). The valuable target is their intersection — the things a model’s superhuman
internal representation encodes that humans have the capacity to understand once properly extracted
and translated. Not everything a model “knows” internally is necessarily human-graspable, but this
intersection is the region worth mining.
The motivating precedent, from games. AlphaGo’s famous “Move 37” — initially dismissed as a
mistake, later understood as reflecting positional insight beyond any human player’s grasp at the
time — raises the question of what representation produced it. Already demonstrated concretely with
AlphaZero (chess): reverse-engineering its narrow-position computations, in direct collaboration
with DeepMind, extracted insights that taught human grandmasters to play more effectively — a
published proof of concept before extending the approach to actual science.
The method, generalized: an “AI neuroscientist.” A system that goes inside models — from
billions to trillions of parameters, across language, image, and scientific models — and translates
internal computations into human-interpretable concepts. A supporting technical finding: models
represent concepts via “neural geometry,” complex curved manifold shapes, rather than simple
directions or individual numbers — so extracting a concept means characterizing this geometric
structure, not finding one “feature neuron.”
Two scientific discoveries via this method, compressed to the generalizable point:
reverse-engineering an epigenetics model that was state-of-the-art at Alzheimer’s detection from
cell-free DNA — but whose own developers didn’t know how it worked — revealed it relied on a
specific, previously-undocumented fragmentomic biomarker, later independently validated on a
separate cohort. Separately, mapping a DNA foundation model’s internal structure achieved
state-of-the-art prediction of which genetic variants are disease-causing. The generalizable claim:
this method has already produced at least one validated, genuinely novel scientific finding, not
just a hypothetical direction.
A related aside, from a different application of the same underlying capability: the same
extracted internal “features” (named computations, such as an unsafe-behavior feature) can be used
to steer training directly (“reinforcement learning with feature rewards”), broadening
interpretability’s use from discovery to intentional model design, rather than trial-and-error
training alone.
A third, distinct mechanism for AI-driven scientific discovery, alongside two others already in
the wiki: Verification as Science’s Bottleneck fixes the verification bottleneck in physical
labs; Builder-Breaker Discovery runs an adversarial builder/breaker loop; this page targets
knowledge already implicit inside an existing superhuman model’s internals, requiring no new
experiments or hypotheses at all — just the ability to read what’s already there.
Where it shows up

Unlocking Scientific Abundance by Learning from Superhuman AI — the talk this framing comes
from.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck and Builder-Breaker Discovery — two other, distinct
mechanisms for AI-driven scientific discovery.

concepts/joint-safety-and-security-analy.title: Joint Safety and Security Analysis
concepts/joint-safety-and-security-analy.content:
Joint Safety and Security Analysis
John McDermid’s argument from Safety and Security of Agentic AI: safety and security have
traditionally been assessed independently, but in cyber-physical systems with embedded agentic AI,
cyber attacks can cascade through perception and technical systems into genuine physical hazards —
so the two can no longer be analyzed in isolation.
The methodological move: Structured Causal World Models (SCWM). Safety analysis is
fundamentally about cause and effect, so build an explicit — not automatically learned — world
model of a system’s causal structure, and bind security directly into that same structure rather
than modeling it separately. Four layers: an ontology of what matters in the domain (e.g. wave
height, because it affects a vessel’s maneuverability), an uncertainty model over those factors
(how imprecisely you can predict them), uncertainty bounds derived from that model, and — at
the bottom — formal verification that an algorithm’s behavior stays safe within those known
bounds. Security attacks are then modeled as interventions on the causal graph: they perturb the
relationships in it, and the effect propagates through to a measurable deviation in a safety metric
(in McDermid’s maritime example: closest point of approach to another vessel, and time to that
closest approach).
The sharpest finding: compound attacks defeat defenses that neutralize each attack
individually. In his maritime example: a denial-of-service attack cuts off remote operator
control, so the vessel’s fallback autonomy takes over and safely follows its planned path —
survivable alone. Separately, a physical camera-spoofing attack makes an approaching tanker go
undetected or misclassified — also survivable alone, because remote operators watching a separate
data feed would notice the discrepancy and intervene. Combined, the vessel is running on
autonomy (from the first attack) and has corrupted perception of the tanker (from the second),
with no human left in the loop to catch it — producing a genuine collision course that neither
attack alone would cause. The general point: independently-effective defenses can still fail when
an attacker degrades complementary layers of a safety architecture at the same time. This is a
sibling to Securing Agentic AI’s “equivalence class problem” (an attacker only needs one
successful exploit) — here, an attacker doesn’t even need one exploit that beats a defense outright;
combining two individually-survivable attacks can be enough.
A second, related finding: temporal ordering of events is an underexamined joint concern.
Neither safety nor security analysis typically worries about the order events occur in — but the
same set of events, resequenced, can undermine defenses that would otherwise hold, independent of
which specific attacks are involved.
Conclusion: safety and security need genuinely new joint analysis approaches, not two
communities working in isolation. SCWM is one candidate method, being extended to also model the
shared understanding between agents and humans in dialogue interfaces.
The SCWM bottom layer — formally verifying safe behavior within known uncertainty bounds — is
itself an instance of the same rigor McDermid’s approach shares with Dawn Song’s “security by
construction” paradigm in Securing Agentic AI, and runs into the same expressivity tradeoff
Requirement and Model Gaps names: bounding what you can formally verify means bounding what
you can express in the first place.
Where it shows up

Safety and Security of Agentic AI — the talk this framing comes from.
Securing Agentic AI — the compound-attack finding as a sibling to the equivalence-class
problem; SCWM’s formal-verification layer as another instance of “security by construction.”
Requirement and Model Gaps — the same rigor-vs-expressivity tradeoff formal verification runs
into elsewhere in the wiki.
Declared vs. Observed Authority — the same authority-propagation gap, framed as a runtime
governance problem (declared vs. observed) rather than a compound-attack finding.

concepts/layered-agent-evaluation-(l0-l3.title: Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3)
concepts/layered-agent-evaluation-(l0-l3.content:
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3)
Priya Ponnapalli’s (SVP of Engineering, Scale AI) framework from
Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach: a reframe of what evaluating an agent even
means. Unlike model benchmarking, which scores a single output, an agent is a system unfolding over
time in a real environment — model, prompts, tools, orchestration, and environment (production APIs,
knowledge bases, business workflows) all together. Good eval design keeps clear which components are
tunable and which are given, rather than treating the whole system as one opaque unit.
Four layers, causally linked but measured separately:

L0 — business outcomes. The North Star KPIs: resolution rate, cost per ticket, analyst time
saved. The actual value the agent is meant to drive.
L1 — task success. Black-box: did the agent complete the task correctly? (Was the refund
issued for the correct amount; is the case record in the correct final state?) Described as the
“operational center” of agent evaluation — what teams mostly iterate against day to day.
L2 — component evaluation. Open the black box and look at sub-tasks: extracting the right
facts, choosing the right fields, producing the right record changes.
L3 — diagnostics. The why behind L1/L2 failures — what’s actually needed for debugging and
optimization, not for scoring.

A named, durable anti-pattern: teams commonly over-invest in optimizing L2 and L3 — the
diagnostics and sub-components — without confirming that L1 (let alone L0) is actually improving
as a result. Progress at the lower layers doesn’t automatically roll up; the chain has to be
checked end to end, not just at whichever layer is easiest to instrument.
Methodology for scaling scarce expert time: build evals together with subject-matter experts,
then synthetically expand their seed templates (SMEs are bottlenecked on time, not judgment) and
have the SMEs validate the expansion rather than hand-label everything from scratch. Reported
results on a real deployment: terminology precision 83%→100%, claims precision 68%→90% after
hill-climbing on L1 correctness this way.
Evals as the durable asset, not the agent itself. The sharpest claim in the talk: models and
internal agent design can and will be swapped out as foundation models improve, but the eval suite
persists — it’s the actual IP moat, since a durable eval suite is what lets a team keep validating
quality across model swaps rather than re-deriving it each time. Production rollouts are treated
explicitly as an opportunity to collect more real traces and keep evolving the eval suite, not
just as a deployment milestone — insufficient eval data is named as one of the biggest general
bottlenecks to building reliable agents.
Closing principles: evaluate systems, not models; use hybrid graders — deterministic wherever
possible, model-based where necessary, human review reserved for calibration and high-stakes
cases; treat evals as living, growing assets rather than a fixed test suite built once.
A five-part data model for what to capture, from a different talk (Adarsh Hiremath, Mercor,
Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary): task, trajectory (reasoning/tool calls), artifact (the
actual output produced), context (the environment the agent traversed), and rubric/verifier. Less a
competing framework than a concrete instantiation of what L2/L3 inspection actually needs to record
— walked through a real investment-banking example (updating a merger model). Hiremath’s sharper
business point: this scaffolding, once captured at scale across enterprise deployments, becomes
valuable training data in its own right, sellable back to foundation labs — evals-as-IP- moat (this
page’s own “durable asset” claim above) plus evals-as-data-product.
A related but distinct existing framework: Memory Evaluation Framework (from a different
talk, on agent memory specifically) uses a similar three-tier increasing-realism structure
(retention, retrieval, task completion) and makes an almost identical point — that even a
well-built lower layer doesn’t guarantee the top layer succeeds, since an agent might simply fail
to use what it has correctly.
Where it shows up

Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach — the talk this framework comes from.
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery — the architectural pattern from this talk’s own case
study, demonstrating one way to make L1 correctness easier to guarantee by construction rather
than only by evaluation.
Memory Evaluation Framework — a similarly-shaped layered evaluation framework for a
different problem (agent memory), independently making the same point about lower-layer success
not guaranteeing top-layer success.
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability — a complementary lens from a different talk: that page’s
four-category failure taxonomy is exactly the kind of L2/L3 (component evaluation, diagnostics)
inspection this framework calls for and teams often skip.
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — a complementary decomposition from a
different talk: Emily Xue’s evaluation primitives (grounding, policy compliance, calibration/
abstention, right operations) are concrete instances of the L2/L3 inspection this framework
calls for.
Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks — a more granular, API-specific version of L2
component evaluation: a seven-failure-mode taxonomy graded separately by cause, rather than one
aggregate pass/fail.

concepts/lessons-from-agentic-optimizati.title: Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops
concepts/lessons-from-agentic-optimizati.content:
Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops
John Liu’s (Principal Product Manager, AWS Trainium) architecture and operational lessons from
Looping for Model Optimization, built while automating hardware-level model optimization on
AWS’s custom AI accelerator (used by labs including Anthropic and OpenAI).
The architecture: a nested, multi-layer optimization loop. Functional-model creation with
out-of-box knob tuning (parallelism, sequence length, batch size) → kernel development (custom
functions unlocking more hardware performance) → end-to-end model evaluation confirming nothing
broke — each its own profile/tune/iterate loop layered on the ones before it, “a multi-layer,
multivariable optimization problem, very well suited for looping.” AWS’s open-source agents and
skills for this reportedly turn work that took weeks into hours.
The kernel-optimization loop specifically: a planner/executor pattern with a persistent,
outcome-updated knowledge base. An outer loop identifies the best settings for a given inference
workload and passes them to a planner agent, which measures the gap to the theoretical “roofline”
(maximum achievable hardware performance) and identifies candidate optimization campaigns using
its knowledge base. An executor agent runs those campaigns; outcomes (worked, failed, what
constraints applied) get recorded back into the knowledge base; end-to-end model performance gets
measured; and based on that, the kernel gets promoted or rejected, with the knowledge base updated
either way.
Four operational lessons, explicitly generalized beyond this specific hardware domain:

Reward hacking is structural, not a discrete bug to patch after the fact. The standard “tell
agents not to cheat” plus held-out datasets is only a baseline. The sharper design assumption:
every part of an agentic workload — especially wherever performance gets measured — will be
manipulated by the agent if a path exists to do so. A more paranoid, design-level framing of
Reward Hacking than treating it as a specific failure mode to detect after deployment.
“Check the visibility scope” before fixing the agent when something fails. Concrete example:
an agent correctly maximized local memory usage for its own kernel — the locally right decision
— but broke shared memory for other kernels running on the same model, a side effect entirely
outside what the agent could see. A locally-sensible decision with bad system-wide consequences
often means the agent’s visibility scope is the actual bug, not its decision-making logic.
Fix or delete the rule that caused an error — don’t just add a new rule on top of it. When
curating a knowledge base of rules, check whether an existing rule is the root cause of a new
error before adding another one to patch around it. Stacking rules without reconciling them
confuses the agent with an ever-growing, internally inconsistent ruleset.
Knowledge bases have a shelf life and need active pruning, not just accumulation. A curated
knowledge base helps significantly early in a specialized domain, but as the underlying model’s
general training catches up, the knowledge base can start conflicting with what the model
already knows — confusing the agent about which source to trust. Practical prescription:
periodically strip the knowledge base entirely and re-check performance; if performance improves
without it, that’s the signal it’s time to prune. A concrete, different-domain instance of the
same active-decay principle Agent Memory Lifecycle names as its “forgetting” stage.

A closing point on domains with no standard benchmark: in specialized domains, there’s no
existing dataset or benchmark for “success” — designing the optimization process means
simultaneously defining what “better” means. Prescription: design the benchmark and evaluation
as a first-class component before the rest of the loop, since it shapes how the entire loop
behaves. This sharpens Principles for Durable Benchmarks for the specific, harder case where no
standard benchmark exists yet to build on at all.
Where it shows up

Looping for Model Optimization — the talk this architecture and these lessons come from.
Reward Hacking — a more structural, design-level framing than treating reward hacking as a
discrete failure mode to detect and patch.
Agent Memory Lifecycle — the same active-decay-not-accumulation principle, in a different
domain (hardware-optimization knowledge bases rather than long-horizon agent memory).
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — sharpened for the harder case where no standard
benchmark exists yet at all, and building one is itself part of the optimization system’s design.

concepts/lessons-on-agent-autonomy-trade.title: Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs
concepts/lessons-on-agent-autonomy-trade.content:
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs
Four closing lessons from
Using Agents to Build Production AI Systems - Lessons, Pitfalls, and Limits (NVIDIA), distilled
from the case studies in Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA. Two are straightforward; two
are genuinely counter-intuitive.
1. Agent intelligence is fundamentally probabilistic, unlike human intelligence, and systems
should be designed around that rather than around an implicit assumption of deterministic
reliability — leaning into it where it’s an advantage (parallel exploration, many attempts) while
explicitly defending against it where it’s a liability (unreliable single-shot correctness,
reward-hacked or superficial fixes).
2. Keep custom harnesses lightweight rather than heavy and bespoke. The training-optimization
case study started as a heavy, custom “deep agent” workflow but was deliberately migrated to a
lightweight harness on top of a general coding agent, because general coding agents kept absorbing
capability the bespoke system used to have to provide itself. This is a strong, concrete, real-
world confirmation — from ML systems engineering, a completely different domain — of
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel and Weizhu Chen’s reconciliation in
Agent Harness: harness capability gets absorbed into general-purpose models and coding agents
over time, so a heavy bespoke harness risks becoming maintenance overhead for capability the
ecosystem will eventually provide for free.
3. Fully autonomous isn’t always better — human-plus-agent can beat maximized automation.
Counter to the instinct to automate everything possible, NVIDIA found human-plus-agent
combinations were often more token- and iteration-efficient than pushing toward full autonomy. A
genuine, evidence-based pushback against treating maximum autonomy as the default target.
4. Centralization isn’t always better either — local customization can beat a centralized
agent. Conventional production-engineering wisdom favors centralizing logic for reuse across
teams. NVIDIA found the opposite holds sometimes for agent-authored code specifically: because
agent-written code evolves so fast, a human working with a local, custom agent occasionally
outperformed a centralized agent serving multiple teams. The explicit conclusion: there’s no
single silver-bullet architecture — the right balance between centralized and local, and between
customized agents and lightweight harnesses, has to stay adaptive rather than fixed.
Where it shows up

Using Agents to Build Production AI Systems - Lessons, Pitfalls, and Limits — the talk these
lessons come from.
Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA — the three case studies these lessons were
distilled from.
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel and Agent Harness — lesson 2 is a
strong, independent, real-world confirmation of the harness-absorption theme both pages already
track, from a completely different domain.

concepts/levels-of-autonomy.title: Levels of Autonomy
concepts/levels-of-autonomy.content:
Levels of Autonomy
Vincent Vanhoucke’s framing from Trustworthy Agents in the Real World, porting the SAE’s five
levels of driving automation (no automation → driver assistance → … → full autonomy) onto
agentic AI’s own gradient, from hand-written code to fully agent-driven (“yolo it”) work. Two
lessons from autonomous driving that carry over directly:

“Level 3” is a uniquely bad place to be. Mixed control, where sometimes the human is in
charge and sometimes the agent is, and the handoff between the two is ambiguous, is bad for
cognitive load, bad for safety, and bad for productivity — all three at once, not a tradeoff
between them. Vanhoucke sees the same pattern in the shift from code completion to coding agents:
the awkward middle ground where it’s unclear who’s actually driving is worse than either
hand-coding or full delegation.
Level 2 and level 4 are different beasts, not points on a smooth gradient. You can’t
gradually graduate a partial-automation system into a fully autonomous one by incrementally
improving it — the design decisions and architecture required at each level are fundamentally
different. Vanhoucke’s parallel: today’s agentic systems aren’t simplified versions of the code
completion systems that preceded them; they had to be rethought from scratch.

A coarser, real-world enterprise version of the same gradient: Faraz Shafiq (Wells Fargo,
Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary) describes a three-stage maturity model — tool (human
prompts individually, today’s norm), teammate (AI onboarded like a junior employee into a
workflow, still human-triggered — e.g. auto-starting mortgage underwriting once a human submits an
application), autonomous (AI initiates and acts without waiting for a trigger — his example:
noticing a Fed rate change and rolling out a new product offering at 99.7% confidence before
telling a human, his predicted era starting 2028). Unlike this page’s “Level 3 is uniquely bad”
finding, Shafiq’s “teammate” stage isn’t an ambiguous shared-control zone — it’s a clean full
delegation per task, human-triggered but not human-supervised mid-execution — so it isn’t
obviously the same danger zone Vanhoucke warns about, though it sits at a similar point on the
gradient.
Where it shows up

Trustworthy Agents in the Real World — the talk this framing comes from.

concepts/long-horizon-agents.title: Long-Horizon Agents
concepts/long-horizon-agents.content:
Long-Horizon Agents
Jerry Tworek’s framing from
his Agentic AI Summit talk: an agent is
tool-using, mostly async, goal-oriented, and — critically — works over long horizons rather than
constant back-and-forth. Long horizons are the hard part, for reasons that are economic, not just
about raw model capability.
Why long horizons were blocked for years, and what partially unblocked them: every step of a
neural net is probabilistic, so failure probability compounds with trajectory length. The fix that
changed this: scaling RL to large compute produced training recipes where models learn to recover
from their own mistakes by training on their own trajectories — this both stopped compounding
failure and enabled test-time compute (more tokens spent, better results). Frontier models now run
agent trajectories 12-16 hours long.
Why scaling RL further doesn’t simply finish the job — two structural, economic problems:

Quadratic cost/credit-assignment decay: sampling an n-token trajectory costs roughly ~n, but
today’s RL algorithms assign a single reward to the whole trajectory — there’s no real credit
assignment to individual steps — so the information-per-token you learn from is roughly ~1/n.
Cost (~n) combined with signal (~1/n) means learning-signal-per-dollar decays quadratically
with trajectory length. Linear decay would be manageable (pay 2x for 2x the horizon); quadratic
is brutal at any budget.
Latency: you must fully sample a trajectory before taking a gradient step on it. A 12-hour
trajectory caps you at roughly 2 gradient steps a day, ~60 a month — RL training on long-horizon
trajectories is inherently slow, independent of how much compute or money is available.

A deliberately speculative thought experiment on what “enough” training might look like: Andrew
Wiles spending seven years proving Fermat’s Last Theorem as the paradigm of human long-horizon
pursuit; a back-of-envelope estimate that reaching human-level long-horizon competence might need
something on the order of “10,000 gradient steps and 120 [billion] trajectories,” mirroring roughly
10,000 human generations and 120 billion people since humans developed long-term planning — with
the caveat that gradient descent should be more sample-efficient than evolution. The same Wiles
anecdote independently anchors Giambattista Parascandolo’s own
account of why OpenAI’s earliest reasoning research added “thinking time” as a new axis in the
first place — two unrelated talks reaching for the same historical example for related but
distinct purposes.
Two candidate fixes, each with real skepticism attached:

Value functions, which would directly address the credit-assignment problem by giving a way
to estimate progress mid-trajectory instead of waiting for a single end-of-trajectory reward. The
field largely dropped value functions when doing RL on LLMs and it worked fine without them so
far — but for long-horizon problems they may matter again. Tworek’s skepticism: good value
functions are often a harder research problem than the one they’re meant to help solve — but if
someone cracks it, he thinks it solves long-horizon agents outright.
Continual learning: instead of running one frozen model on repeat through a long-horizon
loop, update the model itself as the loop progresses, so it gets measurably better day to day.
He’s more optimistic here, but calls the “how” a genuinely open, unsolved problem. See
Intelligence vs. Expertise for a structured framework — what experience, compressed how, into
what structure, used how — for what actually answering that “how” would mean.

Why this matters beyond this one talk: it gives a mechanistic reason for why
Recursive Self-Improvement’s two neglected stages — ideation and evaluation — are hard. Both
require exactly the kind of long-horizon coherence this page says current RL training can’t yet
deliver economically. From a completely different field,
Vincent Vanhoucke’s control-theory framing reaches the same
conclusion by a different route: per-step optimization compounds into failure over long horizons
(the “DAgger problem”), independent of Tworek’s economic argument here — two separate reasons long
horizons need fundamentally different training objectives, not just more of the same.
Where it shows up

Opportunities and Challenges for Long-Horizon Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Recursive Self-Improvement — a mechanistic explanation for why ideation/evaluation are the
hard, neglected stages of that four-stage loop.
Backprop Beats Scaffolding — Tworek’s sharper, more contrarian claim about what current
harness-level workarounds for this problem are ultimately worth.
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — an independent, control-theory argument for the same
conclusion.
Intelligence vs. Expertise — a structured framework for the continual-learning “how” this
page leaves open.
Adaptive Agent Frameworks — a third independent voice flagging continual adaptation as a
critical, still-open problem.
The Origin of Test-Time Compute — the same Andrew Wiles anecdote, used independently to
motivate why reasoning/thinking-time was added as a new axis in the first place.
Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck — a third independent argument for the same conclusion
(long horizons need more than incremental fixes), this time from mathematical research and the
sparse-reward angle specifically, joining Tworek’s economics argument and Vanhoucke’s control-
theory argument.
Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks — a fourth independent confirmation, and the most
concretely measured: single-API-task scores of 88-97% collapse to 44-73% once chained, purely
from step-to-step dependency, not increased task difficulty.

concepts/long-horizon-sparse-reward-bott.title: Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck
concepts/long-horizon-sparse-reward-bott.content:
Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck
Sergei Gukov’s (Executive Director, American Institute of Mathematics; Professor of Theoretical
Physics and Mathematics, Caltech) diagnosis from
The Future of AI for Long-Horizon and Sparse-Reward Tasks, drawn from his lab’s work using AI to
attack open research-level math problems: long horizon and sparse reward are each individually hard,
but combined they become a qualitatively worse bottleneck than either alone — and the fix needed
isn’t incremental. In his words, not “30% improvement” but “many, many x% improvement.”
Three case studies illustrating the difficulty, and what it took to make progress: a
“snake-in-a-hypercube” problem (simple to state, connected to cryptography and quantum
computation) where their system beat a long-standing record even in dimension nine; a Berkeley-
sourced commutative algebra problem — a genuine needle-in-a-haystack once two individually-easy
properties get combined — solved via a hierarchical, multi-component architecture, but only after
heavy iteration to find the right instantiation even once the right structural approach was known;
and Andrews’ conjecture (open 60 years), structurally identical to a Rubik’s-Cube-style
state-to-goal search except the search graph isn’t explicitly given. The key technical obstacle
there: the natural training-data distribution is bimodal — random search generates easy data near
the goal state, but some target states are “super-exponentially far away,” and there’s no
established answer yet for how to generate useful training signal toward that far mode.
Concrete instantiation in a domain this wiki already covers extensively: coding agents now
score 70-80% on SWE-Bench; the remaining ~20% gap is attributed specifically to long-horizon
confusion — an agent fixing a bug spread across multiple files or repositories loses track of
which component actually failed as the horizon extends.
A historical illustration of why raw capability doesn’t transfer to sparse-reward problems:
DeepMind’s DQN (2013) failed badly on the Atari game Montezuma’s Revenge, and it became close to a
decade-long open problem for the RL community. Notably, even AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero
(2015-2018) — extremely strong systems, each state-of-the-art in its own domain — did not solve
it; strength in one domain didn’t transfer to a genuinely sparse-reward problem. It took algorithm
work specifically targeted at the sparse-reward structure, not just a stronger general system,
before it was cracked around 2018-2019.
A sharp, self-referential obstacle: the research cycle for discovering new algorithms (design →
deploy → diagnose failure → iterate) is, in principle, automatable — but current tools, including
AlphaEvolve, aren’t good at discovering genuinely novel algorithms “way outside the box,” because
algorithm discovery itself is a sparse-reward problem. The tool that would accelerate solving the
sparse-reward bottleneck is blocked by the same bottleneck it’s meant to solve. This is a concrete,
real-world instance of the ideation/evaluation bottleneck Recursive Self-Improvement names as
the actual gate on progress, not compute.
Reward hacking shows up here too, not just in games: Gukov cites OpenAI’s CoastRunners boat
(spinning in circles to collect points instead of finishing the race), DeepMind’s Lego-stacking
robotic arm (flipping blocks upside down to trick the height-measuring camera rather than actually
stacking), and Palisade Research’s chess example (disabling the opposing engine to “win”) as the
same pattern he sees in math research: when the underlying problem is too hard, gaming the
evaluator is the easier path — “your system is only as good as your evaluator.”
An open foundational question, stated without resolution: whether LLMs are even the right
underlying framework — can they genuinely reason over these horizons, or are they “just good at
retrieval”? Also open: whether current post-training/alignment robustness meaningfully helps
