Declared vs. Observed Authority — a mechanistic answer to the theoretical problem this page
names: Thales’s runtime trust plane, comparing declared authority against observed behavior,
only makes sense once you accept the Good Regulator Theorem’s premise — that governing
delegation requires an actual model of what the delegate is doing, not just a policy document
describing what it’s supposed to do.
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — Emily Xue’s oversight-policy and human-
review-surface framework is the operational answer this page’s theoretical argument calls for:
accountability requires a specific, designed point where a human with a good-enough model signs
off before deployment.

concepts/the-origin-of-test-time-compute.title: The Origin of Test-Time Compute
concepts/the-origin-of-test-time-compute.content:
The Origin of Test-Time Compute
Giambattista Parascandolo’s historical account, from
When Language Models Learned to Reason, of the earliest reasoning research at OpenAI.
The motivating picture: a wheel of subject × difficulty. Imagine a colorful wheel — angle =
subject (math, physics, biology, and so on), radial distance from the center = difficulty.
Pretraining scaling (GPT-2 → GPT-3 → GPT-4) expanded this circle outward from the middle across all
subjects at once, solving progressively harder problems as it grew. The open question at the time:
would this process ever reach the hardest problems sitting at the very edge?
The Andrew Wiles anecdote as the motivating intuition — independently used for a related but
distinct purpose in Jerry Tworek’s own talk: Wiles spent seven years
solving Fermat’s Last Theorem, not because he could solve everything, but because even one truly
hard problem can demand years of sustained, focused work. Spreading capability broadly across
subjects at moderate difficulty — what pretraining does — seemed unlikely to naturally produce that
kind of prolonged, single-problem focus.
The conceptual move: adding “thinking time” as a genuinely new third axis, orthogonal to
subject and difficulty — tilting the wheel into 3D and asking whether capability could expand along
a time axis instead of just across the subject/difficulty plane. This is the literal origin of
what the field now calls test-time compute.
The initial obstacle: at the time, simply giving a model more wall-clock time produced the
exact same answer — it computed a response in milliseconds regardless and had no mechanism to use
extra time productively. Reasoning had to be actively elicited as a behavior, not assumed to emerge
from idle compute. A practical constraint of the era: context windows were only a few thousand
tokens, mechanically capping “thinking” at a few seconds’ worth of text.
An open substrate question, resolved empirically: should reasoning happen in a recurrent
network doing internal steps, or something else? Plain text — what became chain-of-thought — turned
out to work well, meaning reasoning didn’t need a new computational substrate, just eliciting a
specific behavioral pattern from the existing architecture.
The discovery process — just asking the model to think, with zero training for it.
Parascandolo’s own first project at OpenAI: prompting an untrained-for-this GPT-3 to “think about
it” before answering. Illustrative examples from the era: a simple word-arithmetic problem GPT-3
got flatly wrong until prompted to reason first; a musical-instrument-counting problem fixed by
breaking it into steps; a counting problem where the correct answer’s raw probability, measured
directly, was 2% under direct prompting and rose substantially once the model was prompted to
enumerate its work.
The quantitative payoff — the first “more thinking → higher accuracy” plots. As increasingly
explicit instructions (“think step by step,” “show all your work”) were layered on, the model’s
average generated-solution length grew, and accuracy rose in tandem — the earliest empirical trace
of the scaling relationship underlying today’s reasoning models.
Where it shows up

When Language Models Learned to Reason — the talk this framing comes from.
Long-Horizon Agents — Tworek’s independent use of the same Andrew Wiles anecdote, for a
different purpose (estimating training scale for long-horizon competence, rather than motivating
why a time axis was needed at all).

concepts/the-software-factory.title: The Software Factory
concepts/the-software-factory.content:
The Software Factory
Eno Reyes’s (Co-Founder & CTO, Factory AI) framing from Building the Software Factory: the
next stage after autocomplete → chatbots → agents, reached in roughly three and a half years.
The loop, made explicit. A software factory is the process by which signals flow into an
organization (customer feedback, internal telemetry, an executive deciding to pivot), get triaged
(today almost entirely inside human heads, essentially never represented in any real system),
planned (loosely encoded in tools like Jira, Notion, or Confluence — usually unstructured), turned
into code, validated, shipped, and deployed — after which the deployed software generates more
signals, closing the loop. This implicit feedback loop exists at nearly every company that builds
software; an explicit model of it exists almost nowhere.
The sharp reframe: coding is the easy part. Everything around writing code — triage, planning,
validation, deployment, incident response — is the hard part, the part that leads to mess. This
explains the gap between “AGI is here, 100x productivity” claims and what most companies actually
observe: today’s AI tooling typically automates one narrow, autocomplete-shaped slice (ask the
machine, get a result back) while the rest of the loop stays a human-driven, synchronous workflow.
The goal isn’t removing humans from the loop — it’s letting signals flow all the way to deployed
software without requiring human intervention at every step, which redefines rather than
eliminates the human role (see Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories for what that
redefined role looks like).
Three explicit design principles for building or buying into a software factory:

Model independence. Model vendors have strong incentives to argue you should verticalize —
couple your harness tightly to their model. Reyes reports finding this empirically false: you
want to aggregate and commoditize the model layer, to actually access the Pareto frontier of
cost and quality across models rather than betting on one vendor’s trajectory.
Sovereignty. You should control your own software factory regardless of which vendors come
and go — Factory itself sells SaaS for this, but still offers on-prem and air-gapped
deployment, because “your software factory is your company”: if you build software, the
software factory is literally the new version of your business, and vendor lock-in at this
layer is an existential risk, not a convenience tradeoff.
Full organizational scope. The software factory should span every action across product and
engineering, not just writing code — code review, security analysis, testing, documentation,
incident response all belong inside it.

A fourth, architectural stance: the shared agent core. Rather than a proliferation of
hyper-specialized micro-agents (a dedicated code-review agent, a dedicated incident-response
agent, each independently optimized), Reyes argues for one shared agent core operating across many
surfaces — different workflows (code review vs. incident response) differ in context and content,
but at a high level they’re all the same underlying pattern: computer control on top of an agent
with context. Building this per-surface fragments what should be one system. This directly builds
on Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice (Daniel Homola’s talk, delivered immediately before
this one) — Reyes explicitly references it, taking Homola’s runtime-delegation framing as the
argument for why a shared core, not fragmented specialized agents, is the right shape for a
production system operating across many workflows.
Where it shows up

Building the Software Factory — the talk this framing comes from.
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — the talk this one directly builds on for its shared-
agent-core argument.
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy — the operational half of this same talk: what it actually
takes, environment-wise, for a software factory to run with less human intervention.
Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories — the governance and human-role half of
this same talk.

concepts/three-level-runtime-control.title: Three-Level Runtime Control
concepts/three-level-runtime-control.content:
Three-Level Runtime Control
From Reasoning as Control: Adaptive Test-Time Compute for Planning Agents:
self-improvement in agentic systems isn’t just a model-capability property — the runtime
infrastructure around the model can also be continually improved, which may matter even more for
vertical, enterprise- specific applications. This extends Recursive Self-Improvement’s
harness-vs-model-weights split and Agent 2.0/Architect Agents’s “structure itself can
improve” theme with a specific three-level hierarchy of where that improvement can target.
Level 1 — token/thinking-level steering. There’s an elegant closed-form solution for steering a
base model toward a reward via an additive signal, but a real mismatch exists: reward models are
naturally trajectory-level, while you want to steer generation as early as possible, token by
token. The naive correct approach (generate a full completion, then score it) works but is
prohibitively slow — reported at roughly 14 hours to generate 500 tokens on a single academic GPU.
The fix: a purpose-built token-level reward model, cutting cost by orders of magnitude and
making runtime steering genuinely practical. Payoffs: no base-model training required at all,
“weak-to-strong guidance” (a small model steering a much larger one — echoing
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern’s weak-teaches-strong finding), and real-time
multi-objective alignment adapted to different user needs without retraining.
Level 2 — action control via “genuine self-reflection.” Naive imitation learning from expert
demonstrations produces a “stuck loop” failure mode — an agent repeatedly retries an action until
it terminates or exhausts its budget. Imitating a stronger model’s self-reflection style helps
somewhat but isn’t satisfying, since it’s mimicry rather than real reflection. The fix: force the
agent to judge which action is better at a given decision point using its own judgment —
effectively building an internal, mini world model of what works in what state — while also forcing
it to articulate why. This improved both imitation-learning and RL outcomes, generalized notably
better out-of-distribution, and beat prior state-of-the-art. Strikingly, this narrow,
environment-specific training also improved general reasoning capability, despite having nothing
directly to do with general reasoning — a genuinely surprising, durable finding.
Level 3 — workflow control via a precomputed, reusable bank. Should agent workflow and topology
be fixed for everything (“one for all”) or custom-designed per individual query (“one for each”)?
Neither extreme is good — one sacrifices task fit, the other sacrifices efficiency, since designing
a bespoke workflow per query is expensive. The middle path: precompute a bank of workflows during
training, then select and adapt from that bank efficiently at deployment time. This complements
Agent 2.0 and Architect Agents with a distinct emphasis — efficient reuse of previously-
discovered good structure, not building or discovering structure from scratch every time.
Closing framing: self-improvement can target compute allocation under a limited budget, early
steering of the thinking process, action control via genuine self-reflection, and workflow control
via reusable precomputed structure — three distinct levers, not one monolithic “make the model
smarter” lever.
Where it shows up

Reasoning as Control: Adaptive Test-Time Compute for Planning Agents —
the talk this framing comes from.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the harness-vs-model-weights split this hierarchy sharpens into
three specific levels.
Agent 2.0 and Architect Agents — the same “structure itself can improve” theme, with this
page adding efficient reuse via a precomputed bank as a distinct emphasis.
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern — the same weak-to-strong pattern, here for steering
rather than distillation.

concepts/tool-sensitivity-and-the-lethal.filePath: concepts/Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta.md
concepts/tool-sensitivity-and-the-lethal.title: Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta
concepts/tool-sensitivity-and-the-lethal.content:
Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta
Itsik Mantin’s risk framework from When Good Agents Go Rogue, following from
Poison Entry Vectors.
The core risk-scaling principle: connecting a tool to an agent hands the agent the keys to that
capability — and if the agent is hijacked, those keys pass to the attacker. Blast radius scales
directly with the sensitivity of the tool:

Database access → deletion, corruption, theft, or manipulation of data.
Bash / code execution → remote code execution, ransomware, conscription into a botnet.
Financial-action tools → fraud, money theft.
Internet access → the actual exfiltration channel, and often the force-multiplier that makes
data stolen via other tools actually consequential.
Messaging tools → impersonation attacks on colleagues (a message that appears to come from
you, convincing someone to take a damaging action).

A sharp concrete example: a security researcher got a coding agent to overwrite its own
security-configuration file, disabling the “every operation requires human-in-the-loop” safeguard —
turning a seemingly mundane file-write capability into the key to a far more devastating attack.
The exercise this leaves you with: identify the most powerful tools connected to your agent, and
consider what happens if an attacker takes control of them.
Simon Willison’s “lethal trifecta” — a simplified, citable risk-assessment model, independent
of this talk’s specific framing. An agent sits in the danger zone when it simultaneously has: (1)
exposure to untrusted data, (2) access to sensitive data, and (3) a channel for external
communication. All three together is what makes exfiltration and hijacking possible; removing any
one substantially cuts the risk.
A concrete mitigation checklist: least privilege; treat all incoming content as untrusted by
default; vet connectors and skill sources, using only trusted ones; require human-in-the-loop for
consequential actions; sandbox code execution so it can’t do real harm even if hijacked; build
shared infrastructure (an “AI firewall”) that all agents and products route through, rather than
reinventing security per product; and invest in a dedicated AI-security research function to build
institutional threat understanding over time.
Where it shows up

When Good Agents Go Rogue — the talk this framing comes from.
Poison Entry Vectors — how the payloads that exploit this risk actually get in.

concepts/train-inference-mismatch.title: Train-Inference Mismatch
concepts/train-inference-mismatch.content:
Train-Inference Mismatch
From
Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent - A Case Study of SGLang and Miles: an
RL post-training run typically uses two different pieces of software for two different roles — an
inference engine (e.g. SGLang) to generate rollouts, and a separate training backend (e.g. NVIDIA
Megatron) to compute gradients and update weights. If those two engines compute even slightly
different numerical results for the same model and inputs — different kernels, different precision,
different implementation details — the rollout policy the trainer thinks it’s updating and the
rollout policy that actually generated the data silently diverge.
Why this matters more than it sounds like it should: RL algorithms generally assume the data
they’re training on was generated by the current policy (on-policy). Train-inference mismatch
breaks that assumption without any obvious symptom — there’s no error, no crash, just a training
run that’s quietly become more off-policy than intended, degrading in ways that are hard to
diagnose because nothing looks broken. The talk frames this as “a very popular topic in frontier
labs” right now — a known, recurring failure mode of production RL infrastructure rather than an
edge case.
Three named fixes, addressing it at different layers:

Deterministic kernels — the most direct fix: make the inference and training engines
numerically match exactly (described as achieving “zero KL” divergence between them), removing
the mismatch at its source rather than compensating for it downstream.
Chat-template / token alignment (“token in, token out”) — ensure multi-turn agentic chat
templates are handled identically across turns in both engines, so tokenization or formatting
differences don’t reintroduce mismatch even after kernels are aligned.
Algorithmic correction — when some mismatch is unavoidable, correct for it in the training
algorithm itself: rollout routing replay, and truncated importance sampling to down-weight
rollouts whose generating policy has drifted too far from the current one.

Where it shows up

Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent - A Case Study of SGLang and Miles
— the talk this concept comes from.
Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance — a related but distinct source of train/rollout
divergence: that page’s staleness is intentional policy lag traded for throughput; train-
inference mismatch is unintentional numerical divergence between two engines that should in
principle agree.

concepts/trajectory-based-agent-reliabil.title: Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability
concepts/trajectory-based-agent-reliabil.content:
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability
Srijith Rajamohan’s (formerly Head of AI Research, Redis) findings from
Spec-Driven Agents - Hierarchical Specs, Tooling, and Trajectory-Based Evaluation, built
diagnosing a real production agent for the Redis query engine: evaluating only the final result is
insufficient — many failure modes are invisible there and only show up in how the agent got to its
answer.
A four-category failure taxonomy, three about the final result and one about the trajectory:

Correctness — the result is wrong: hallucinated paths, misread metrics.
Completeness — only part of the issue got diagnosed, the rest left unresolved.
Usefulness, with two distinct sub-failures: information overload (too much or too generic
information to be actionable) and, sharper, advice that’s technically correct but violates the
user’s actual semantic intent — telling someone whose query is slow to “reduce the number of
search terms” is technically true but doesn’t serve the real need. Correctness and usefulness are
not the same property.
Efficiency (trajectory-only, invisible in the final result) — repeated reads, backtracking,
dead-end searches. Wastes tokens, but the sharper finding is that inefficient trajectories also
directly hurt accuracy — trajectory quality and correctness aren’t independent concerns.

A named principle: “the only thing worse than a system that doesn’t work is something that
just works occasionally.” Consistency is not a secondary concern to correctness — an agent that’s
right most of the time but unpredictably wrong is a worse production asset than one with a known,
stable failure rate.
Two measured architectural fixes, neither involving a bigger model:


Setup tools vs. discretionary tools. Setup tools always run at startup — an onboarding
pattern: give the agent the lay of the land (what’s happening, who’s who) before it starts
acting — while discretionary tools are called situationally, based on the specific problem.
This shrinks the tool-selection decision space the agent navigates at each step. Measured
effect: even when aggregate quality metrics looked similar between configurations, drilling
into the actual trajectories showed far more variance and inconsistency without setup tools —
reducing the number of decisions an agent has to make at each point reduces variance and
improves consistency, independent of raw capability.


Tool overload is real, and tool orthogonality matters more than tool coverage. Three
configurations were tested: an auto-generated baseline (slow, debatable quality); a “minimal”
domain-informed tool set; and a “full” superset adding composite/convenience tools (e.g. a
direct get_slowest_shard tool alongside the more primitive get_shard_info). Counter-
intuitively, “full” performed worse — slower, marginally lower quality — because ambiguity
between overlapping tools (poor separability: when should the agent call tool B versus tool C?)
is itself a reliability problem, independent of whether the agent has enough raw capability to
solve the task.


The “diagnostic playbook.” Replacing raw documentation with a router plus a set of
handbooks: the router maps a user’s concern, expressed in their own words, to a symptom or
problem type, then routes to the relevant handbook(s) — doing the concern-to-symptom
translation work up front rather than leaving the agent to search raw docs at retrieval time.
Measured results: 43% reduction in total tokens, 48% reduction in total error rate, and
improved instruction-following as a side effect. The causal claim worth preserving: making
information easier to access reduced cost and reliability failures together — not a tradeoff
between the two.


Two closing takeaways, stated explicitly: measure the trajectory, not just the final answer,
since many real issues never surface in the final result; and be deliberate about which knowledge
and tooling is baseline/mandatory context versus discretionary/exploratory, rather than exposing
everything and letting the agent sort it out.
Cross-cutting connections: the “technically correct but violates semantic intent” usefulness
failure is the same underlying gap Taste as a Benchmark Metric names from a benchmark-design
angle — correctness alone doesn’t capture whether an answer is actually good. And “many failure
modes are invisible in the final result” is a trajectory-specific instance of the same structural
problem Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability’s “invisible errors” barrier names more
generally — Klein’s iceberg, applied specifically to multi-step agent trajectories rather than
single model outputs.
Where it shows up

Spec-Driven Agents - Hierarchical Specs, Tooling, and Trajectory-Based Evaluation — the talk
this framework comes from.
Taste as a Benchmark Metric — the same underlying insight (technically correct isn’t the
same as actually good) from a benchmark-design angle rather than a production-agent-diagnosis
angle.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — this page’s core finding (failures invisible in
the final result) is a trajectory-specific instance of Klein’s “invisible errors” iceberg.
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — a complementary evaluation lens from a different talk:
that page’s L2/L3 (component evaluation, diagnostics) is exactly the kind of trajectory-level
inspection this page argues is necessary and often skipped.
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — the same “technically correct but violates
semantic intent” pattern in a different, higher-stakes domain: Emily Xue’s healthcare policy-
compliance example (correct diagnosis, wrong process) is this page’s usefulness failure mode
seen in a regulated enterprise setting.
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — the same measure-the-path-not-just-the-final-answer
principle, applied specifically to which agent a multi-agent system delegated to and how, rather
than to one agent’s own internal trajectory.

concepts/transferable-prompt-injection-m.title: Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms
concepts/transferable-prompt-injection-m.content:
Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms
Findings from Devina Jain’s month-long attacker/defender prompt-injection competition (22 teams, run
with Berkeley RDI), presented in
Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations.
Why prompt injection is architecturally hard, not just an alignment gap: LLMs process
instructions and data in the same channel, and can’t reliably distinguish “this is an instruction
to follow” from “this is content to ingest.” (One real-world illustration: an EchoLeak-style
incident where an attacker’s email, never opened by the victim, was read and acted on by an AI
assistant, exfiltrating the victim’s inbox with zero user interaction.)
A rubric for a meaningful red-teaming scenario, distinguishing signal from noise:

Difficulty — a model attacking a copy of itself should land near a balanced (~50%) win rate.
Sensitivity — a strong model against a weak one should show a clear capability gap.
Non-triviality — the scenario shouldn’t collapse to a deterministic exploit in one round.
Their example of a bad scenario: an “HR hack” whose target is a single number (a salary band),
attackable by pure binary search with no actual injection needed. Fixed by using a secret only
the defender knows, so success requires an actual attack rather than search.

Under sustained adversarial pressure, defenses improve faster than attacks do. Over the
month, attacker performance improved early, then flattened; defender performance kept climbing
substantially further. Practical implication for continuous red-teaming: rotate the attacker pool
and keep rerunning, rather than reusing one static attacker, since a defender under constant
adversarial pressure keeps learning past what a fixed attacker can teach it. This is a live,
measured confirmation of the “automatic red-teaming as an optimization loop” idea already in
Securing Agentic AI.
Public leaderboards hide overfitting. Running the same teams against a private, held-out set
of scenarios dropped the median attack-success rate by about 6 points. Most teams (15 of 22) held
roughly steady, but a handful fell sharply — these turned out to have hard-coded, scenario-specific
harnesses keyed to known text rather than genuinely robust strategies. A few improved. Lesson: never
trust a public eval number alone; always maintain a private holdout.
The sharpest finding: a small set of attack mechanisms transferred across 14 unrelated scenario
domains. Ten mechanism clusters were identified overall; four transferred broadly: “just ask
nicely” (models often can’t distinguish a harmful request from an ordinary one — asking directly
for a password sometimes just works; also observed in a real production support chatbot), “the
findings were wrong” (append content claiming prior, correctly-incriminating evidence was
mistaken, and the model discounts what it should still trust), “fake pre-approval” (claim an
authority — a VP, a manager — already approved the requested action), and “workflow
impersonation.” The same mechanisms worked identically on an expense-approval agent (a fake VP
pre-approval got a budget-exceeding cost approved) and an industrial-supply agent (the same
mechanism got an order approved at 50x the normal unit count), despite the domains sharing nothing
else. The general implication: build defenses around these general mechanism classes, not
per-scenario filters — scenario-specific patching misses attacks that transfer straight across
domains.
Near-miss testing, imported directly from self-driving collision analysis. In self-driving,
many near-collisions have an “identical failing twin” — nearly the same conditions, but a small
change in speed or angle is the difference between a collision and a miss. The security-arena
analog: roughly 10% of successful attacks had a near-identical unsuccessful twin, where changing
just a few words flipped the outcome (their example: adding “owner confirmed via mobile app” — four
words — turned a failed attack into a successful one). Implication: a single pass/fail test on one
prompt proves very little; you need to test the neighborhood of near-miss variants around both
successes and failures, not just the point outcome.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations — the talk this
framing comes from.
Securing Agentic AI — a live, measured confirmation of the automatic-red-teaming-as-an-
optimization-loop idea already there.
Declared vs. Observed Authority — the same authority-propagation gap “fake pre-approval”
exploits, this time framed as a runtime governance problem rather than an attack mechanism.
Poison Entry Vectors — a complementary taxonomy, of entry channels rather than attack
mechanisms.

concepts/triple-a-benchmark-standardizat.title: Triple-A Benchmark Standardization
concepts/triple-a-benchmark-standardizat.content:
Triple-A Benchmark Standardization
Eson’s argument from Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation:
agent evaluation lags model evaluation because agents lack a common interface the way LLM APIs have
one — different agents use different interfaces, tools, environments, and execution models, so
running an agent on a new benchmark usually requires benchmark-specific engineering. Combined with
limited access to private agents/models, this makes agent evaluation hard to reproduce and hard to
scale.
A sharper diagnosis: most existing benchmarks are built around swapping the model, not the
full harness (prompts, tools, memory, workflow, control logic) wrapped around it. Testing a
genuinely different agent — a different harness — usually requires modifying the benchmark’s own
code, creating high integration overhead and a possible mismatch between the tested system and the
system actually used in production. With N benchmarks and M agents, naive pairwise integration
requires up to N×M separate integration efforts — impractical at scale. This sharpens
Harness Matters More Than Model: it isn’t just that the harness affects outcomes, it’s that
most benchmarks can’t even properly measure a different harness in the first place.
The fix — turn benchmarks into agents too. Instead of directly integrating every benchmark with
every agent, both sides integrate through standard agent-to-agent protocols (A2A, MCP) — the same
protocols agents already use to talk to each other. An added “assessment control protocol” defines
a unified evaluation workflow for consistency and reproducibility. This separates benchmarks from
the agents being evaluated, reduces benchmark-specific integration work, and makes multi-agent
evaluation natural rather than a special case, since agents already communicate this way.
AgentBeats — the concrete open platform instantiating this paradigm: supports benchmark
development, agent evaluation, collaboration, and leaderboard-based result tracking, across
single-agent and multi-agent settings, with multiple operational modes for different privacy and
data constraints. Validated via a real competition spanning 70 evaluation tracks and 12 agent
categories, with hundreds of benchmarks and agents integrated through the Triple-A paradigm.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation — the talk this
framing comes from.
Harness Matters More Than Model — the claim this sharpens: benchmarks often can’t even
measure a different harness, not just that harness affects outcomes.
Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic — a structurally different answer to the same
underlying problem: rather than standardizing a fixed benchmark to properly measure any harness,
randomize the harness/orchestrator directly in live production traffic and measure the treatment
effect.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — a related but different problem in the same space: this
page addresses the interface mismatch between benchmarks and harnesses; that page addresses
the content quality of the benchmark tasks themselves.

concepts/verifiable-agent-red-teaming.title: Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming
concepts/verifiable-agent-red-teaming.content:
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming
Bo Li’s platform design from Securing AI Agents (“DecodingTrust-Agent”), worth preserving as a
checklist for what a good agent red-teaming platform needs.
Realistic sandboxes connected to external tools, not an isolated file system. Vulnerabilities
specifically emerge once an agent connects to external tools and MCP servers — an isolated sandbox
misses most of the real attack surface. Their platform includes 50+ such environments.
Combinable attack strategies verified against actual system state, not an LLM judge. A
red-teaming agent generates strategies (tool injection, skill injection, prompt injection, and
combinations of these), but success is checked against ground truth — did a transaction actually
happen, was a file actually deleted — rather than relying on an uncertain LLM judge to grade whether
an attack succeeded. This is a durable methodological point independent of this specific platform:
outcome verification should check real state whenever the task allows it.
Domain-scoped coverage rather than a single fixed test count. Organized across 14 domains
(finance, healthcare, and others), each incorporating that domain’s own specific policies — no claim
that any fixed number of test cases is universally “enough.”
A generalizable point buried in the design: the platform evaluates helpfulness and safety
jointly, because safety is a property of the model-and-harness combination, not the model alone —
the same underlying point as Harness Matters More Than Model, here applied to security
specifically rather than raw task performance.
Where it shows up

Securing AI Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
Agent Security Taxonomy — the broader taxonomy this platform instantiates the “risk
assessment” bucket of.
Harness Matters More Than Model — the same model-plus-harness-jointly-determines-the-outcome
point, applied to security here rather than task performance.
Frontier Cyber Evaluation — the same sandbox-must-actually-contain-the-agent principle, from
a different security-evaluation platform, plus real incidents where it was violated.

concepts/verifiable-code-generation.title: Verifiable Code Generation
concepts/verifiable-code-generation.content:
Verifiable Code Generation
Joy’s argument from Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation:
AI-generated code can look right, pass its tests, and still hide subtle bugs no human can fully
catch by inspection at scale. The fix: require the agent not just to generate code, but to prove
the code satisfies a formal specification, with that proof checked by a deterministic verifier
(e.g., Lean) — correctness proved, not merely assumed or empirically tested.
A sharp, quotable framing: formal verification and LLMs solve each other’s bottleneck. Formal
verification traditionally requires deep expertise and is very time-consuming, which has kept it
out of reach for ordinary software; LLM agents can automate much of that labor, scaling formal
guarantees to software that could never previously afford them. In the other direction, formal
verification gives LLM-generated code the correctness guarantee it’s otherwise missing.
Verina — measuring foundational skills on standalone tasks. 189 competition-style, easy-level
tasks measuring how well models generate code, a formal specification, and a proof, with support
for measuring different task compositions. A striking capability jump: about a year before this
talk, the strongest model solved roughly 5% of proof tasks; by the time of this talk, the current
strongest agentic provers solve essentially all of them.
VeriRepo — does that success transfer to real, repository-scale software? A repository-level
verifiable-code-generation benchmark built from real-world repositories across several languages:
43 manually-curated repositories, roughly 700 implementation obligations, and 2,700 formal
specifications, each repository put through a rigorous curation pipeline with manually-checked
specifications. Two evaluation modes: proof-only (given a reference implementation, prove every
specification correct) and code-plus-proof (implement every API and prove your own
implementation correct).
A methodologically important design choice: the benchmark scores whether an entire repository
is fully proved, not individual specifications in isolation — specifically to prevent agents from
gaming the score by solving only easy specifications and leaving hard ones unsolved. Even the
strongest tested combination solves only a modest fraction of full repositories, sometimes failing
to prove even a single specification within a given repository, making this a genuinely
frontier-resistant benchmark.
The diagnosed bottleneck: agents can close local proof obligations but struggle to formally
reason about global invariants that span an entire repository — the missing piece is a coherent
proof library with shared invariants, not just per-function proof skill.
Forward-looking directions: better formalizing human intent so specifications actually reflect
what was meant, not just what’s easy to state formally; scaling to harder properties (security,
concurrency, temporal behavior); and building agentic provers that reason coherently at the
whole-repository level rather than only locally.
Where it shows up

Workshop: Future of Agent Evaluation — the talk this
framing comes from.

concepts/verifiable-substrate.title: Verifiable Substrate
concepts/verifiable-substrate.content:
Verifiable Substrate
Manmohan Chandraker’s architecture from
Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition,
illustrated with a fully agent-run discovery loop targeting 3D Gaussian splatting for pedestrian
perception in autonomous driving. The only human input is a high-level directive; agents define the
specific sub-problem, generate hypotheses, and specialist agents launch parallel experiments.
Evaluation via an ELO-rated tournament: candidate methods are validated and falsified against
each other competitively, with the highest-rated survivor implemented on real GPU hardware so gains
are measurably real rather than simulated — a distinct evaluation mechanism from
Builder-Breaker Discovery’s adversarial builder/breaker pair, though both are answers to the
same underlying problem of driving discovery through structured falsification. A writer/reviewer
agent team then produces a paper about the surviving result. A validation result, kept
appropriately skeptical (self-reported, small sample, informal review): 3 of 4 agent-produced
papers submitted to an actual CVPR workshop, with organizer permission, were accepted, one with
high praise.
The core reusable contribution — a precise, three-part definition of what makes a discovery
substrate verifiable:

A context-free grammar constraining idea generation to genuinely grounded claims, not free-form
assertion.
Every candidate method is a mutation on top of an already-verified reproduction — starting from
something known-real, not generated from scratch with no anchor.
Every claim traces back to a real log, a real line of code, or a real GPU run — nothing is
asserted without a concrete, inspectable artifact.

This complements, without duplicating, Builder-Breaker Discovery (an adversarial discovery
mechanism) and Verification as Science’s Bottleneck (a diagnosis of why verification is scarce)
— this page’s contribution is a precise recipe for what verifiability actually requires
structurally.
A bootstrap method: reverse-engineer a verifiable substrate from existing literature. Given a
paper never publicly implemented (verified not already known to frontier models, ruling out
memorization), analyze it to determine what’s genuinely novel and what specifically drives its
reported improvements, produce code implementing those ideas, and physically verify that code
against real data — creating the same verified-reproduction-plus-traceable-claims structure without
building from scratch.
Where it shows up

Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
— the talk this framing comes from.
Intent Loops — the human-participation framework built on top of this substrate, from the
same talk.
Builder-Breaker Discovery and Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — related but distinct
approaches to the same underlying problem of trustworthy AI-driven scientific discovery.
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — a fourth approach that goes a different
direction than this page’s every-claim-traceable recipe: it removes the external verifier from
the evolution loop entirely rather than making verifiability structurally rigorous.
Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — states the same simulatability-enables-
verification link at a higher level of abstraction: Socher’s claim that “everything you can
simulate, you can verify” is the general principle this page’s three-part recipe makes structural.

concepts/verification-as-science's-bottl.title: Verification as Science's Bottleneck
concepts/verification-as-science's-bottl.content:
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck
Mengdi Wang’s argument from LabOS: scientific research runs through three stages —
hypothesize (reason, dig deep into a problem), compute (simulate to find the best
candidates), and validate/verify. AI has massively accelerated the first two. The third hasn’t
moved, and it’s the one that actually determines whether new knowledge exists at the end of the
process.
Evidence — the reproducibility crisis: a Nature-adjacent survey found 70% of biomedical
research papers aren’t reproducible by others, and 50% aren’t even reproducible by the original
authors — consistent across chemistry, biology, physics, and earth sciences. This isn’t a new
problem AI created, but it’s the ceiling AI-accelerated hypothesis generation runs into.
Why physical science specifically lacks the scaffolding that makes digital auto-research
tractable: training a model gives you checkpoints you can backtrack to; a physical experiment at a
bench or in a clean room doesn’t. There’s no log to debug, no way to inspect and improve “the
harnessing” of an experiment the way Chuan Li’s auto-research tooling
uses a git branch per idea to make results reproducible and comparable. Physical science is missing
the equivalent of that scaffolding entirely.
The sharpest claim — “with AI, science is not faster, science is actually getting slower.”
Submission volume at major research venues has exploded, while verification capacity hasn’t scaled
to match — more AI-generated hypotheses and papers without a matching increase in verified,
trustworthy findings just worsens the signal-to-noise ratio of the literature. This is a concrete,
science-specific version of the same point Recursive Self-Improvement makes more abstractly:
Oriol Vinyals argues evaluation and ideation, not compute, are what actually gate progress — Wang’s
talk shows exactly that bottleneck playing out in a real domain, at scale, right now.
The proposed fix: turn every scientific lab into a verifiable environment. LabOS, her group’s
instantiation, is a multimodal AI-XR agent (worn as smart glasses) that makes every action and
state-change in a physical lab observable to AI in real time — catching errors, digitizing physical
workflows, and providing troubleshooting guidance as a researcher works. The goal is essentially to
give physical experimentation the checkpoint-and-log scaffolding digital agent workflows already
have, so verification can eventually scale the way hypothesis generation already has.
The same logic, applied to business task selection rather than scientific discovery: Faraz
Shafiq (Wells Fargo, Agentic AI Summit 2026 Sunday Plenary) names this “verifiers’ law” — tasks
fast to verify are ripe for agentic automation now (Sudoku: hard to solve, trivial to verify;
coding has near-instant test feedback), while tasks with long-delayed or ambiguous verification
resist automation regardless of model capability, since the feedback loop needed to trust or
improve the agent can’t close fast enough. His example: a loan-default decision made today isn’t
verified right or wrong until a default happens, maybe 5 years later. Same underlying claim as this
page’s own diagnosis — verification speed, not intelligence, gates what can actually be automated —
just used here as a forward-looking planning heuristic (what to automate first) rather than a
retrospective diagnosis (why science has slowed).
Where it shows up

LabOS — the talk this framing comes from.
Autonomous Research Agents — the digital-auto-research scaffolding (reproducibility via
git-branch-per-idea) that physical science is missing an equivalent of.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the same evaluation-is-the-bottleneck claim, made abstractly
there and concretely, in a real domain, here.
Builder-Breaker Discovery — a candidate mechanism for addressing this bottleneck: fold
falsification directly into the discovery loop rather than treating verification as a separate,
downstream step.
Interpretability as Scientific Discovery — a third, distinct discovery mechanism: extract
knowledge already implicit inside an existing superhuman model, rather than generating and
verifying new hypotheses.
End-to-End AI Research — the same verification-is-the-real-cost claim, from security
research rather than physical-lab science.
Verifiable Substrate — a precise, structural recipe for what verifiability actually requires,
complementing this page’s diagnosis of why it’s scarce.
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — a fourth discovery mechanism, with a
strategically different move than the others: rather than making verification faster or more
rigorous, it sidesteps the need for an external verifier during evolution entirely, using
intrinsic model signals (log-probabilities, diversity) as a self-supervising fitness function.
Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — a fourth independent voice on the
ideation/validation bottleneck (Socher’s ideation/implementation/validation triad almost exactly
mirrors Wang’s hypothesize/compute/validate), plus the claim that simulatability is precisely what
makes verification free.

concepts/verifier-free-evolution-via-int.title: Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness
concepts/verifier-free-evolution-via-int.content:
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness
“Squeeze Evolve,” Together AI’s approach from
Unified Orchestration System for Verifier-Free Evolution (Ben, Senior Director, Core ML): a
unified, multimodal orchestration system for scientific-discovery agents that removes the external
verifier from the evolution loop entirely.
The standard discovery-loop architecture it builds on (from prior work, “SkyDiscover”): a
context builder injects problem context, ideas, guidance, and reflections on prior mistakes
and successes into the prompt; a solution generator (an LLM with access to environments — code
execution, web lookup) produces candidate solutions; an evaluator scores them and produces
logs, feedback, and artifacts; a solution selector picks samples to feed back into the context
builder for the next iteration.
The problem this addresses: verification is the expensive part. Prior discovery frameworks
typically require an external evaluator, and in physical science specifically that evaluation step
— real experiments, expensive simulation — can be costly and slow. The driving question: what’s
the upper bound of an evolution system without verification in the loop at all, and can that also
cut cost? This is the same diagnosis Verification as Science’s Bottleneck makes (verification,
not hypothesis generation, is what actually gates scientific progress) — but where that page’s
Builder-Breaker Discovery and Verifiable Substrate mechanisms both still fold verification
into the loop (adversarial falsification; precise verifiability criteria), Squeeze Evolve takes a
different strategic stance: it sidesteps the need for an external verifier during evolution
altogether, rather than making verification faster or more rigorous.
A second problem: single-model evolution degrades. Using one model repeatedly for evolutionary
refinement tends to degrade solution quality over successive generations — there’s only so much
entropy and creativity a single model keeps producing before it converges rather than continuing to
explore.
The mechanism: multi-model diversity, routed by difficulty, scored by intrinsic signals.
Solutions from prior and current generations get assigned fitness scores using token log-
probabilities and solution diversity — an intrinsic, self-supervising signal rather than an
external verifier’s judgment. Difficult solutions get routed to expensive, powerful models;
solutions judged easy enough to evaluate and combine get routed to a cheaper model — increasing
diversity and cost-effectiveness together. Structurally close to Runtime Agent Optimization’s
ensemble-portfolio and difficulty-based escalation strategies, applied here specifically to
evolutionary scientific discovery.
Measured results: the full pipeline (10 evolution steps, Gemini 3.1 Pro) reaches 97.5% on
ARC-AGI at roughly 7/task. Mixing in a cheaper model (Gemini 3.0 Flash) retains the *same*
accuracy in just 2 evolution steps at roughly 5.90/task — fewer steps and lower cost for equal
accuracy. For vision-based tasks, dropping the vision component at the aggregator stage where it
isn’t actually needed further improves cost-effectiveness. Most notably, in the heterogeneous
(mixed powerful-plus-cheap-model) case, the system didn’t just match the single-strong-model
baseline more cheaply — it outperformed it, suggesting model-heterogeneity diversity produces
genuinely better solutions, not merely cheaper equivalent ones. Integrated into NVIDIA Dynamo; a
Claude Code plugin is available.
Where it shows up

Unified Orchestration System for Verifier-Free Evolution — the talk this method comes from.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — the diagnosis this method responds to, with a
strategically different move than the wiki’s other discovery mechanisms: avoiding the need for
external verification during evolution, rather than making verification itself faster or more
rigorous.
Builder-Breaker Discovery and Verifiable Substrate — sibling discovery mechanisms in this
wiki, both of which still fold verification into the loop rather than removing it.
Interpretability as Scientific Discovery — a fourth distinct discovery mechanism: extracting
knowledge already implicit inside an existing model, rather than generating and scoring new
candidates.
Runtime Agent Optimization — the same ensemble-portfolio and difficulty-based escalation
strategy, applied here to evolutionary scientific discovery specifically.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — this method is a concrete escape from “anthropic bounds”:
scoring evolution via intrinsic model signals rather than any human-labeled ground truth, which is
what caps how far ELO/human-label benchmarks can measure above human baseline.

concepts/visual-imagination-in-multimoda.title: Visual Imagination in Multimodal Models
concepts/visual-imagination-in-multimoda.content:
Visual Imagination in Multimodal Models
Raja Giryes’ research narrative from
On the Visual Capabilities of Multimodal Models, building from a diagnostic pattern to a sharp
technical finding.
A meta-point framing the whole talk: once a research community starts asking the right
diagnostic question about a capability gap, focused progress tends to follow within a year or two
— a methodological observation complementary to the evaluation-bottleneck theme elsewhere in the
wiki. Here, the right diagnostic evaluation is what catalyzes rapid targeted progress, rather than
evaluation itself being the limiting factor.
Diagnostic background: earlier multimodal models struggled with compositional reasoning in
captioning — treating an image as “a bag of words,” mixing up counts and entities — fixed in prior
work by decomposing captions into tree structures for denser, better-aligned training signal. More
recent diagnostic work found two further imbalances: most of the actual reasoning in multimodal
understanding happens in the LLM component, not the visual component, since so much more training
investment has historically gone into language; and in-context learning, which scales well with
more text examples, actually confuses multimodal models when given too many images — both
symptoms of multimodal training leaning too heavily on the language side rather than genuinely
developing visual reasoning capacity.
Spatial cognition, and a well-documented, rapid improvement trajectory. A study from roughly two
years before this talk tested frontier models on named spatial-cognition tasks: mental rotation (is
this the same shape, rotated?), perspective-taking (what’s the angle between two objects from a
given viewpoint?), maze completion, and shortcut discovery (having seen a non-shortest walkthrough
of a space, can the model find the actual shortest path?). At that point, frontier models performed
close to chance on all of them. A follow-up study roughly a year and a half later found models had
progressed to about a three-year-old child’s level on these tasks. A further comparison found
current frontier models can solve spatial-cognition tasks that take a human roughly ten seconds — a
real but modest ceiling. On individual tasks: perspective-taking went from near-chance to close to
100% for some frontier models within two years; maze completion and shortcut discovery, still weak
just a few months prior, also showed a sharp recent jump.
The sharpest finding: models internally “imagine” visual transformations, even without any
image-generation ability. A study run with Apple collaborators tested models in an “open-loop”
setting — shown only the first frame of a scenario, asked what step to take next, never shown
subsequent frames — and probed internal weights and activations, including in models that can only
receive images, never generate them. Finding: the model’s internal representations were
reconstructing the visual transformation needed to solve the task — for a “are these two shapes the
same after rotation” question, internal weights reconstruct something functionally like the mental
rotation itself; similarly, for character-assembly tasks, internal weights represent the assembly
process. The model does this internal visual “imagination” despite having no mechanism to output
an image at all — capability doesn’t require an explicit output modality. The practical payoff:
having found this latent behavior, explicitly supervising and training toward it measurably
improved task performance.
Closing framing, in the speaker’s own two points: asking the right question matters enormously
for advancing science; and for multimodal models specifically, it matters that models genuinely
attend to and develop visual processing, not just lean on the language side — doing so measurably
helps.
Where it shows up

On the Visual Capabilities of Multimodal Models — the talk this framing comes from.

concepts/world-models-for-closed-loop-ag.title: World Models for Closed-Loop Agents
concepts/world-models-for-closed-loop-ag.content:
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents
Vincent Vanhoucke’s framing from Trustworthy Agents in the Real World, drawing on control
theory and robotics.
The “DAgger problem”: in a multi-step system, optimizing to minimize error at each individual
step (an open-loop, imitation-learning style objective) can still fail badly, because small
per-step errors correlate and compound — the system drifts into states its training never covered,
and ends up somewhere very different from the intended outcome. This is why long-horizon planning
and reinforcement learning use different objective functions than step-wise imitation: you have to
optimize for closed-loop behavior over the whole trajectory, not just the next step. This is a
distinct argument, from a different field, for a conclusion Long-Horizon Agents also reaches
via RL training economics (quadratic cost/credit-assignment decay) — two independent reasons long
horizons need fundamentally different training objectives, not just more of the same.
World models as the mechanism for closed-loop optimization: rather than optimize one step at a
time, imagine the long-horizon future a candidate action leads to, and optimize against that
imagined rollout. Waymo built its own world model for this — a learned simulator judged on three
properties:

Realism — grounded in real-world physics and visuals, not just plausible-looking generative
output (built from a video generation model, fine-tuned toward real-world rather than
video-game-style physics).
Controllability — able to render counterfactual actions and conditions on demand (turn left
instead of right; change the time of day, weather, or the position of any car or pedestrian) so
you can evaluate “what if” without needing to have observed it.
Generalization — able to extrapolate beyond the training distribution into scenarios never
observed. Vanhoucke’s illustration: Waymo has never seen an elephant on the road. Trained naively,
the model renders no elephant at all when asked; pushed toward generalization without enough
care, it renders elephant-shaped trucks (borrowing truck knowledge, unable to square it with
“elephant”); done right, it renders a genuine elephant — a clean illustration of the gradient
between underfit, confused, and correctly generalized behavior.

The closing challenge: Vanhoucke asks agentic AI builders working on non-physical agents
directly — “what is your world model?” — arguing that a high-fidelity, controllable simulation of
your environment is a prerequisite for long-horizon planning and resilience, not a nice-to-have,
and most non-physical agent systems don’t have one.
Independently, Requirement and Model Gaps names world models — learning parts of the model
through direct interaction with the deployment environment, rather than assuming it upfront — as
one of the few structural ways to narrow the model gap specifically. Two unrelated talks
converging on world models as the fix for two related but distinct problems (long-horizon planning
here; model-reality mismatch there) is a stronger signal than either alone.
Where it shows up

Trustworthy Agents in the Real World — the talk this framing comes from.
Long-Horizon Agents — an independent, economics-based argument for the same conclusion (long
horizons need different training objectives than step-wise optimization).
Requirement and Model Gaps — an independent argument for world models as a way to narrow the
model gap.
Intelligence vs. Expertise — expertise, in that talk’s framing, is itself an internalized
world model of a specific “micro-world” — the same underlying concept from a different angle.
World Motion Models — a direct sharpening: the right abstraction level for a world model is
task-dependent, not always full pixel-level generative fidelity.
Market Models — the same structural move (a dedicated model class for
a domain’s actual dynamics) applied to business decision-making instead of physical robotics.
Sidewalk Autonomy — a concrete instance of video-reconstruction-based world modeling, closing
the sim-to-real gap for a different physical-AI domain (sidewalk robots, not road vehicles).
Interactive World Model Architecture — Sanja Fidler independently names the same
realism/controllability/generalization properties and uses the identical elephant-on-the-road
generalization test, without having seen this talk; her talk supplies the architecture recipe
(base model, domain post-training, causal action-conditioning, distillation for real-time speed)
this page’s framing doesn’t detail.

concepts/world-motion-models.title: World Motion Models
concepts/world-motion-models.content:
World Motion Models
Trevor Darrell’s argument from Real-World Reasoning Agents: full pixel-level video-generation
world models are impressive, but often overkill for a specific task. If the actual task is, say,
tightening a bolt on a wheel as it passes, you don’t need to predict what the trees are doing or
most of the car — you need to predict the affordance or geometry of the specific part in motion.
The approach: model 3D rigid-body trajectories directly rather than pixels — SE3 poses
(six-degree-of-freedom pose frames), tokenized and stacked over time across multiple reference
frames, one per object or rigid body part in a scene. Trained via denoising, similar in spirit to
pixel-based world models but operating at a far more compact, task-relevant level of abstraction.
The resulting general framework supports prediction (given the past), action-conditioned
prediction, inpainting/motion-planning, and retargeting, all over this pose-trajectory
representation.
Why this matters: it directly sharpens World Models for Closed-Loop Agents, already in the
wiki from Vincent Vanhoucke’s talk — the right level of abstraction for a world model depends on
what the downstream task actually needs. Full pixel-level generative fidelity is not always
necessary, or even desirable, when geometry/motion-level prediction is sufficient and far cheaper.
Where it shows up

Real-World Reasoning Agents — the talk this framing comes from.
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — the general world-model concept this sharpens: the
right abstraction level is task-dependent, not always pixel-level.
Interactive World Model Architecture — Sanja Fidler’s ground-plane-only physics (no collision
checking against other scene complexity) is a concrete, practical instance of the same
cheaper-abstraction-where-sufficient tradeoff this page argues for in general.
Stateful Visual Encoders and Tactile Reactivity and Multi-Process Architecture — two
other projects from the same talk.
Market Models — the same structural move (a dedicated model class
matched to a domain’s actual dynamics), applied to business decision-making instead of physical
robotics.

concepts/zero-ops-(concept).title: Zero Ops
concepts/zero-ops-(concept).content:
Zero Ops
Shamir Abdul Aziz’s framing from
Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern: “Zero Ops is not about removing humans from
operations. It’s about removing the operations from humans.” The goal is taking mundane operational
work off humans so they move to higher-value work — innovation, governance — not eliminating human
involvement.
“Models are not the moat.” Models are swappable and keep improving on their own; the durable
investment is context, governance, and tools. The actual moat: source code, production telemetry,
institutional knowledge, and the skills and tools given to the system. This directly reinforces
Agent Harness’s recurring theme — multiple independent talks now converge on exactly this
point: the value that persists isn’t the model, it’s what surrounds it.
“Outcome-based engineering” — humans review outcomes, not diffs. An agent fixing a performance
regression could just create a pull request, leaving a human to review it line by line — or it
could create the PR, deploy it to a test environment, validate the regression is actually gone, and
present that validated outcome for human confirmation. The shift is from reviewing process to
reviewing evidence.
A refined crawl-walk-run-fly maturity model, with a precise definition of “fly.” Not just “the
agent executes unsupervised” — the top tier specifically means the agent executes, validates its
own outcome, and presents the validated result for human confirmation. This nuances
Spectrum of Agency: full autonomy here isn’t “no human at all,” it’s “agent-validated outcome,
human confirms” — a more precise notion of maturity than raw unsupervised execution.
Enterprise trust requirements: audit, control, evaluate, roll back with confidence, and prove
with evidence that what an agent did was correct — standing requirements for enterprises to deploy
agents at scale, without which trust (and adoption) doesn’t follow no matter how capable the agent
is.
Where it shows up

Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern — the talk this framing comes from.
Agent Harness — the same “the model isn’t the moat, the harness/context around it is” theme.
Spectrum of Agency — a complementary autonomy-calibration framework; this page sharpens what
“full autonomy” should actually mean at the top of that spectrum.
Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents — a third, domain-specific autonomy-tier
taxonomy (mental health), independently converging on the same underlying design question.

entities/aditya-grover.title: Aditya Grover
entities/aditya-grover.content:
Aditya Grover
Co-Founder and CTO of Inception Labs. Auto-captions render his name as “Adit Grover” / “Adita.” In
Redefining the Token Efficiency Frontier with Diffusion LLMs, argues diffusion — already
dominant for image and video generation — is the next foundation for language models, reading each
generational leap in AI as the same underlying idea, parallelization, applied at a different layer
(Parallelization as AI’s Throughline). Co-founded Inception to commercialize
diffusion-based text generation after a research breakthrough from a
co-founder’s lab reached parity with GPT-2; the company’s Mercury and Mercury 2 models are built on
this approach.
Talks

Redefining the Token Efficiency Frontier with Diffusion LLMs (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/anastasios-angelopoulos.title: Anastasios Angelopoulos
entities/anastasios-angelopoulos.content:
Anastasios Angelopoulos
Co-Founder & CEO of LMArena (arena.ai). Started Arena as a Berkeley PhD student project (advised by
Mike Jordan and Jitendra Malik, in collaboration with Ion Stoica) before it grew into an
independent evaluation company — introduced the Bradley-Terry/Elo-based pairwise leaderboard
methodology to AI model evaluation, and has since extended it to agents via causal, treatment-
effect-based evaluation on real production traffic.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on Agent Arena’s methodology: reality as the only judge that
matters, and randomizing the orchestrator/model in live agentic sessions to measure causal
treatment effects at scale. See Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic.
Where it shows up

Agent Arena - Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World
Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic

entities/ankit-goyal.title: Ankit Goyal
entities/ankit-goyal.content:
Ankit Goyal
Principal Staff Software Engineer on the AI Platforms team at LinkedIn.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on re-architecting infrastructure for long-running production
agents: three infra shifts (UX, compute, trust), a harness-code-with-code-defined-evaluators
architecture to prevent reward hacking, an agent-scoped identity/sandboxing security model, and a
custom warm-pool control plane for agent-scale job launching. See
Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents.
Where it shows up

Infrastructure for Long-Running Agents
Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents

entities/aravind-segu.title: Aravind Segu
entities/aravind-segu.content:
Aravind Segu
Software Engineer at Databricks, working on Omnigent. Introduced on stream as “Arvind”; full name
from the event schedule. Co-presented, with
Dhruv (Databricks), the Omnigent workshop at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, demoing the
meta-harness’s multi-harness orchestration, live collaboration, and smart-routing features. See
Meta-Harness Architecture.
Where it shows up

Omnigent - A Meta Harness for AI Agents
Meta-Harness Architecture

entities/ben-athiwaratkun.title: Ben Athiwaratkun
entities/ben-athiwaratkun.content:
Ben Athiwaratkun
Senior Director, Core ML (Turbo) at Together AI. Only the first name was given on stream; surname
from the event schedule.
Presented “Squeeze Evolve” at the Agentic AI Summit 2026: a unified orchestration system for
verifier-free scientific-discovery evolution, using intrinsic model signals (log-probabilities,
diversity) as fitness instead of an external verifier, with difficulty-based routing across
cheap and expensive models. See Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness.
Where it shows up

Unified Orchestration System for Verifier-Free Evolution
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness

entities/ben-burtenshaw.title: Ben Burtenshaw
entities/ben-burtenshaw.content:
Ben Burtenshaw
Community Engineer at Hugging Face. In Open Source Agentic RL Environment, argues RL
environments are the mechanism by which capabilities move from domain experts into model weights —
and are currently at the pre-standardization stage model checkpoints were at years ago
(RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer) — and introduces OpenEnv, an open standard and
hub for sharing agentic RL environments.
Talks

Open Source Agentic RL Environment (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/bo-li.title: Bo Li
entities/bo-li.content:
Bo Li
Professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Co-Founder & CEO of Virtue AI, a
unified AI security and compliance platform for enterprises (finance, healthcare, retail); Virtue
AI recently joined Meta Superintelligence Labs. In Securing AI Agents, presents a three-bucket
taxonomy for agent security work — risk assessment, protection, certification
(Agent Security Taxonomy) — and DecodingTrust-Agent, a red-teaming platform verified against
real system state rather than an LLM judge (Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming).
Talks

Securing AI Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/bolei-zhou.title: Bolei Zhou
entities/bolei-zhou.content:
Bolei Zhou
Professor at UCLA, also working with Coco Robotics (a last-mile food-delivery robotics startup). In
Scaling Sidewalk Autonomy with World Models, argues sidewalk robots face a distinct, socially
denser and more resource-constrained autonomy problem than road vehicles
(Sidewalk Autonomy), and describes video-reconstruction-based simulation (V2) and its
follow-on, scene-graph-based variation generation (UrbanVerse, “digital cousins”) for closing the
sim-to-real gap and enabling counterfactual post-training
(Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins).
Talks

Scaling Sidewalk Autonomy with World Models (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/chuan-li.title: Chuan Li
entities/chuan-li.content:
Chuan Li
Also captioned as “Sean” (auto-caption error; matched to the published panelist list by role).
Chief Scientific Officer at Lambda (GPU cloud provider) and a member of its founding team, shaping
both the hardware and software of the cloud since joining in 2017. Did his PhD and postdoc at Max
Planck and Utrecht before moving from research into infrastructure.
Talks

A Lab Notebook for Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)

entities/dan-klein.title: Dan Klein
entities/dan-klein.content:
Dan Klein
Professor at UC Berkeley and Co-Founder/CTO of Scaled Cognition, a lab focused on high-reliability
agentic models with verifiable behavior. Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, stepping into a
featured-talk slot after the scheduled speaker (David Chew) couldn’t attend.
His talk laid out five structural, named barriers to agent reliability and argued that reliability
lagging other axes of intelligence — not raw capability — is the real gap between an impressive
demo and a shippable product. See Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability.
Where it shows up

Superintelligence vs. Super-Reliability
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability

entities/dan-roth.title: Dan Roth
entities/dan-roth.content:
Dan Roth
Chief AI Scientist at Oracle and Professor at the University of Pennsylvania (20+ years). In
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities, argues the real architectural shift is decoupling agents
from models entirely (see Model-Hardware Co-Design), and points out that even a verifier
enforcing what agents can communicate to each other can be defeated if the agents evolve their own
encoding (see Securing Agentic AI). His own dedicated talk lays out why making enterprise data
usable by agents is much harder than it looks, and why fixing one visible agent error can silently
introduce a new one — see Data for Agents.
Talks

AI for Data and Data for AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary panel)

entities/daniel-fink.title: Daniel Fink
entities/daniel-fink.content:
Daniel Fink
AI Engineering Lead at Cognizant AI Lab, a roughly 30-40 person applied research group (San
Francisco, with a Bangalore presence). Captioned “Daniel Frink.” Built Neuro SAN, an open-source,
config-driven multi-agent framework.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on Neuro SAN’s architecture, the agentic-webs and agent-
generated-agent-network capabilities that emerged from being fully config-driven, and a validated
production deployment inside Cognizant’s own corporate IT (~200 leaf agents, ~30% ticket-volume
reduction). See Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks.
Where it shows up

Scaling Up Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks with Neuro SAN
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks

entities/daniel-homola.title: Daniel Homola
entities/daniel-homola.content:
Daniel Homola
Lead AI Engineer at BMW Research, working on system-level architecture for agentic AI customer
products, including GUI/computer-use agents that operate screens the way users do.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on reframing multi-agent orchestration around the runtime
delegation decision rather than naming patterns, and on the bounded-tool-call-vs-unbounded-agent-
delegation distinction. See Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice.
Where it shows up

From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice

entities/dawn-song.title: Dawn Song
entities/dawn-song.content:
Dawn Song
Professor at UC Berkeley and Co-Director of Berkeley RDI — the research institute that organizes
the Agentic AI Summit this corpus comes from — most recently VP of AI Research at Meta
Superintelligence Labs. A recurring speaker across the Saturday Plenary: the AM fireside chat with
Jasjeet Sekhon, this keynote, and the “Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities” panel later the same
day. Long-running research focus on AI trustworthiness evaluation and the impact of frontier AI on
cybersecurity, including automatic red-teaming systems and formally-verified “security by
construction.”
Talks

Towards Building Safe and Secure Agentic AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)

entities/devina-jain.title: Devina Jain
entities/devina-jain.content:
Devina Jain
Research Engineer at Lambda, working on model evaluations and safety; background in physical AI and
self-driving. Introduced on stage as “Davina”; full name from the event schedule. In
Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations, presents findings
from a month-long attacker/defender prompt-injection competition run with Berkeley RDI: a rubric for
building meaningful (not just noisy) red-teaming scenarios, why defenses improve faster than attacks
under sustained pressure, why public leaderboards hide overfitting, and — the sharpest finding —
four attack mechanisms that transferred across 14 unrelated scenario domains
(Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms). Also imports “near-miss” testing directly from her
self-driving background: small wording changes can flip an attack’s success the way small changes in
speed or angle separate a collision from a near-miss.
Talks

Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations (Agentic AI Summit
2026, Atlas)

entities/dhruv-(databricks).title: Dhruv (Databricks)
entities/dhruv-(databricks).content:
Dhruv (Databricks)
Works on Omnigent at Databricks. Surname not stated on stream — not to be confused with
Dhruv Batra (Co-Founder & CEO, Yutori), a different person. Co-presented, with
Aravind Segu, the Omnigent workshop at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, covering the
server/runner architecture and its composition/collaboration/control payoffs. See
Meta-Harness Architecture.
Where it shows up

Omnigent - A Meta Harness for AI Agents
Meta-Harness Architecture

entities/dhruv-batra.title: Dhruv Batra
entities/dhruv-batra.content:
Dhruv Batra
Chief Scientist and Co-Founder of Yutori. Auto-captions render his name as “Duvatra”/“Duru
Batra”/“Duv” and the company as “URI”/“Ytori.” In
Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs, argues against the popular claim that
agents will interact with an “agentified” web primarily through APIs — the web’s long tail will
never get clean APIs, and reading raw HTML can’t substitute for rendering a page, since a large
class of real queries only have an answer after client-side JavaScript executes
(Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail). His group builds Navigator, a vision-based computer-use
model that predicts human-like browser actions from a screenshot.
Talks

Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/doga-kerestecioglu.title: Doga Kerestecioglu
entities/doga-kerestecioglu.content:
Doga Kerestecioglu
Principal Applied Scientist at Microsoft, on the Fabric AI team — the group within Microsoft Fabric
building long-running agents for the real-time intelligence space, i.e. agents with access to
high-volume streaming data. On stream the speaker self-identifies only by team (“I’m from the
Microsoft Fabric AI team”) and the MC’s introduction renders as “DOA” in the auto-captions; the
name here is resolved from the event schedule.
In Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks, describes a
five-stage agent memory lifecycle inspired by human memory (Agent Memory Lifecycle) and a
three-tier evaluation methodology for memory systems (Memory Evaluation Framework).
Talks

Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks (Agentic AI
Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/ed-chi.title: Ed Chi
entities/ed-chi.content:
Ed Chi
VP of Research at Google DeepMind, leading ML research on LLM applications (including Lambda);
involved in the Bard and Gemini launches, now working on universal assistant agents (Project
Astra). Previously principal scientist at Xerox PARC. ACM Fellow; SIGCHI Academy member. Co-author
of the original Chain-of-Thought prompting paper — describes personally funding the API costs
(~$10K, on his own credit card, circa January 2021) for the early GPT experiments with Danny/Denny
Zhou that produced it, after being unable to get internal compute access at Google.
At the Agentic AI Summit 2026, gave a personal retrospective (“The Future of Personalized Universal
Agents”) on the ideas he considers to have actually mattered across his career — indexing,
vector-space models, and deep learning/ranking from the first two decades; sequential transduction
(Transformers), chain-of-thought, and post-training from 2015–2025 — with the opinion that “large
language models” should have been called “large reasoning models.” His prediction for 2025–2035:
personalization moving past sorting/ranking into genuine judgment and taste; his own current focus
is reasoning and planning.
On a Sunday Plenary frontier-research panel (likely — the transcript’s speaker attribution is
unreliable at this exact point), floats “anthropic bounds”: benchmarks scored against human
judgment (ELO from human raters, human-designed labels) have a ceiling built into the metric
itself, since 100% means matching every human label. See Principles for Durable Benchmarks.
Where it shows up

Principles for Durable Benchmarks

entities/emily-xue.title: Emily Xue
entities/emily-xue.content:
Emily Xue
Head of Enterprise AI at Scale AI; billed on the event schedule as Yuan (Emily) Xue, and captioned
“Emily Zhu.” Previously spent 11 years at Google as a core member of the
Gemini team, contributing to Gemini development and building the team behind Google’s cloud-agent
benchmark.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on the structural tension between developer-facing capability
benchmarks (which deliberately preserve headroom) and enterprise deployment-readiness needs
(near-ceiling reliability for a specific use case), plus a concrete taxonomy of enterprise
