evaluation primitives. See Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks.
Where it shows up

The Exam Before Enterprise Deployment
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks

entities/eno-reyes.title: Eno Reyes
entities/eno-reyes.content:
Eno Reyes
Co-Founder and CTO of Factory AI. Auto-captions at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 rendered his name as
“Anno Reis” — corrected here.
Spoke on the “software factory” concept: the implicit, mostly-human signal-to-deployed-software
loop every software company runs, three design principles for building or buying into one (model
independence, sovereignty, full organizational scope) plus a shared-agent-core architecture,
environment quality as the actual gate on agent autonomy, and governance/measurement practices for
scaling agents in production. See The Software Factory, Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy,
and Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories.
Where it shows up

Building the Software Factory
The Software Factory
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy
Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories

entities/eric-ho.title: Eric Ho
entities/eric-ho.content:
Eric Ho
CEO and Co-Founder of Goodfire, an AI interpretability research company. In
Unlocking Scientific Abundance by Learning from Superhuman AI, argues interpretability can be
used as a scientific discovery method — reverse-engineering superhuman models to extract genuinely
new, human-legible knowledge from their internals (Interpretability as Scientific Discovery),
building on his co-founder’s prior work reverse-engineering AlphaZero in direct collaboration with
DeepMind.
Talks

Unlocking Scientific Abundance by Learning from Superhuman AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/frank-coyle.title: Frank Coyle
entities/frank-coyle.content:
Frank Coyle
Computer science educator teaching at UC Berkeley, with roughly 30–35 years in the field. Two
pieces of background that visibly shape his argument: an early career in neuroscience — which he
describes as becoming relevant again now that agentic AI is pulling cognitive science back into
the conversation — and direct involvement in 1980s expert systems, the symbolic-AI wave that
failed to scale and gave way to the AI winter. That history is why his position in
Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies is not “symbolic AI was right all along” but the narrower
claim that symbolic methods return usefully as a checking layer around a probabilistic core, not
as the whole system (Neurosymbolic AI, Ontology as Agent Guardrail).
Runs the site codesupreme.ai, named after John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme.
His stated teaching philosophy, which bookends the talk — from Sister Corita Kent, popularized
by the avant-garde composer John Cage: “Nothing is a mistake. There is no win. There’s no fail.
There’s only make.” Paired with a claim about handwriting: writing by hand engages the whole
sensory system, where typing occupies the brain with locating letters on a keyboard, so you learn
faster with a pen and a notebook. Recorded here as context on the speaker rather than as a wiki
claim — it’s off-topic for this vault’s subject matter, and the handwriting assertion is offered
without evidence.
Talks

Why Agentic Systems Need Ontologies (AI Engineer conference, 2026)

entities/giambattista-parascandolo.title: Giambattista Parascandolo
entities/giambattista-parascandolo.content:
Giambattista Parascandolo
At OpenAI; goes by “GB.” In When Language Models Learned to Reason, presents genuinely old
internal slides from his own first project at OpenAI — the earliest reasoning research, before any
model was trained to reason — describing “thinking time” as a new third axis alongside subject and
difficulty, and the first empirical discovery that simply prompting a model to think before
answering raised its accuracy (The Origin of Test-Time Compute).
Talks

When Language Models Learned to Reason (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/hadar-sharvit.title: Hadar Sharvit
entities/hadar-sharvit.content:
Hadar Sharvit
VP of Large Market Model & Machine Learning at Fetcherr; formerly Director of Deep Learning there.
In Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents, demonstrates an architecture for delegating
high-stakes quantitative decisions to grounded, purpose-built tools rather than an LLM’s own
reasoning (Grounded Capability Delegation), and a comparison experiment where a vanilla coding
agent and a capability-grounded agent reached opposite pricing recommendations from identical
data — the vanilla agent confusing correlation with causation, the grounded agent correctly
identifying demand elasticity through genuine counterfactual analysis.
Talks

Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/ian-fischer.title: Ian Fischer
entities/ian-fischer.content:
Ian Fischer
Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Poetiq, a startup entirely focused on building recursive self-improving
(RSI) systems, co-founded with Shumeet Baluja — both former Google DeepMind researchers who had
worked together for over a decade. In An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement,
offers a more rigorous, two-condition definition of RSI than is common in the field (recursive and
self as a strict pair — see Recursive Self-Improvement), and describes Poetiq’s own mechanism
for achieving genuine, systems-oriented RSI cheaply: Self-Optimizing Optimizers.
Before Poetiq: research scientist at Google / Google DeepMind, known for work on information
bottleneck theory (Deep Variational Information Bottleneck, Conditional Entropy Bottleneck).
Before that, co-founder and CTO of Apportable, a Y Combinator company acquired by Google in 2015.
Talks

An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/igor-babuschkin.title: Igor Babuschkin
entities/igor-babuschkin.content:
Igor Babuschkin
Started at DeepMind (WaveNet, StarCraft agents), then OpenAI (scaling transformer models), then
co-founded xAI with Elon Musk, reaching the frontier within under two years. Now Co-Founder/CEO of
River AI, focused on “personal AI” — giving individuals more control and ownership over their own
AI experience.
Moderated the Agentic AI Summit 2026’s Sunday Plenary “frontier research” session — including
Richard Socher’s talk and the closing panel — framing the session around one
shared difficulty across all the speakers’ directions: reward signals are getting harder to
generate as the field moves past correctness-checkable domains like coding.
Also spoke on personal AI and continual learning: five unsolved problems (RL training specific to
the personal-AI use case, personalization, memory/long-context, privacy/security — a much scarier
prompt-injection surface than usual, since a compromised personal agent leaks everything about
you — and cost), framed as a possible way to claw back individual control from AI companies
following the arc PC → smartphone → cloud AI (a step away from individual control) → personal AI
(a step back toward it). Argues personal AI needs both in-context and weight-level memory, and
built River AI’s own multi-tenant LoRA system to make per-user weight-level personalization cheap.
See Agent Memory Lifecycle for the weight-vs-context memory distinction.
Where it shows up

Agent Memory Lifecycle

entities/itsik-mantin.title: Itsik Mantin
entities/itsik-mantin.content:
Itsik Mantin
Head of AI Security Research at Intuit; 25 years in cybersecurity, started working with LLM threats
five years before this talk. In When Good Agents Go Rogue, catalogs the channels through which
“agent goal hijacking” payloads reach an agent’s context (Poison Entry Vectors) and how the
blast radius of a successful hijack scales with connected-tool sensitivity, introducing Simon
Willison’s “lethal trifecta” as a risk model (Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta).
Talks

When Good Agents Go Rogue (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/james-zou.title: James Zou
entities/james-zou.content:
James Zou
Professor at Stanford University, where he leads the AI-for-Science lab. No org/ tag — the
affiliation is purely academic, consistent with how Mengdi Wang’s page is handled.
In Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science, argues for a scaling axis
distinct from building bigger models: scaling the number of collaborating scientist agents, from
tens to millions, and watching for capabilities that only emerge at that scale
(Scaling by Agent Count). What makes that tractable is organizational structure rather than a
flat swarm — his Virtual Lab of 5-10 agents scales into a Virtual Biotech of tens of thousands,
each mirroring a real institutional hierarchy.
Two supporting arguments run alongside it. Scientific databases are built for humans, so agents
should get their own substrate rather than reaching through human-facing APIs
(Agent-Native Data Infrastructure). And a published paper is better treated as an executable
agent than a passive artifact — a “virtual author” that can apply its own method to new data, check
its reproducibility, and collaborate with other paper agents (Paper Agents).
Talks

Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/jerry-tworek.title: Jerry Tworek
entities/jerry-tworek.content:
Jerry Tworek
CEO and co-founder of Core Automation; previously VP of AI Research at OpenAI, where he led the
team that scaled reinforcement learning to the point of producing o3 (“the first really agentic
model,” per his own framing). In Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities, argues the transformer
architecture itself is becoming the bottleneck to further AI progress (see
Model-Hardware Co-Design), and frames reward hacking as a direct, predictable consequence of
environment design rather than a mysterious emergent quirk (see Reward Hacking). His own
dedicated talk lays out the economics of why training genuinely long-horizon agents is hard — see
Long-Horizon Agents and Backprop Beats Scaffolding.
Talks

Opportunities and Challenges for Long-Horizon Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday
Plenary)
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary panel)

entities/jianfeng-gao.title: Jianfeng Gao
entities/jianfeng-gao.content:
Jianfeng Gao
Microsoft Research. Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on internalizing agent harness capability
into models via training, and the environment/training infrastructure (Orchard and UltraEnv)
built to run that loop at scale.
Live captions render his name as “Jen Gao”/“Jang”; the spelling here is confirmed against the
event schedule, which bills him as Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President, Microsoft Research.
Where it shows up

Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel
Orchard and UltraEnv
Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning

entities/johann-schleier-smith.title: Johann Schleier-Smith
entities/johann-schleier-smith.content:
Johann Schleier-Smith
Senior Staff Engineer at Temporal, on the AI foundations team. Auto-captions render his name as
“Johan Shyler Smith”/“Johan Schlersmith.” In Systems Foundations for Agentic AI, describes
durable execution — separating systems concerns like crash recovery from application logic via a
runtime layer (Durable Execution) — and argues the right level of agent autonomy is task-
dependent, not something to maximize by default (Spectrum of Agency).
Talks

Systems Foundations for Agentic AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/john-liu.title: John Liu
entities/john-liu.content:
John Liu
Principal Product Manager for AWS Trainium, AWS’s custom AI accelerator used by leading frontier
labs including Anthropic and OpenAI. Captioned “John Lou.”
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on agentic hardware-optimization loops: a planner/executor
architecture with a persistent knowledge base, and four portable operational lessons on reward
hacking, agent visibility scope, knowledge-base rule hygiene, and knowledge-base pruning. See
Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops.
Where it shows up

Looping for Model Optimization
Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops

entities/john-mcdermid.title: John McDermid
entities/john-mcdermid.content:
John McDermid
Director of the Centre for Assuring Autonomy at the University of York — a ~100-person research
center — with 40 years working on safety of software-intensive systems. Auto-captions render his
name as “John McDermad.” In Safety and Security of Agentic AI, argues safety and security can
no longer be assessed independently once agentic AI is embedded in cyber-physical systems, using
Structured Causal World Models to analyze both together and demonstrating that compound attacks can
defeat defenses that neutralize each attack individually (Joint Safety and Security Analysis).
Talks

Safety and Security of Agentic AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/jonathan-cohen.title: Jonathan Cohen
entities/jonathan-cohen.content:
Jonathan Cohen
Also captioned as “John” (auto-caption error). VP of Applied Research at NVIDIA. Leads, among
other things, the team behind the Nemotron family of open reasoning models — a Nemotron-based
system recently earned a gold-medal-equivalent score at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
His work spans the full agent stack: inference microservices, guardrails, and RL infrastructure.
Career spent at the intersection of GPUs and the software that makes them useful.
Talks

Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)

entities/josh-albrecht.title: Josh Albrecht
entities/josh-albrecht.content:
Josh Albrecht
At Imbue. In Building Punk Software: An Open Agent Stack, argues
dependency on third-party AI platforms is existential risk to your business specifically, and
proposes “punk software” — a five-part rubric (individual, decentralized, open, anti-monopolistic,
moral) for DIY, fully-open AI tooling (Punk Software) — demonstrated with three of Imbue’s own
tools: Manager, Manager Donate, and Mines.
Talks

Building Punk Software: An Open Agent Stack (Agentic AI Summit 2026,
Atlas)

entities/jun-yang.title: Jun Yang
entities/jun-yang.content:
Jun Yang
Senior Director of Compute Architecture at NVIDIA. The MC introduces him as “Junyang” and the
auto-captions render his self-introduction as “Gian from NVIDIA”; the name here is resolved from
the event schedule.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on NVIDIA’s own production use of agents around TensorRT-LLM:
a bug-fixing autobot, a new-model bring-up pipeline, and a training-optimization agent, plus four
closing lessons on agent autonomy tradeoffs. See Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA and
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs.
Where it shows up

Using Agents to Build Production AI Systems - Lessons, Pitfalls, and Limits
Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs

entities/krishnakumar-sharma.title: Krishnakumar Sharma
entities/krishnakumar-sharma.content:
Krishnakumar Sharma
CEO of Omokai, building a physical-AI operating
system for robots and drones; formerly Head of AI at Amazon Germany. In
Agentic Coding, the Boring Way, diagnoses the costs of undisciplined agentic coding in legacy
and enterprise systems, and proposes the D3 discipline (Discover, Plan, Deliver) developed at
Amazon (The D3 Framework).
Talks

Agentic Coding, the Boring Way (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/krishnaram-kenthapadi.title: Krishnaram Kenthapadi
entities/krishnaram-kenthapadi.content:
Krishnaram Kenthapadi
Chief Scientist for Oracle Health’s healthcare AI efforts; two decades of prior work on
trustworthiness (data privacy, bias/fairness, explainability, observability). In
Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned,
describes the orchestration architecture behind Oracle’s clinical AI agent
(Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration) and the system-wide challenges of scaling it into a
trustworthy multi-agent healthcare system — most sharply, why recall matters far more in clinical
summaries than in typical search (Healthcare AI System Challenges).
Talks

Trustworthy Multi-Agent AI Systems for Healthcare: Challenges & Lessons Learned
(Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/manmohan-chandraker.title: Manmohan Chandraker
entities/manmohan-chandraker.content:
Manmohan Chandraker
At UC San Diego. In
Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition,
describes an agent-run scientific discovery architecture for physical AI research — an
ELO-tournament evaluation pipeline and a precise, three-part definition of a “verifiable substrate”
(Verifiable Substrate) — and a framework for keeping humans meaningfully engaged as that
automation increases, built on harnessing tacit expertise and traceable attribution
(Intent Loops).
Talks

Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
(Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/markus-buehler.title: Markus Buehler
entities/markus-buehler.content:
Markus Buehler
Professor at MIT (material science) and Founder & CTO of Unreasonable Labs. In
Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery, argues real discovery requires “breaking the world
model” — an AI system able to actually change what’s believed to be true — via an adversarial
builder/breaker loop (Builder-Breaker Discovery), and describes decentralized, self-organizing
agent swarms with full experiment traceability as a structural fix for publication bias
(Decentralized Science Swarms).
Talks

Superintelligence for Scientific Discovery (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/matt-white.title: Matt White
entities/matt-white.content:
Matt White
Former Global CTO of AI at the Linux Foundation; previously Executive Director and CTO of the
PyTorch Foundation; visiting scholar at Columbia University. In
Open Source Agentic RL Environment, frames the tension between rising AI capability and
openness coming under genuine political pressure, and argues “an agent is not simply a model, an
agent is a stack” — if any one layer (model, harness, tools, environment, guardrails, RL system,
evaluation infrastructure, compute) becomes closed and vertically controlled, the whole ecosystem
becomes less portable, competitive, and resilient (An Agent Is a Stack).
Talks

Open Source Agentic RL Environment (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass — opening framing)

entities/mengdi-wang.title: Mengdi Wang
entities/mengdi-wang.content:
Mengdi Wang
Professor at Princeton University. Auto-captions render her name as “Mingdi Wang” / “Mangdi Wang.”
In LabOS, argues verification, not hypothesis generation, is the real bottleneck for
AI-accelerated science — physical experimentation lacks the checkpoint-and-log scaffolding that
makes digital auto-research tractable (Verification as Science’s Bottleneck) — and describes
LabOS, her group’s AI-XR system for making physical lab work observable and verifiable in real
time.
Talks

LabOS (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/milad-nasr.title: Milad Nasr
entities/milad-nasr.content:
Milad Nasr
Research Scientist at Anthropic; background in network security, now machine learning security. In
End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model, demonstrates a genuine end-to-end AI
research result — a scoped cryptanalysis improvement on reduced-round AES — and argues that “ideas
are cheap, execution is everything” may be inverting now that models can generate and test
thousands of ideas cheaply (End-to-End AI Research).
Talks

End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/milind-naphade.title: Milind Naphade
entities/milind-naphade.content:
Milind Naphade
SVP of AI Foundations at Capital One, leading all AI research and development across the bank.
Previously CTO of Metropolis at NVIDIA, with earlier stints at Cisco and IBM. PhD; 25 years applying
AI to business and scientific problems.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on Capital One’s “Macaw” architecture: a four-agent production
decomposition (understanding/planner/evaluator/explainer) with an independent evaluator agent that
checks plans against policy before execution, explicitly designed as a nondeterministic
reject-and-loop-back system rather than deterministic automation. See
Advancing the State of the Art - The Frontier of Enterprise Agentic AI.
Where it shows up

Advancing the State of the Art - The Frontier of Enterprise Agentic AI
Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent

entities/mohamed-nabeel.title: Mohamed Nabeel
entities/mohamed-nabeel.content:
Mohamed Nabeel
Senior Principal Researcher at Palo Alto Networks; also Adjunct Professor at National University San
Diego. Works in web security, recently focused on how the proliferation of LLMs and agents reshapes
that attack surface. In
Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks,
argues LLM hallucination is itself a supply-chain attack surface, generalizing prior findings on
hallucinated PyPI/npm packages and domain names to browser extensions specifically
(Hallucination-Squatting).
Talks

Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks
(Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/neil-lawrence.title: Neil Lawrence
entities/neil-lawrence.content:
Neil Lawrence
Chief Scientist and Co-Founder of Trent AI (captioned inconsistently as “Trend”/“Trent”; the
event schedule spells it Trent AI). Trent AI’s focus is cybersecurity, where its stated
product stance is to support security engineers rather than replace them, since they remain the
accountable party within their organizations.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on AI safety as fundamentally an accountability problem,
grounding the argument in the 1970 Good Regulator Theorem and naming the resulting failure mode
“agentic debt.” See The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt.
Where it shows up

Viable Systems, Judgment, and AI Safety
The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt

entities/nikhil-chandhok.title: Nikhil Chandhok
entities/nikhil-chandhok.content:
Nikhil Chandhok
Chief Product & Technology Officer at Circle, the issuer of USDC, leading product, technology, and
AI strategy. Previously led product for AR/smart-glasses at Meta (Spark AR Studio); earlier, ran
product at YouTube (turned YouTube Music profitable, launched the first YouTube iPhone app).
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on why agents need a fundamentally different payment substrate
than humans do — programmability, absolute finality, and the privacy-vs-auditability tension — and
Circle’s agentscircle.com marketplace for agent-to-agent task commerce. See
Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy.
Where it shows up

Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy
Agent-Native Payment Rails

entities/ori-goshen.title: Ori Goshen
entities/ori-goshen.content:
Ori Goshen
Co-Founder & CEO of AI21 Labs, an AI lab based in Tel Aviv. Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on
continuous, automated runtime optimization of agent configurations — model choice, harness, and
execution strategy — toward a target cost/quality/latency operating point. See
Runtime Agent Optimization.
Where it shows up

Self Optimizing Agents
Runtime Agent Optimization

entities/oriol-vinyals.title: Oriol Vinyals
entities/oriol-vinyals.content:
Oriol Vinyals
VP of Research at Google DeepMind and Gemini tech lead. In
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities, argues the bigger near-term opportunity is in the
agent/system layer around a model — memory, context compression — rather than a new core
architecture, since transformers have already absorbed a decade of tweaks (see
Model-Hardware Co-Design). Gives his own dedicated talk earlier the same session defining
Recursive Self-Improvement — DeepMind has treated reinforcement learning as the definition of
“agent” for over a decade, starting from sandboxed games (Go, StarCraft) before the current
LLM-agent wave.
Talks

Self-Improvement and Recursive Self-Improvement (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary panel)

entities/philip-rathle.title: Philip Rathle
entities/philip-rathle.content:
Philip Rathle
CTO of Neo4j. In Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI, argues that knowledge, context,
semantics, memory, and ontology converge in practice into one recurring architectural pattern — an
enterprise knowledge layer, best represented as a graph rather than flat tables, opaque vectors, or
model weights (Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer).
Talks

Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/priya-ponnapalli.title: Priya Ponnapalli
entities/priya-ponnapalli.content:
Priya Ponnapalli
SVP of Engineering at Scale AI. Leads work building reliable AI systems for governments (including
the US Department of Defense and the Defense Innovation Unit) and regulated enterprises
(healthcare, finance, telco).
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on an evals-first methodology for reliable agents: a layered
L0-L3 evaluation framework, and an architectural pattern (deterministic core, agentic periphery)
demonstrated via an oil-well casing-design agent. See Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) and
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery.
Where it shows up

Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3)
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery

entities/rahul-bakshi.title: Rahul Bakshi
entities/rahul-bakshi.content:
Rahul Bakshi
Director of Applied Science, Edge AI at Amazon. Leads the applied science team responsible for
Amazon’s custom silicon, including the chip that powers last year’s Echo devices.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on physics-bounded compute escalation for edge agents: a
biological power ceiling for wearables, a three-tier escalation model (escalate only when the task
calls for it), and the gap in composable, task-aware runtimes. See
Physics-Bounded Compute Escalation.
Where it shows up

Scale Compute to the Signal
Physics-Bounded Compute Escalation

entities/raja-giryes.title: Raja Giryes
entities/raja-giryes.content:
Raja Giryes
Professor at Tel Aviv University. In
On the Visual Capabilities of Multimodal Models, traces a research narrative from diagnosing
why multimodal training leans too heavily on the language side to a sharp finding: models
internally “imagine” visual transformations even when they have no mechanism to output images at
all, and explicitly supervising this improves performance
(Visual Imagination in Multimodal Models).
Talks

On the Visual Capabilities of Multimodal Models (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/ramesh-raskar.title: Ramesh Raskar
entities/ramesh-raskar.content:
Ramesh Raskar
Professor at MIT, leading Project NANDA (AI agents in decentralized architecture) — an
11-12-year-old research effort on what an open, non-corporate-owned internet of AI agents would
look like. Auto-captions render his name as “Romesh Rascar.” In
The Agentic Web and the Bazaar Era of AI, argues AI is shifting from a centralized “factory
era” to a “bazaar era” of billions of transacting agents (The Bazaar Era of AI), and frames the
central stakes as whether that web stays open or fractures into walled gardens the way the mobile
and social web did.
Talks

The Agentic Web and the Bazaar Era of AI (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/ranjan-sinha.title: Ranjan Sinha
entities/ranjan-sinha.content:
Ranjan Sinha
IBM Fellow, CTO and VP for watsonx Enterprise AI at IBM. Captioned “Runja Singha”; name confirmed
against the event schedule. In
Speaking the Same Language: NLIP for Agent Interoperability, presents
NLIP, an ECMA-standard protocol positioned as “the HTTP of intent” — semantic interoperability
relying on intelligence at both endpoints, instead of requiring identical schemas on both ends
(Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability).
Talks

Speaking the Same Language: NLIP for Agent Interoperability
(Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/rao-surapaneni.title: Rao Surapaneni
entities/rao-surapaneni.content:
Rao Surapaneni
Leads agent governance and Gemini Enterprise deployment across Alphabet at Google Cloud.
Co-creator of the A2A and AP2 interoperability standards; contributor to UCP, ARD. Mantra: “better
governance unlocks more agent autonomy.”
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on enterprise agent governance: the “agent as intern” framing,
minted agent identity as the fix for identity-inherited access breaking down under agent sharing
and cross-silo multi-agent orchestration, and context-aware runtime permission checking. See
Enterprise AI - Agent Governance.
Where it shows up

Enterprise AI - Agent Governance

entities/richard-socher.title: Richard Socher
entities/richard-socher.content:
Richard Socher
NLP pioneer credited with early work on neural networks in language (word vectors, contextual
vectors, recursive neural nets) and one of the most-cited researchers in the field. Founded
MetaMind, then You.com, and now Recursive (raised $650M) — a company built to pursue recursive
self-improving superintelligence for scientific research.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on the “Eureka Machine”: a four-pillar framework for what AI
needs to automate scientific discovery, the distinction between auto-research and genuine
self-targeted recursive self-improvement, and a concrete result — his system beating years of prior
human research on AI-research benchmarks (nanochat, nanoGPT speedrun, an NVIDIA kernel benchmark)
within days. See The Eureka Machine.
Where it shows up

The Eureka Machine
Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery

entities/romil-bhardwaj.title: Romil Bhardwaj
entities/romil-bhardwaj.content:
Romil Bhardwaj
Co-Founder of SkyPilot, an open-source cross-cluster compute orchestration project originating at
UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab. Auto-captions render his name as “Raml Bardage”/“Romel”/“Romeo.”
In AI Needs an Open Compute Layer, argues AI organizations need a layer that manages across
their inevitably fragmented compute — not a better single-cluster scheduler — since Slurm and
Kubernetes, however good individually, are both fundamentally single-cluster managers
(An Open Compute Layer).
Talks

AI Needs an Open Compute Layer (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/ryan-lopopolo.title: Ryan Lopopolo
entities/ryan-lopopolo.content:
Ryan Lopopolo
Also captioned as “Leopollo” (auto-caption error). Founding engineer of OpenAI’s Seattle office;
led engineering on several of ChatGPT’s workplace products, including Code Interpreter, Record,
and Connectors; author of OpenAI’s public thinking on harness engineering; led a project at OpenAI
called Dark Factory. Opens Harness Engineering by disclosing he moved to Google two weeks
before the talk (Agentic AI Summit 2026, 2026-08-01) and is speaking in a personal capacity, not on
Google’s behalf.
Talks

Harness Engineering (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)

entities/sanja-fidler.title: Sanja Fidler
entities/sanja-fidler.content:
Sanja Fidler
Professor at the University of Toronto; was VP of AI Research at NVIDIA until announcing her
departure the day before this talk, and presents NVIDIA’s work as a departing affiliate (the
auto-caption of her name is badly garbled; the spelling here is confirmed against the event
schedule, which lists the same bio). In World Models for Physical AI Simulation, traces
simulation for physical AI through three technological stages
(Simulation Evolution for Physical AI) and details the architecture behind NVIDIA’s real-time,
interactive generative world models (Interactive World Model Architecture).
Talks

World Models for Physical AI Simulation (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/saurabh-tiwary.title: Saurabh Tiwary
entities/saurabh-tiwary.content:
Saurabh Tiwary
Also captioned as “Sarb.” VP at Google DeepMind. Previously GM of Google AI for Cloud, where he
led Vertex AI and brought Gemini to enterprise customers; before that, spent over a decade at
Microsoft as a CVP/Technical Fellow, where he founded Project Turing — an early effort to stand up
large GPU clusters and train some of the first large language models.
Talks

From Models to Agents to Discovery (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)

entities/sergei-gukov.title: Sergei Gukov
entities/sergei-gukov.content:
Sergei Gukov
Executive Director of the American Institute of Mathematics and John D. MacArthur Professor of
Theoretical Physics and Mathematics at Caltech, where he leads a lab using AI to attack open,
research-level mathematics problems.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on the combined long-horizon/sparse-reward bottleneck facing
AI-for-math specifically (and long-horizon agentic tasks generally), illustrated with real research
problems his lab has worked on, and proposed a shift from “data stack” to “reward stack” as the
field’s next defining scarce resource. See Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck and
Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack.
Where it shows up

The Future of AI for Long-Horizon and Sparse-Reward Tasks
Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck
Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack

entities/shamir-abdul-aziz.title: Shamir Abdul Aziz
entities/shamir-abdul-aziz.content:
Shamir Abdul Aziz
Principal Product Manager at Microsoft. In
Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern, distills two years of building and running agents at
Microsoft: removing operations from humans rather than humans from operations, “models are not the
moat,” outcome-based engineering, and a refined maturity model for agent autonomy
(Zero Ops).
Talks

Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/shiva-kasiviswanathan.title: Shiva Kasiviswanathan
entities/shiva-kasiviswanathan.content:
Shiva Kasiviswanathan
Principal Applied Scientist at AWS, working on AI agents for monitoring and observability in
large-scale cloud operations. In Toward Adaptive Agent Frameworks, lays out three research
directions for mission-critical agent deployment: budget-aware execution as a constrained MDP,
parallel reasoning learned during training, and continual adaptation without catastrophic
forgetting (Adaptive Agent Frameworks).
Talks

Toward Adaptive Agent Frameworks (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/silas-alberti.title: Silas Alberti
entities/silas-alberti.content:
Silas Alberti
SVP of Research and founding team member at Cognition, makers of Devin and Windsurf. In
Scaling RL for Coding Agents, walks through a year-long scaling journey across four
increasingly ambitious RL training runs, identifying entropy collapse as RL’s fundamental diversity
ceiling (Entropy Collapse) and asynchronous RL’s staleness tolerance as the lever that made an
intercontinental training run — spread across four countries — practically possible
(Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance).
Talks

Scaling RL for Coding Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/srijith-rajamohan.title: Srijith Rajamohan
entities/srijith-rajamohan.content:
Srijith Rajamohan
Formerly Head of AI Research at Redis (captioned “Sreejit Rajmohan”). Led the team that built a
diagnostic/remediation agent for Redis query-engine issues, aimed at unblocking customer support
cases before they escalated to the development team.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on trajectory-based agent reliability: a four-category failure
taxonomy, and two measured architectural fixes (setup vs. discretionary tools; a “diagnostic
playbook” knowledge structure). See Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability.
Where it shows up

Spec-Driven Agents - Hierarchical Specs, Tooling, and Trajectory-Based Evaluation
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability

entities/tim-hockin.title: Tim Hockin
entities/tim-hockin.content:
Tim Hockin
Distinguished Engineer at Google; co-creator of Kubernetes. Auto-captions render his name as “Tim
Hulkin” throughout the raw transcript. Approaches agentic AI as an infrastructure problem from the
bottom up: in Is Kubernetes Good for Agents?, argues agent
workloads’ bursty, untrusted/ single-tenant, latency-sensitive profile (Agent Workload Shape)
breaks the assumptions general orchestration platforms are built on, and describes Google’s
open-sourced “Agent Substrate” project as an architectural fix (Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern).
Talks

Is Kubernetes Good for Agents? (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Compass)

entities/trevor-darrell.title: Trevor Darrell
entities/trevor-darrell.content:
Trevor Darrell
At UC Berkeley. In Real-World Reasoning Agents, presents three linked research projects on
agents that see, feel, and reason about the physical world: stateful visual encoders that detect
small state changes standard encoders are invariant to (Stateful Visual Encoders); T-Rex, a
tactile-reactive, multi-process manipulation architecture built with NVIDIA collaborators
(Tactile Reactivity and Multi-Process Architecture); and world motion models that predict 3D
rigid-body trajectories instead of pixels (World Motion Models).
Talks

Real-World Reasoning Agents (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/uri-yerushalmi.title: Uri Yerushalmi
entities/uri-yerushalmi.content:
Uri Yerushalmi
Chief AI Officer and Co-Founder of Fetcherr (auto-captions render the name as “Urieli”).
Background in algorithmic/high-frequency trading and computational neuroscience (PhD). In
Market Models - The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents, argues language models
alone can’t make good quantitative business decisions, since price/supply/demand aren’t first-class
citizens of a language model’s representation, and proposes “market models” — trained directly on
market dynamics, structurally parallel to world models for physical robotics — as the missing piece
(Market Models).
Talks

Market Models - The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents (Agentic AI Summit
2026, Nexus)

entities/venkat-bhat.title: Venkat Bhat
entities/venkat-bhat.content:
Venkat Bhat
Psychiatrist and clinician scientist; Director of the AI for Mental Health Program at the University
of Toronto, and national mental health community-of-practice lead within Canada’s temerity center
for AI in medicine. Runs multi-year clinical trials across depression, PTSD, anxiety, and mental
health/Alzheimer’s. In
Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration,
brings a distinctly rigorous, skeptical clinical-trialist lens to agentic AI: an
assistive/collaborative/ semi-autonomous maturity taxonomy, and the sharp caution that sandbox
success isn’t real-world evidence (Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents), plus a
genuinely novel finding that agent guardrails degrade as task complexity rises
(Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity).
Talks

Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration
(Agentic AI Summit 2026, Nexus)

entities/vijay-ganesh.title: Vijay Ganesh
entities/vijay-ganesh.content:
Vijay Ganesh
Professor of Computer Science at Georgia Tech, working in formal methods and neuro-symbolic AI for
mathematics, physics, and code.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on semantic alignment for auto-formalization: training a model
1,000x smaller than frontier models to outperform them on translating natural-language math into
formal, machine-checkable math, via a contrastive cross-modal training recipe that generalizes to
code translation. See Semantic Alignment for Cross-Modal Translation.
Where it shows up

Semantic Alignment Models for Math and Software Engineering
Semantic Alignment for Cross-Modal Translation

entities/vincent-chen.title: Vincent Chen
entities/vincent-chen.content:
Vincent Chen
VP and founding member of Snorkel AI, where he leads research. Captioned “Vincent Sun Chen” and
billed on the event schedule as “Vincent Sunn Chen” — the middle name’s spelling is still
uncertain, the first and last are not.
Spoke at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 on what makes benchmarks durable rather than “bench slop,” and
on Senior SWE-Bench, a benchmark for senior-level (not junior-level) software engineering that
introduces an explicit “taste” metric alongside correctness. See
Principles for Durable Benchmarks and Taste as a Benchmark Metric.
Where it shows up

The Art & Science of Benchmarking Agents
Principles for Durable Benchmarks
Taste as a Benchmark Metric

entities/vincent-vanhoucke.title: Vincent Vanhoucke
entities/vincent-vanhoucke.content:
Vincent Vanhoucke
At Waymo. In Trustworthy Agents in the Real World, argues physical AI (autonomous driving,
robotics) hit agentic AI’s hard problems roughly 20 years early, and reads off lessons robotics
already learned: reliability at scale is a “game of nines” requiring redesign per
order of magnitude, not incremental tuning; agentic systems inherit AV’s
autonomy-level pitfalls (mixed human/agent control is uniquely bad; partial
and full autonomy are different systems, not points on a gradient); and long-horizon planning needs
world models to escape the compounding-error trap of
step-wise optimization.
Talks

Trustworthy Agents in the Real World (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/weizhu-chen.title: Weizhu Chen
entities/weizhu-chen.content:
Weizhu Chen
Also captioned as “Wu Chen” (auto-caption error). Technical Fellow and Corporate VP at Microsoft
AI, co-leading foundation model development including coding and agentic models. Last author of
LoRA, the industry-standard technique for efficient LLM fine-tuning. In
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities, describes a framework where the model designs and builds
its own agent components on the fly, raising whether harness engineering stays a human discipline
(see Agent Harness). His own dedicated talk argues data matters more than model architecture
for continuous improvement (see Data Over Architecture) and reframes most of ML as distillation
(see Distillation as the Core ML Pattern).
Talks

Continuous Model Improvement (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary)
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Plenary panel)

entities/woosuk-kwon.title: Woosuk Kwon
entities/woosuk-kwon.content:
Woosuk Kwon
Co-creator of vLLM, the open-source LLM inference engine started during his PhD at UC Berkeley
(~88k GitHub stars as of this talk). Co-Founder and CTO of Inferact, a startup built around vLLM
(the company name renders as “Infact”/“Infirect” in the auto-captions). In vLLM, argues agents
stress inference infrastructure along three axes (large models, long context, exploding token
demand) and describes vLLM’s answers: workload-aware model
parallelism with no universal winner, hardware diversification driven by flipped token economics
(Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity), and dynamic KV-cache partitioning and offloading
for hybrid attention and long-lived sessions (Dynamic KV-Cache Management).
Talks

vLLM (Agentic AI Summit 2026, Atlas)

entities/zach-mueller.title: Zach Mueller
entities/zach-mueller.content:
Zach Mueller
Head of Developer Relations at Lambda. In
Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations (“the model is not
the agent”), presents measured evidence that a model’s harness materially changes its performance
and cost — sometimes by double-digit percentages — with the winning model-harness pairing often
unpredictable in advance (Harness Matters More Than Model). Describes Lambda’s project
generating and releasing an open, license-clean dataset of ~150 million agent traces per source
model, and challenges the room to try running familiar models in unfamiliar harnesses.
Talks

Workshop: Open-Source Agent Investigations (Agentic AI Summit
2026, Atlas)

entities/zelin-wan.title: Zelin Wan
entities/zelin-wan.content:
Zelin Wan
Senior AI Engineer at Postman. On stream the speaker self-identifies only as “an engineer from
Postman” and the MC’s introduction is garbled in the auto-captions (“Jayen Juan”); the name here is
resolved from the event schedule.
Presented APIFlow Bench at the Agentic AI Summit 2026: a benchmark showing that API-agent
reliability collapses on chained, dependent tasks (44-73%) even though single-task performance
looks solved (88-97%), plus a three-gate methodology for trusting synthetically-generated
benchmark tasks. See Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks.

Concepts

Agentic AI Full Stack — layered framework (hardware → models → data → security → platform
→ agents) for running agentic AI at scale.
Reward Hacking — agents optimizing the literal measurement instead of the intended task;
documented via a Tetris-playing agent bypassing its own game and exploiting a Turing-complete
chat template.
Autonomous Research Agents — agents running open-ended research loops with no human in the
middle; the Lab supplies reproducible infrastructure, while the Crouzeix prompt supplies an
explicit search policy for portfolio management, memory, falsification, and persistence.
Recursive Self-Improvement — the SI vs. RSI distinction (sharpened by Fischer’s stricter
recursive+self two-condition test), a four-stage ideation/implementation/experimentation/
evaluation loop, three tiers of evaluating progress toward it, and why it may arrive slower than
expected (evaluation/ideation bottlenecks, physical limits, asymptotes).
Long-Horizon Agents — why training genuinely long agent trajectories is economically brutal:
quadratic cost/credit-assignment decay and gradient-step latency, plus value functions and
continual learning as candidate fixes.
Backprop Beats Scaffolding — today’s harness-level tricks (/goal, plan mode, sub-agents)
aren’t trained end-to-end, and whatever ML can eventually backpropagate through tends to displace
what it can’t — a durable tension with treating the harness as a permanent architecture.
Data for Agents — the two-way AI/data relationship, why enterprise data access is harder
than it looks (the retrieval myth, planning over access order, conflicting sources), and “silent
regression on correction” as a durable agent-reliability failure mode.
Data Over Architecture — of the three engines driving model improvement (compute, data,
architecture), data and inference-cost/efficiency matter more than raw architecture quality.
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern — nearly all of ML is distillation from humans or other
models; multi-teacher and weak-teaches-strong distillation both work, contrary to the strong-only
intuition.
Model-Hardware Co-Design — AI infrastructure as a systems problem: chip diversity is
inevitable, models and chips are both multi-year bets that must be planned together, and
abstraction between developers and hardware should be minimized for performance. Also covers an
open, unresolved debate on where the next AI capability gains come from — core architecture,
the agent/system layer, or decoupling agents from models entirely.
Agent Harness — the infrastructure/context/constraints wrapped around a raw model that turn
probabilistic capability into safe, reliable, goal-directed action; synthesized from NVIDIA’s
and OpenAI/Google’s independent framings of the same idea.
Securing Agentic AI — attack surface grows with agent flexibility/autonomy/privilege;
automatic red-teaming as an optimization loop; three historical defense paradigms culminating in
formally-verified “security by construction.”
Agent Workload Shape — agent workloads are bursty, untrusted/single-tenant, and
latency-sensitive, breaking the assumptions general-purpose orchestration platforms (Kubernetes)
are built for.
Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern — the architectural fix for that mismatch: snapshot idle agents
and multiplex them onto a shared pool of pre-warmed workers instead of running one process per
agent for its whole (mostly idle) lifetime.
Game of Nines — each additional order of reliability at scale requires redesigning the
system, not incrementally improving it.
Levels of Autonomy — mixed human/agent control (“level 3”) is uniquely bad; partial and full
autonomy are different systems, not points on a smooth gradient.
World Models for Closed-Loop Agents — per-step optimization compounds into failure over long
horizons (the “DAgger problem”); a good world model needs realism, controllability, and
generalization to fix it.
Scaling by Agent Count — a fourth scaling axis alongside compute/data/architecture: scale the
number of collaborating agents, structured via real organizational hierarchy, not a flat swarm.
Agent-Native Data Infrastructure — scientific databases built for humans are too brittle for
agents; converting them into agent-native virtual file systems is faster, cheaper, and more
accurate than traditional API/MCP access.
Paper Agents — turning a published paper into an interactive “virtual author” agent that can
apply its method to new data, check its own reproducibility, and autonomously collaborate with
other paper agents.
Requirement and Model Gaps — user intent is always broader than what’s specified (the
requirement gap), and the real world is always broader than any tested-against model (the model
gap); both can be narrowed but never certified closed, and AI agents make them far more
consequential via context asymmetry, speed, and scale.
Intelligence vs. Expertise — intelligence (expansive problem-solving capacity) and expertise
(contractive, accumulated, situated competence) are largely orthogonal; continual learning is the
bridge, and a strong-enough algorithm could yield “unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence.”
Parallelization as AI’s Throughline — each generational AI advance (hardware, architecture,
algorithm) is the same idea, parallelization, applied at a different layer.
Diffusion Language Models — breaking the autoregressive, one-token-at-a-time paradigm via
parallel denoising; reframes the target metric as intelligence per unit of time/cost/compute.
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck — AI has sped up hypothesis generation but not
verification; physical experiments lack the checkpoint/log scaffolding digital auto-research has,
risking a world where “science is not faster, science is actually getting slower.”
Joint Safety and Security Analysis — safety and security can’t be assessed independently in
cyber-physical agentic systems; Structured Causal World Models analyze both together, and
compound attacks can defeat defenses that neutralize each attack individually.
Self-Optimizing Optimizers — Poetiq’s mechanism for cheap RSI: a general-purpose optimizer,
first pointed at a target, then pointed at itself.
The Bazaar Era of AI — AI shifting from a centralized “factory era” to a “bazaar era” of
billions of transacting agents; four infrastructure bottlenecks (DNS, passports, interoperability,
attestation) stand between that and walled gardens; the “X for agents” reframing.
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity — no default model-parallelism configuration
wins across model/cluster/workload combinations; flipped token economics forces hardware
diversification beyond a single vendor.
Dynamic KV-Cache Management — hybrid attention needs dynamic, not static, GPU memory
partitioning between attention types; idle KV cache from long, intermittent agent sessions gets
offloaded and restored rather than recomputed.
Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms — a handful of attack mechanisms (“just ask nicely,”
“fake pre-approval,” “findings were wrong,” “workflow impersonation”) transfer across unrelated
scenario domains; public leaderboards hide overfitting; near-miss testing catches what pass/fail
outcomes alone can’t.
Harness Matters More Than Model — swapping a model’s harness changes measured performance and
cost by double-digit percentages; a model’s apparent behavior is partly a harness artifact, not a
fixed property of the model.
Builder-Breaker Discovery — real discovery requires “breaking the world model”; an adversarial
loop where a builder proposes a simplicity-penalized model and a breaker actively hunts for
evidence that falsifies it.
Decentralized Science Swarms — self-organizing agent swarms with no imposed hierarchy, full
traceability of every experiment (including failures) as a fix for publication bias.
Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail — the web’s long tail will never get clean APIs (economics)
and raw HTML can’t substitute for rendering (a large class of answers only exist post-JavaScript);
vision-grounded computer-use agents, not API standards, are what reaches it.
Reasoning Graphs — a model and a harness are both compression into an executable form; a
layered graph of agents (data → reasoning → action) suited to long-horizon, high-consistency
processes.
Architect Agents — the reasoning graph for each use case is built by an agent, not
hand-coded, and the architect agent compounds intelligence at the meta-skill of harness-building.
An Open Compute Layer — AI orgs inevitably end up with fragmented, multi-cluster compute;
Slurm and Kubernetes are both single-cluster managers; the missing piece is a layer that
orchestrates across clusters and lets training/serving dynamically share the same GPU pool.
The Origin of Test-Time Compute — reasoning/thinking-time as a third axis alongside subject
and difficulty; the first empirical discovery that prompting a model to think before answering
raised accuracy, before any model was trained to reason.
Interpretability as Scientific Discovery — reverse-engineer superhuman models’ internals to
extract genuinely new, human-legible scientific knowledge, rather than only using
interpretability for safety or trust.
Entropy Collapse — behavioral diversity within an RL training run decays over time; once it
collapses, no further improvement is possible regardless of compute, until the recipe itself
changes.
Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance — decoupling trainer and rollout generation lets a
more stable algorithm tolerate more staleness between them, keeping inference engines fully
utilized and enabling training across geographically scattered compute.
Durable Execution — separating systems concerns (crash recovery) from application logic via
a runtime layer; three reasons agentic/LLM workloads are a genuinely new kind of systems problem.
Spectrum of Agency — how much autonomy to give an agent is task-dependent; more agency isn’t
automatically the better choice.
Stateful Visual Encoders — standard visual encoders are invariant to small, meaningful
changes by design; a targeted fix makes them change-aware instead.
Tactile Reactivity and Multi-Process Architecture — manipulation needs feeling, not just
seeing/planning/acting; physical agentic systems need a dual- or multi-process architecture.
World Motion Models — predicting geometry/motion rather than pixels when that’s all a task
needs; full pixel-level fidelity isn’t always necessary or desirable.
Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer — graphs bridge human and machine understanding in a
way vectors and model weights don’t; a knowledge layer is active computation, not passive
storage; a fourth take on “the data layer built for one purpose isn’t the one agents need.”
Market Models — a dedicated model class trained on market dynamics,
not text — the same structural move as world models, applied to business decisions; probabilistic
“voxels” as its basic unit; “decision regimes” for multi-modal reward landscapes that shift over
time.
Grounded Capability Delegation — delegate high-stakes quantitative decisions to grounded,
purpose-built tools rather than an LLM’s own reasoning; a vanilla agent confused correlation with
causation where a capability-grounded agent correctly found genuine demand elasticity.
Punk Software — platform dependency is existential risk to your business; a five-part rubric
(individual, decentralized, open, anti-monopolistic, moral) for DIY, fully-open AI tooling.
Semantic vs. Schema-Rigid Interoperability — protocols requiring identical schemas on both
ends vs. protocols relying on intelligence at both endpoints instead; protocol choice should be
guided by workload characteristics, not a single default.
Visual Imagination in Multimodal Models — models internally reconstruct visual
transformations needed to solve spatial-cognition tasks even with no image-generation ability;
explicitly supervising this measurably improves performance.
An Agent Is a Stack — an agent is model, harness, tools, environment, guardrails, RL system,
evaluation infra, and compute; closing any one layer makes the whole ecosystem less portable,
competitive, and resilient.
RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer — environments are the mechanism by which
capabilities move from domain experts into model weights, and are at the pre-standardization
stage model checkpoints were at years ago; OpenEnv’s fix, and a three-way usage taxonomy.
Declared vs. Observed Authority — observability and governance aren’t substitutes; a runtime
trust plane compares declared agent authority against observed behavior, categorizing drift
rather than treating any variance as a binary alarm.
Agent Security Taxonomy — three buckets for agent security work: risk assessment, protection
(fundamental vs. plug-and-play), and certification/self-improvement.
Verifiable Agent Red-Teaming — a red-teaming platform design verified against real system
state rather than an LLM judge, with domain-scoped coverage instead of a fixed test count.
End-to-End AI Research — a two-years-ago >10-year prediction for end-to-end AI research
turned out very wrong; models generate and test thousands of ideas rather than reasoning like a
human researcher, inverting “ideas are cheap, execution is everything.”
Poison Entry Vectors — a taxonomy of channels (email, calendar invites, images, ultrasonic
audio, skills, MCP tool descriptions) through which agent goal-hijacking payloads reach context.
Tool Sensitivity and the Lethal Trifecta — blast radius from a hijacked agent scales with
connected-tool sensitivity; Willison’s lethal trifecta (untrusted data + sensitive access +
external communication) as a simplified risk model.
Hallucination-Squatting — LLM hallucination is a supply-chain attack surface: attackers
register the exact fictitious artifact names a model confidently recommends, exploiting fast
growth, snapshot-learner blindness to deletions, and uneven brand recognition.
Zero Ops — remove operations from humans, not humans from operations;
“models are not the moat”; outcome-based engineering; a refined maturity model where “full
autonomy” means agent-validated outcomes, not unsupervised execution alone.
The D3 Framework — “agentic hangover”: more AI use isn’t automatically more productivity;
Discover/Plan/Deliver as a disciplined alternative to agent swarms and loop engineering.
Clinical Multi-Agent Orchestration — routing clinical queries across structured/unstructured
data with cost-aware model selection; sub-agents structured around a real clinical protocol
(ABCDE) with a synthesizer resolving conflicting outputs.
Healthcare AI System Challenges — offline/online evaluation mismatch; recall matters far more
in clinical summaries than in typical search; domain knowledge encoded via a semantic knowledge
graph.
Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents — a mental-health-specific autonomy maturity
taxonomy; sandbox/simulation success is not evidence of real-world efficacy; declaring a system’s
appropriate severity range rather than overclaiming generality.
Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity — an agent’s safety guardrails degrade as task
complexity rises; guardrail strength materially affects how an agent doing therapy is perceived.
Triple-A Benchmark Standardization — most benchmarks are built around swapping the model, not
the full harness; turn benchmarks into agents so both sides integrate through the protocols
agents already use to talk to each other.
Agents’ Last Exam — agent benchmarks concentrate on programming/math (~7% of real
employment); a methodologically serious fix built from an authoritative occupation taxonomy; no
single agent wins everywhere.
Frontier Cyber Evaluation — four benchmarks spanning the vulnerability lifecycle; evaluation
infrastructure is itself part of the attack surface.
Verifiable Code Generation — formal verification and LLMs solve each other’s bottleneck;
agents close local proof obligations but struggle with repository-wide invariants.
Agent 2.0 — minimal scaffolding letting agents spawn sub-agents and write their own tools and
memory during execution, rather than pre-specifying topology and tools upfront; validated against
a real DEF CON qualifier competition; current models haven’t fully learned to build their own
agents yet.
Adaptive Agent Frameworks — budget-aware execution as a constrained MDP; parallel reasoning
learned during training, not assembled at inference; continual adaptation without catastrophic
forgetting.
Three-Level Runtime Control — token-level steering via a purpose-built reward model, action
control via “genuine self-reflection” that also improves general reasoning, and workflow control
via a precomputed, reusable bank rather than a fixed or fully bespoke structure.
Small-Model Coding Agent Design — minimize context, take tiny verified steps, and reserve
reasoning for recovery loops; small models still specifically struggle to verify their own work.
Agent Memory Lifecycle — ingest/consolidate/forget/retrieve/reconsolidate; consolidation
cadence is domain-dependent, not temporal; “logs are not memories.”
Memory Evaluation Framework — retention, retrieval, and task-completion as three increasingly
realistic, expensive, and important evaluation tiers for agent memory systems.
Verifiable Substrate — a three-part definition of what makes AI-driven scientific discovery
verifiable: grounded idea generation, mutation on top of verified reproductions, and claims that
trace to real logs, code, or hardware runs.
Intent Loops — harnessing tacit expertise (why experts act, not just what they do) so agentic
automation sustains human participation through traceable attribution rather than squeezing
humans out.
Sidewalk Autonomy — sidewalk robots face a distinct, socially denser and more
resource-constrained autonomy problem than road vehicles; simulation built from real video closes
the sim-to-real gap.
Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins — video reconstruction gives one environment per video (a
digital twin); scene-graph-based object swapping generates multiple variations (digital cousins)
from a single capture.
Simulation Evolution for Physical AI — three stages of robotics simulation: artist-built
graphics, reconstruction (NeRF/Gaussian splats, bounded by what was captured), and generative
world models (fully data-driven, can hallucinate uncaptured scenarios).
Interactive World Model Architecture — the technical recipe for real-time, action-conditioned
generative world models: base video model, domain post-training, causal architecture,
distillation for speed.
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel — harness capability (information,
execution, feedback) gets distilled permanently into model weights via training, generation over
generation; a counterpoint on a different time horizon to harness-as-moat.
Orchard and UltraEnv — container-native environment-execution infrastructure (UltraEnv) and
orchestration (Orchard) for running many agents against many environments at scale.
Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning — EvolveLab: agents improving across attempts by
distilling lessons from experience rather than replaying raw traces.
Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts — trainer/rollout-generator/sandbox decomposition for
RL, illustrated with a Qwen3-8B case study; RL taught harness-compliance, not new reasoning.
Harness Diversity as Data Augmentation — Kimi K3 randomizes harness features during training
for robustness, versus Cursor Composer 2’s opposite bet to specialize to one harness.
On-Policy Distillation of Expert RL Models — Kimi K3’s final model is nine reasoning-level ×
domain expert models distilled into one via on-policy distillation.
Train-Inference Mismatch — divergence between an RL rollout engine and training engine
silently degrades training from on-policy toward off-policy; fixes span kernels to algorithms.
Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving — agentic workloads shift serving priorities
toward cache reuse and disaggregation, away from single-turn-chat throughput optimization.
Structural Barriers to Agent Reliability — five named barriers (invisible errors, soft
prompt control, the metacognition gap, non-verifiable RL, cost) explaining why reliability lags
other axes of intelligence.
Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic — randomizing the orchestrator/model in live
agentic sessions to measure treatment effects, rather than scoring against a static benchmark.
Meta-Harness Architecture — a server/runner orchestration layer above existing harnesses,
giving composition, collaboration, and session-level control without absorbing harnesses into
the model.
Runtime Agent Optimization — continuously optimizing an agent’s model/harness/execution-
strategy configuration against a Pareto frontier of cost, quality, and latency.
Principles for Durable Benchmarks — research-agenda thesis, roadmap-setting, researcher UX,
task quality, difficulty/headroom, and rigorous QC, versus “bench slop” and benchmark gaming.
Taste as a Benchmark Metric — Senior SWE-Bench’s “tasteful solve”: codebase and practice
alignment scored explicitly, beyond raw correctness.
Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3) — evaluating an agent as a system across business outcomes,
task success, component evaluation, and diagnostics; evals as the durable asset.
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery — keeping an agent entirely off the numerical-
computation path so fidelity is guaranteed by construction, not evaluation.
Trajectory-Based Agent Reliability — a four-category failure taxonomy and measured tool/
knowledge-architecture fixes (setup vs. discretionary tools, a diagnostic-playbook structure).
Long-Horizon Sparse-Reward Bottleneck — long horizon and sparse reward combine into a
bottleneck needing many-x, not incremental, improvement; illustrated via open math-research
problems.
Reward Stack Replaces Data Stack — reward/environment design as the field’s new scarce,
defining resource, replacing data curation’s role in the pretraining era.
Semantic Alignment for Cross-Modal Translation — a contrastive training recipe letting a
1,000x-smaller model beat frontier models on auto-formalization and code translation.
Deployment Readiness vs. Capability Benchmarks — capability benchmarks and enterprise
deployment-readiness needs are structurally opposed; the path to improvement is economic
(reducing oversight cost), not a rising score.
The Good Regulator Theorem and Agentic Debt — a 1970 cybernetics theorem explaining why
delegating authority to a poorly-modeled system is structurally unsafe; the resulting failure
mode named “agentic debt.”
Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice — multi-agent orchestration reframed as a runtime
delegation decision with multi-valued ground truth, distinct from bounded tool selection because
agent delegation can start an unbounded, never-returning loop.
The Software Factory — the implicit signal-to-deployed-software loop every software company
runs; model independence, sovereignty, full org scope, and a shared agent core as design
principles.
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy — agent autonomy is gated by deterministic, verifiable
feedback in the environment, not model capability alone; a fifth instance of the wiki’s
environments-as-bottleneck theme.
Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories — governance as a platform
responsibility, guardrails scaled to the org size you’re growing into, and outcome metrics over
token counts.
Config-Driven Multi-Agent Networks — Neuro SAN: JSON-described agents/tools, a credential
side-channel, agentic webs, agent-generated agent networks, and a 200-leaf-agent production
deployment.
Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks — single-API-task scores of 88-97% collapse to
44-73% once chained, from step dependency alone; a three-gate methodology for trustworthy
synthetic benchmark tasks.
Production Agent Case Studies at NVIDIA — measured results from a bug-fixing autobot, a
new-model bring-up pipeline, and a training-optimization agent on TensorRT-LLM.
Lessons on Agent Autonomy Tradeoffs — probabilistic agent intelligence, lightweight
harnesses, and two counter-intuitive findings: full autonomy and centralization aren’t always
better.
Physics-Bounded Compute Escalation — a biological power ceiling for wearables and a
three-tier escalation model: escalate compute only when the task actually calls for it.
Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops — a planner/executor architecture for hardware
optimization, plus four portable lessons on reward hacking, visibility scope, rule hygiene, and
knowledge-base pruning.
Verifier-Free Evolution via Intrinsic Fitness — removing the external verifier from
scientific-discovery evolution entirely, using token log-probabilities and diversity as fitness
instead.
Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents — three infra shifts (UX, compute, trust),
a harness-code architecture with code-defined evaluators, and a warm-pool control plane for
agent-scale job launching.
Four Pillars of AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — knowledge, measurement, simulation, and
physical experimentation as what AI needs to automate discovery; a self-targeted RSI result that
may update Vinyals’ “hasn’t happened yet” claim.
Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent — Capital One’s four-role architecture (understanding/
planner/evaluator/explainer) with an explicit reject-and-loop-back path; contrasted with
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery as two different answers to high-stakes agent reliability.
Agent-Native Payment Rails — three structural reasons agents need a different payment
substrate than humans (programmability, finality, privacy-vs-auditability), plus an open-
architecture fix and a live micropayment marketplace for agent-to-agent task commerce.
Neurosymbolic AI — a probabilistic LLM wired to a formal symbolic layer; hallucination as the
feature you fence rather than fix, the Aristotle→Gruber and 1956→agents lineages, and why
symbolic AI returns as a checking layer rather than as the whole system.
Ontology as Agent Guardrail — an ontology-backed reasoner inside the tool-use loop: “Pydantic
at the door, ontology at the ledger”, side-effect-free agents, the RDFS/OWL constructs that do
the checking, and three error classes free text can’t catch.
