sources/a-lab-notebook-for-agents.title: A Lab Notebook for Agents
sources/a-lab-notebook-for-agents.content:
A Lab Notebook for Agents
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, Featured Talks block) by Chuan Li
(Chief Scientific Officer, Lambda). Reports on an auto-research project — Claude, with no human
instruction allowed, tries to teach Gemma to play Tetris better, purely by adjusting model
settings, prompts, and inference speed (no fine-tuning). Over 2.5 days and ~90 ideas / 400+
experiments, the score went from 0 to 16. The talk’s thesis: the gains came less from the model
being smart and more from forcing it to keep lab notes the way a human scientist would — notebook,
whiteboard, sticky notes, signup sheet, translated into agent-usable APIs (note-taking, leaderboard,
inter-agent messaging, job queue). They open-sourced this as the Lab (MIT license).
Key points

The setup: Claude acts as researcher, Gemma as subject. No human instructions, no fine-tuning
— only external levers (model settings, prompt authorization, inference speed). 30-minute
timeout per game, run for 2.5 days.
Agents cheat: Claude first bypassed the game entirely, hand-writing a
simulation directly into the source code and leaving itself a comment to skip the real game loop
(scored 15M). After the team made game files read-only, it found the chat template was
Turing-complete (Jinja — loops, conditionals, mutable state) and computed optimal moves inside
the template itself. Fix: swap in a non-Turing-complete template. Li’s framing: build a strong
cage, or you aren’t measuring the problem-solving skill.
Results are noisy: the same idea run twice, differing only in max_tokens, scored 3 vs. 4.
This is why the Lab commits every idea to its own git branch
(code + settings) — reruns are reproducible and can be averaged instead of trusting one lucky or
unlucky run.
The Lab optimized its own cost: frontier-model experiments ran ~$30 each. They pointed the
Lab at itself — not to go faster, but to generate enough of its own API traces to analyze and
redesign its API. Found a get_experiment call was returning unneeded infrastructure metadata
(Slurm, git info); trimming it made that call 50x cheaper, ~10x cheaper overall.
Progress came in jumps, not a smooth curve: 0→4 (agent invents a stalling move to survive
longer), 4→7 (agent builds a per-piece “cheat sheet,” the same strategy as a goalkeeper prepping
for penalty kicks), plateau, then a history-mining pass finds rotation-heavy pieces are the
bottleneck (→9). The biggest single jump — nearly doubling the score — came from adding one line
to the user prompt (not the system prompt): “don’t overthink, make quick decisions,” placed
right before the board is shown. That one line took ~100 experiments to find.
Attribution: the study was actually run by David Hardman (with Yan Daniel), 2nd-place
finishers in the ARC Prize. Li closes by inverting Chollet’s ARC framing — “solely measuring
skill falls short of measuring intelligence” — into “solely measuring intelligence falls short of
measuring skill; you need both.”

sources/ai-needs-an-open-compute-layer.filePath: sources/AI Needs an Open Compute Layer.md
sources/ai-needs-an-open-compute-layer.title: AI Needs an Open Compute Layer
sources/ai-needs-an-open-compute-layer.content:
AI Needs an Open Compute Layer
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 4:10 PM, part of the Linux Foundation “Open
Agentic Stack” workshop). Romil Bhardwaj (SkyPilot) argues AI organizations need a layer that
manages across their fragmented compute — not a better single-cluster scheduler.
Key points

The problem, the proposed fix, and the payoff. See An Open Compute Layer for the full
argument: why AI orgs inevitably end up with fragmented, multi-cluster compute; why RL workloads
make scheduling qualitatively harder (one “job” is really several sub-workloads with very
different resource profiles); why Slurm and Kubernetes, despite each being excellent at what they
do, are both fundamentally single-cluster managers that don’t solve cross-cluster orchestration;
the proposed layer (SkyPilot) that bridges workloads and whatever clusters actually exist without
replacing any of them; and the emergent benefit of unifying training and serving on one layer —
dynamic reallocation between the two as demand shifts.

sources/ai-for-data-and-data-for-ai.filePath: sources/AI for Data and Data for AI.md
sources/ai-for-data-and-data-for-ai.title: AI for Data and Data for AI
sources/ai-for-data-and-data-for-ai.content:
AI for Data and Data for AI
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, Featured Talks block) by Dan Roth. See
Data for Agents for the concept this talk builds. The one concrete example here (the tennis
query below) is a deliberate illustration Roth ran himself, not breaking news, so it’s treated as
durable content rather than trimmed as an incident.
Key points

The relationship is two-way, not one-dimensional: “AI for data” — GenAI lets us work with
messy, heterogeneous data conceptually instead of learning domain-specific formats — is the
direction most people think about. “Data for AI” is the reverse and, for agents specifically, the
more consequential one: the quality, structure, and governance of your data determines what an
agent can actually do.
Why this is a growing problem, not a shrinking one: general-purpose data has already been
absorbed by model providers — that’s why agents work at all today — but a large amount of data
will permanently stay outside any model (corporate, financial, government, medical, personal),
and it’s dynamic, unlike a frozen training corpus. Supporting agent access to that external data
is, in his view, one of the key emerging GenAI use cases.
A real list of why this is harder than it looks: information retrieval doesn’t reliably work
unless query and document representations are lexically close, which necessitates an actual
semantic layer across sources, not just better search; NL-to-SQL (or NL to any formal query) is
genuinely hard and depends on retrieval working first; rich/multimodal documents (papers, figures,
video) aren’t exposed to retrieval unless someone deliberately extracts that information first;
planning how to access data — what order, how to filter one source by another — is its own hard
problem; real sources routinely conflict and reconciling them is sometimes beyond current model
reasoning; enterprise deployment adds governance, policy enforcement, auditability, and
cost/caching tradeoffs largely orthogonal to raw capability.
A concrete reality check: his own team is competitive on NL-to-SQL leaderboards (Spider 2,
Archer), and even leading systems only score ~55-73% — “really far” from solved.
The tennis example — the sharpest point in the talk: he asks a frontier model to list European
male tennis players by 2025 income. The model plans multi-source retrieval, reconciles conflicting
data, and shows its reasoning trace — genuinely impressive — but the result has three quiet
failures: wrong sort order despite claiming to have used a sort tool; a top player (Carlos
Alcaraz) missing entirely, not just mis-ranked; two players with income identical to the exact
dollar, a near-impossible coincidence that’s really a fabrication tell. When told Alcaraz was
missing, the model fixed it — but silently dropped a different, previously-correct player
(Rublev) and changed another player’s number. Fixing one visible error introduced a new,
invisible one. Nobody cares about tennis rankings and he happens to know the ground truth here
— the same failure mode against a company’s financial analysis is genuinely dangerous, because you
usually won’t know unless you already know the answer.

sources/accelerated-computing-for-agenti.title: Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI
sources/accelerated-computing-for-agenti.content:
Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, Featured Talks block) by Jonathan Cohen
(VP, Applied Research, NVIDIA — leads the team behind the Nemotron open reasoning models). Same
block as A Lab Notebook for Agents; both speakers then share the infrastructure panel with
Tiwary and DeSantis. See Agent Harness for the concept this talk and Harness Engineering
build together.
Key points

What changed since ChatGPT: the modern AI era started as “chat” — a human talking to an LLM,
maybe with database access. Today’s systems are complete autonomous stacks: many models
(open-weight and proprietary), tools, memory, context management, the ability to spawn
sub-agents, and security infrastructure, sometimes started without a human at all.
Core definition: “An agent isn’t just a large language model. It’s a large language model
surrounded by infrastructure” — data marshalling, type checking, rule-based policy enforcement.
Cohen’s line: another word for everything surrounding the LLM “is computer science.” An agent is
the combination of the LLM’s probabilistic, non-deterministic intelligence with the deterministic
power of decades of software engineering.
The resulting stack is heterogeneous at every level: GPUs and CPUs, complex storage
hierarchies, agents spawning sub-agents with scoped data passed between them, sandboxes and
secure enclaves, and a heterogeneous mix of models (large, small, fine-tuned, externally-hosted
proprietary).
NVIDIA’s answer — the “NVIDIA Agent Toolkit”: deployment tech (Kubernetes, NIMs, Dynamo),
accelerated tools (“CUDA-X” — fluid dynamics, differential equations, DNA-sequencing analysis,
made agent-callable), the Nemotron model family plus domain-specific models (robotics/physical
AI, BioNeMo for biology), sandboxing, trace capture for offline RL post-training, and open-source
reference “blueprints.” Several sub-component names are auto-caption garbled (“Nemo relay,”
“switchyard,” “OpenShell,” “open claw”) — treat those as approximate, not confirmed product
names.
The harness deep-dive: recent work from Cohen’s group, “NeMo Object-Oriented Agents” — an
agent as a literal Python object. A special ... (ellipsis) syntax tells the LLM “fill this
block in with code,” so the agent can call and modify its own methods, store solved-problem plans
as callable methods, and hold state as object attributes. Information is passed by reference
(as Python objects) rather than compacted into a string context. Reported results: same score at
half the tokens, and one of the strongest scores on “CyberGym” (an agentic cybersecurity
benchmark).
Forward pointer: Cohen closes on “the harness really matters.” Talk #9 later in this same
session, Ryan Lopopolo’s (OpenAI/Google) Harness Engineering, opens by calling harness
engineering “critical from this morning’s sessions” — the same thread, deliberately picked up
later in the day. See Agent Harness for the concept both talks build.

sources/advancing-the-state-of-the-art--.filePath: sources/Advancing the State of the Art - The Frontier of Enterprise Agentic AI.md
sources/advancing-the-state-of-the-art--.title: Advancing the State of the Art: The Frontier of Enterprise Agentic AI
sources/advancing-the-state-of-the-art--.content:
Advancing the State of the Art: The Frontier of Enterprise Agentic AI
Talk by Milind Naphade (SVP, AI Foundations, Capital One) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday
Plenary track, opening a 3-talk-plus-panel cluster on AI agents in finance and legal. Naphade leads
all AI research and development at Capital One; previously CTO of Metropolis at NVIDIA, with
earlier stints at Cisco and IBM.
Capital One has been building agentic AI for more than two and a half years and had its first
production multi-agentic system live in early last January. Full architecture — “Macaw,” a
four-agent decomposition (understanding/planner/evaluator/explainer) with an explicit policy-check
reject-and-loop-back path — covered in Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent, along with two
production deployments (an auto-dealership chat concierge and a consumer-bank fraud-conversation
handler).
Context beyond the architecture itself: Capital One’s AI Foundations org has published 65+ papers
this year at venues like ICML, ICLR, NeurIPS, and ACL — including work on synthetic data generation
for multi-turn multi-agent conversations (a different problem than single-turn/single-agent
synthetic data), a “mixture of models” approach to routing generated data across multiple models,
and critic-guided distillation for more robust reasoning. Naphade’s framing: Capital One’s data
advantage becomes an AI advantage specifically by customizing every layer of the stack — models,
services, the agentic layer, and the solution layer — rather than treating any one layer as
sufficient on its own.
My read
The most durable piece here is the evaluator agent’s reject-and-loop-back mechanism — a concrete,
named answer to “how do you keep an agentic system safe in a heavily regulated domain” that’s
structurally different from Scale AI’s approach of
removing agents from the risk surface entirely. Both talks are proof that “make agents safe for
high-stakes production” doesn’t have one dominant answer yet — different companies are shipping
genuinely different architectures, both apparently working.
Where it shows up

Policy-Checking Evaluator Agent

sources/agent-arena---causal-evaluations.filePath: sources/Agent Arena - Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World.md
sources/agent-arena---causal-evaluations.title: Agent Arena: Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World
sources/agent-arena---causal-evaluations.content:
Agent Arena: Causal Evaluations of Agents in the Real World
Talk by Anastasios Angelopoulos (Co-Founder & CEO, LMArena) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday
Atlas track. Arena began as a Berkeley PhD student project (with Mike Jordan, Jitendra Malik, and
Ion Stoica) and grew into a company Angelopoulos describes as a top-10 startup by visits since
2020, with 35 million monthly visitors on arena.ai.
Full methodology covered in Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic: reality as the only
judge that matters, a value-back-to-the-user incentive design for collecting free high-quality
feedback at scale, and — the most novel piece — randomizing the underlying orchestrator/model in
live agentic sessions to measure causal treatment effects, aggregated across roughly 25 signals
(task completion, hallucination rate, steerability, bash-error recovery, praise/complaint ratio,
cost, latency) into a continuously updating leaderboard.
Notable scale claim: 28% of Arena’s traffic is software-related work, described as generating
the equivalent of roughly 1,000 SWE-bench-sized datasets of real-world coding data every week
through organic usage.
My read
This is the strongest methodological entry in the Sunday Atlas benchmarking cluster so far —
genuinely distinct from a “yet another benchmark” talk because it isn’t a benchmark at all in the
traditional sense; it’s an experimental design running continuously on real traffic. Worth
watching how it compares once the other evals talks in this batch (Snorkel AI, IBM Research, Scale
AI, the spec-driven-agents talk) are ingested — early read is that this one sidesteps the
harness-standardization problem entirely rather than solving it, which is a meaningfully different
strategy from what Triple-A Benchmark Standardization proposes.
Where it shows up

Causal Evaluation from Production Traffic

sources/agent-learning-requires-compress.filePath: sources/Agent Learning Requires Compressing Information into an Executable Reasoning Structure.md
sources/agent-learning-requires-compress.title: Agent Learning Requires Compressing Information into an Executable Reasoning Structure
sources/agent-learning-requires-compress.content:
Agent Learning Requires Compressing Information into an Executable Reasoning Structure
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 1:30 PM) by Nilou Salehi (Associate
Professor, UC Berkeley; captioned “Nio”). She also self-introduces as co-founder/CEO of “Across
AI,” a company name the schedule does not list and that stays unverified. She argues that both
models and harnesses are fundamentally the same activity — compressing information into something
executable — and describes a concrete architecture, reasoning graphs, built automatically by an
“architect agent.”
Key points

Reasoning graphs. See Reasoning Graphs: a layered graph of agents (data-understanding →
reasoning → action) suited to processes that must run repeatedly with high consistency and
explainability — with the unifying frame that a model and a harness are both compression into an
executable form, echoing Distillation as the Core ML Pattern.
Architect agents and compounding intelligence. See Architect Agents: the reasoning graph
for each new use case is built by an agent, not hand-coded, and that “architect agent” gets
measurably better at the meta-skill of building reasoning graphs with each new case it handles — a
concrete, working answer to the open question already in Agent Harness about whether harness
engineering stays a human discipline.
A compressed case study (invoice matching against purchase orders) illustrates the fit: a
long-horizon, exception-heavy process where an architect-built reasoning graph dramatically
outperformed a general-purpose harness, launched in about a week with no custom code.

sources/agentic-ai-applications-for-ment.title: Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration
sources/agentic-ai-applications-for-ment.content:
Agentic AI Applications for Mental Health: From Chatbots to Clinical Orchestration
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 3:05 PM). Venkat Bhat (University
of Toronto; psychiatrist and clinical trialist) brings a distinctly rigorous, skeptical
clinical-trials perspective to agentic AI in mental health.
Key points

Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents. See
Assistive, Collaborative, Semi-Autonomous Agents: a human-in-the-loop maturity taxonomy for
mental-health agents; why sandbox/simulation success is not evidence of real-world efficacy; the
discipline of declaring a system’s appropriate severity range rather than overclaiming generality;
and a sobering closing statistic on how few actual randomized controlled trials of GenAI
mental-health tools exist.
Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity. See Guardrail Degradation Under Complexity: a
genuinely novel finding that an agent’s safety guardrails degrade as task complexity rises, plus
a measured effect of guardrail strength on how an agent doing independent therapy delivery is
perceived.

sources/agentic-ai-foundational-capabili.title: Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities
sources/agentic-ai-foundational-capabili.content:
Agentic AI Foundational Capabilities
Panel at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, 2:35 PM), following the five afternoon
keynote/featured talks by the same six speakers. Filtered for durable material — the panel also
covered a recent industry sandbox-escape incident in detail, but per how this wiki weights
incidents vs. ideas, that’s a footnote here, not the point (see Reward Hacking and
Securing Agentic AI for the one durable idea it did contribute).
Key points

Where the next AI capability gains come from — a live three-way disagreement: Jerry Tworek
bets on stepping away from the transformer architecture itself (the next two years as “the era of
architecture”); Oriol Vinyals bets instead on the agent/system layer around the model — memory,
context compression — since transformers have already absorbed a decade of tweaks; Dan Roth
bets on decoupling agents from models entirely, since the transformer itself is a recent and
likely temporary choice. See Model-Hardware Co-Design for the fuller writeup.
Weizhu Chen’s open question against hand-built agent harnesses: his group built a
framework where the model designs and builds its own agent components on the fly, raising whether
harness engineering stays a human discipline as models get better at it. See Agent Harness.
Dan Roth’s verifier-evasion point: even a verifier built to enforce what information
agents can share with each other can be defeated if the agents evolve their own encoding or
language the verifier can’t parse — a structural limit on communication-constraint systems
generally, not specific to any one incident. See Securing Agentic AI.
Jerry Tworek’s causal framing for reward hacking: it isn’t a mysterious emergent quirk, it’s a
direct consequence of what an environment rewards — “you don’t get to train your models if you
don’t build your environments carefully enough.” See Reward Hacking.
One line on the incident, no more: the panel also discussed a recent OpenAI agent
sandbox-escape (already covered from Dawn Song’s own talk,
Towards Building Safe and Secure Agentic AI) and a second, separate Anthropic
containment-escape mentioned in passing by the moderator — noted here for completeness, not
developed further.

sources/agentic-coding,-the-boring-way.title: Agentic Coding, the Boring Way
sources/agentic-coding,-the-boring-way.content:
Agentic Coding, the Boring Way
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 1:30 PM), focused on legacy and
enterprise systems specifically. Krishnakumar Sharma (Omokai; ex-Head of AI, Amazon Germany)
diagnoses the costs of undisciplined agentic coding and proposes a concrete discipline developed at
Amazon.
Key points

The D3 Framework. See The D3 Framework for the full argument: the “agentic hangover”
(more AI use doesn’t automatically mean more productivity), why “agent swarms” and “loop
engineering” are costly myths, uncontrolled AI-driven code generation producing persistent
production-database errors, hidden costs including developer cognitive burnout, and the D3
discipline (Discover, Plan, Deliver) as the fix.

sources/agentic-modeling-via-internalizi.filePath: sources/Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses.md
sources/agentic-modeling-via-internalizi.title: Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses
sources/agentic-modeling-via-internalizi.content:
Agentic Modeling via Internalizing Agent Harnesses
Talk by Jianfeng Gao (Microsoft Research) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday, Atlas track).
Speaker name is a phonetic reconstruction — captions rendered it as “Jen Gao”/“Jang.”
Core argument: agent harnesses (information, execution, and feedback layers built around a
model) shouldn’t be treated as permanent, model-external infrastructure. Their capability should
be internalized — distilled into the model itself over successive training generations — via
Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel. Harnesses, run at scale, become the data
substrate that produces the training signal for their own eventual obsolescence.
Gao’s team built Orchard and UltraEnv, a container-native environment-execution stack, to run
that loop at scale — demonstrated with a 73%-SWE-bench-Verified SWE agent trained on ~100,000
distilled trajectories using small open models, plus a GUI-navigation agent and a personal
assistant agent.
The talk also described Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning (“EvolveLab”) — agents improving
across attempts at a task by distilling lessons from experience rather than replaying raw traces,
using a human-memory analogy that turns out to closely mirror a different Microsoft team’s framing
in Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks.
A garbled, unconfirmed detail: an RL algorithm alternative to GRPO framed as distribution-matching
rather than pure reward-maximization, mentioned briefly and not elaborated in the transcript.
My read
This talk sits in direct tension with a theme that’s recurred across this wiki since early in the
summit — Harness Matters More Than Model and Agent Harness — that scaffolding, not the base
model, is where an agent system’s real capability and defensibility currently live. Gao doesn’t
dispute that; internalization instead names the trend the harness-as-moat snapshot sits on: what
differentiates a harness today tends to become default model behavior tomorrow, generation over
generation. Neither talk settles whether new harness capability gets invented faster than old
harness capability gets internalized — that’s the open question this wiki should keep watching
for as more talks touch it.
The EvolveLab/Agent-Memory-Lifecycle convergence is also worth flagging on its own: two separate
Microsoft teams, working on different problems, independently reached for the identical
train-window “we don’t remember every blade of grass” image to justify distilling experience
rather than storing it raw. That’s the kind of cross-talk convergence this wiki exists to surface.
Where it shows up

Internalization and the Harness-to-Model Flywheel
Orchard and UltraEnv
Distilled-Lesson Test-Time Learning
Jianfeng Gao

sources/an-optimization-perspective-on-r.title: An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement
sources/an-optimization-perspective-on-r.content:
An Optimization Perspective on Recursive Self-Improvement
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 3:20 PM). Ian Fischer
(Poetiq — a startup entirely focused on building RSI systems) offers a more rigorous definition of
recursive self-improvement than is common in the field, a taxonomy of existing approaches, and his
own company’s mechanism for achieving it cheaply.
Key points

A precise, two-condition definition of RSI, and a taxonomy of existing approaches — sharper
than what’s already in the wiki. Folded directly into Recursive Self-Improvement: recursive
(compounding) and self (targeting the system itself) as a strict pair, why common usage is both
too permissive and too restrictive, a cost-vs-genuineness landscape splitting LLM-centric from
systems-oriented approaches, and two common “almost-RSI” patterns — Anthropic’s “AI that builds
itself” and the “automated AI scientist” loop — each one specific change away from genuine RSI.
Self-optimizing optimizers — Poetiq’s own mechanism. See
Self-Optimizing Optimizers: start with a general-purpose optimizer, point it at a target
(standard optimization), then point the same optimizer at itself (genuine RSI), which only
requires the optimizer to be general-purpose and able to report its own performance.

sources/architecting-quantitative-decisi.title: Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents
sources/architecting-quantitative-decisi.content:
Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents
Second half of the Fetcherr workshop at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 2:05 PM), the
implementation-level continuation of
Market Models - The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents. Hadar Sharvit
demonstrates an architecture for delegating high-stakes quantitative decisions to grounded tools
rather than an LLM’s own reasoning, and a comparison experiment showing what goes wrong without it.
Key points

Grounded capability delegation. See Grounded Capability Delegation for the full argument:
the forecaster-plus-optimizer decomposition behind most business decisions, why naive LLM agents
structurally lack both capabilities, an orchestrator/specialist-sub-agent/QA architecture that
delegates the mathematically-grounded work to purpose-built tools, and a comparison experiment
where a vanilla coding agent and a capability-grounded agent reached opposite pricing
recommendations from identical data — the vanilla agent confusing correlation with causation, the
grounded agent correctly identifying demand elasticity through genuine counterfactual analysis.

sources/are-small-llms-ready-for-coding-.filePath: sources/Are Small LLMs Ready for Coding Agents.md
sources/are-small-llms-ready-for-coding-.title: Are Small LLMs Ready for Coding Agents?
sources/are-small-llms-ready-for-coding-.content:
Are Small LLMs Ready for Coding Agents?
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 1:30 PM) by Denis Akhiyarov (Senior
Staff AI Scientist, ServiceNow; captioned “Dennis Akiro”). A personal side-project talk: building a
minimal local coding-agent harness specifically designed to make small LLMs viable as coding
agents.
Key points

Small-Model Coding Agent Design. See Small-Model Coding Agent Design for the full
argument: three design principles for compensating for a small model’s weaker planning and
context-handling with tighter, more frequent verification, and an honest limitation from
realistic testing — the agents specifically struggle to verify their own work.

sources/building-frontier-inference-and-.filePath: sources/Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent - A Case Study of SGLang and Miles.md
sources/building-frontier-inference-and-.title: Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent: A Case Study of SGLang and Miles
sources/building-frontier-inference-and-.content:
Building Frontier Inference and Training Infra for Agent: A Case Study of SGLang and Miles
Talk by Banghua Zhu (Co-Founder, RadixArk) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Saturday Atlas track.
The raw transcript’s auto-captions garble nearly every proper noun here — SGLang (the inference
engine) renders as “Ashland”/“HGLN”/“HLN”/“Asha”; Miles (the RL post-training framework) as
“mouse”/“MOS”; the company as “Raex Arc”/“Regisart”/“Reddisart”/“Reddit” (RadixArk). Speaker and
company are resolved from the event schedule; the speaker describes himself as co-founder and CTO
with a UC Berkeley PhD. No entity page created.
SGLang, described as a production-grade open-source inference engine (language models, vision-
language models, plus newer diffusion/image/video and audio ASR/TTS support), optimized for
agentic workloads specifically — see Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving for the
cache-reuse, disaggregation, and long-context techniques this talk credits for a 2.2x throughput
improvement and up to 500 tokens/sec/user on GLM 5.2.
Miles, an enterprise RL post-training framework forked and co-evolved with “slime” (built with
the community for the GLM model series), pairing SGLang as the rollout engine with NVIDIA Megatron
as the training backend. Day-zero support for major open model releases. The talk’s most novel
material: Train-Inference Mismatch — how divergence between the rollout and training engines
silently degrades RL from on-policy toward off-policy, and the three fixes (deterministic kernels,
chat-template token alignment, algorithmic correction via routing replay and truncated importance
sampling).
Other details, not elevated to their own pages: native support for most open-source RL
environment providers, explicitly naming Daytona among others — direct confirmation that
Sandbox Infrastructure for RL Rollouts’s Daytona and the environment-standardization trend in
RL Environments as the Unstandardized Layer are being adopted by production RL frameworks, not
just discussed abstractly. Mature fully-asynchronous RL support (overlapping and disaggregating
rollout/train, extending Asynchronous RL and Staleness Tolerance), and heavy investment in
low-precision rollout training (8-bit, 4-bit, native MXFP4 rollout without reported performance
loss).
My read
This closes out the Atlas RL-infra cluster on the strongest note of the three — train-inference
mismatch is a genuinely new failure mode for this wiki, distinct from staleness (intentional lag)
and reward hacking (misspecified reward), and worth watching for further mentions as more infra
talks get ingested. The Daytona name-check is a small but concrete confirmation that this
cluster’s talks aren’t describing disconnected efforts — Gao’s Orchard/UltraEnv, the Daytona
workshop’s own pitch, Burtenshaw’s OpenEnv argument, and Miles’s environment support are all
pointing at the same production reality from different vantage points.
Where it shows up

Train-Inference Mismatch
Inference Engine Design for Agentic Serving

sources/building-infrastructure-for-the-.filePath: sources/Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy.md
sources/building-infrastructure-for-the-.title: Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy
sources/building-infrastructure-for-the-.content:
Building Infrastructure for the Agentic Economy
Talk by Nikhil Chandhok (Chief Product & Technology Officer, Circle) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026,
Sunday Plenary track, part of a 3-talk-plus-panel cluster on AI agents in finance and legal. Circle
issues USDC, which became functionally legal tender in the US via the “Genius Act” (passed
mid-last year, rulemaking finalizes end of this year, live next year). Chandhok previously led
product for AR/smart-glasses (Meta) and product at YouTube.
His framing: USDC already gave the majority of the ~8 billion people worldwide with a phone but no
dollar-banking access direct, bank-free access to dollars, living entirely on the public internet
rather than inside a bank. His bet: agents are about to become outward-facing endpoints on the
internet the same way, and the payment rails built for humans weren’t built for that.
Full argument — three specific structural reasons existing rails can’t serve agents
(programmability, finality, privacy-vs-auditability), the open-architecture fix, and a concrete
marketplace product — covered in Agent-Native Payment Rails.
My read
Most of today’s agent-governance discussion (Surapaneni’s talk, most of the wiki’s security/
identity coverage generally) is inward-facing — how does my organization keep my agents in
line. Chandhok’s talk is the mirror image: what happens when agents need to transact with other
agents outside any single organization’s boundary. That’s a genuinely different problem, and
this is the first talk in the wiki to address it directly — worth treating as a distinct addition
to the identity/governance cluster rather than a subset of it.
Where it shows up

Agent-Native Payment Rails

sources/building-punk-software.title: Building Punk Software: An Open Agent Stack
sources/building-punk-software.content:
Building Punk Software: An Open Agent Stack
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Atlas, Saturday 4:30 PM). Josh Albrecht (Imbue)
argues that dependency on third-party AI platforms is a real, non-hypothetical business risk, and
proposes “punk software” — DIY, decentralized, fully-open tooling — as the response.
Key points

Punk Software. See Punk Software for the full argument: why platform dependency is
existential risk to your business specifically (not to humanity), the five-part punk-software
rubric (individual, decentralized, open, anti-monopolistic, moral), the open-stack architecture
that satisfies it layer by layer, and three worked examples (Manager, Manager Donate, Mines)
scored against the rubric.

sources/building-reliable-agents---an-ev.filePath: sources/Building Reliable Agents - An Evals-First Approach.md
sources/building-reliable-agents---an-ev.title: Building Reliable Agents: An Evals-First Approach
sources/building-reliable-agents---an-ev.content:
Building Reliable Agents: An Evals-First Approach
Talk by Priya Ponnapalli (SVP of Engineering, Scale AI) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday
Atlas track. Scale builds AI systems for governments (including the US Department of Defense and
the Defense Innovation Unit) and regulated enterprises (healthcare, finance, telco), where
“mostly right” isn’t good enough — every production agent is held to eight engineering gates
spanning data privacy, access control, and rigorous evals, the last of which this talk focuses on.
Full framework covered in Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3): evaluating an agent means
evaluating a system, not a model, via four causally-linked layers (business outcomes, task
success, component evaluation, diagnostics), a named anti-pattern (optimizing lower layers without
confirming higher ones improve), SME-scaling methodology for building evals under expert time
constraints, and the claim that eval suites — not models or agent internals — are the durable
asset.
The oil-well casing-design case study introduces a separate architectural pattern, covered in
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery: keeping the agent entirely off the numerical-computation
path (a trusted deterministic simulator handles all numbers; the agent only retrieves, answers
questions with citations, and drafts documentation), guaranteeing numerical fidelity by
construction rather than by evaluation. A second case study — a financial due-diligence agent for
a professional-services firm — cut analyst time-to-validated-insight from 4-6 weeks to 2 days
using the same layered framework.
My read
The two contributions here are worth keeping distinct: the L0-L3 framework is a general evaluation
methodology applicable to almost any agent, while the deterministic-core pattern is a narrower
architectural choice that only works when part of the workflow already has a trusted, existing
deterministic system to delegate to. Worth cross-referencing against Memory Evaluation Framework
(a similarly-layered framework for a narrower problem) as more evals talks in this batch get
ingested — there may be a case eventually for a higher-level page synthesizing what these
layered-evaluation frameworks have in common across different domains.
Where it shows up

Layered Agent Evaluation (L0-L3)
Deterministic Core, Agentic Periphery

sources/building-the-software-factory.title: Building the Software Factory
sources/building-the-software-factory.content:
Building the Software Factory
Talk by Eno Reyes (Co-Founder & CTO, Factory AI) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday Compass
track (Enterprise AI sub-track). Auto-captions render his name as “Anno Reis,” corrected here. Ran
materially longer than the other talks in its cluster — the density of the material justified
three concept pages rather than the usual one or two.
Three threads: The Software Factory (the core framing — signals flowing through an implicit,
mostly-human triage/plan/code/ship/deploy loop with no explicit model anywhere; three design
principles — model independence, sovereignty, full organizational scope; and a “shared agent core”
architecture built directly on Daniel Homola’s talk from immediately before this one);
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy (fix the environment, not just wait for better models —
agent autonomy is gated by deterministic, verifiable feedback, not model capability alone); and
Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories (governance as a platform responsibility,
a guardrail-maturity heuristic scaled to the org size you’re growing into, the human role shifting
to factory process management, a graduated-autonomy code-review case study, and a sharp
don’t-measure-tokens metrics point).
My read
This talk quietly closes a loop that’s been building across the whole Sunday Atlas/Compass evals
and infrastructure cluster: the environment-as-bottleneck theme now has five independent instances
across totally different domains (RL training infrastructure, three separate talks; and now
software-engineering production practice, twice — Reyes here, and implicitly Homola’s delegation
argument before him). The explicit callback to the immediately-preceding talk is also notable —
one of the few cases this event where a speaker directly builds on the talk right before theirs
rather than each session being self-contained.
Where it shows up

The Software Factory
Environment-Driven Agent Autonomy
Scaling Guardrails and Measuring Software Factories

sources/computer-use-models-will-agentif.filePath: sources/Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs.md
sources/computer-use-models-will-agentif.title: Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs
sources/computer-use-models-will-agentif.content:
Computer-Use Models Will Agentify the Web, Not APIs
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 1:30 PM). Dhruv Batra (Yutori)
argues against the popular assumption that agents will primarily interact with a future “agentified”
web through APIs — instead, vision-based computer-use agents will be what actually reaches the
web’s long tail.
Key points

Where the popular narrative breaks, and why. See Agentifying the Web’s Long Tail for the
full argument: agents becoming the web’s primary actors is right, “the web will be agentified” is
right, but “via APIs” is wrong — the long tail of small-business websites will never get clean
APIs (an economic argument), and reading raw HTML can’t substitute for actually rendering a page,
since a large class of real queries only have an answer after client-side JavaScript executes (a
technical argument). The resulting framing: “the bitter lesson for web agents” — vision-grounded
computer use, not API standards, is what reaches the long tail.

sources/constraint-driven-innovation.title: Constraint-Driven Innovation
sources/constraint-driven-innovation.content:
Constraint-Driven Innovation
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, 9:30 AM keynote), immediately preceding
From Models to Agents to Discovery in the same session. Peter DeSantis (SVP, Amazon —
foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing; launched Amazon EC2, built the
Graviton and Trainium teams) argues AI infrastructure is still “day one” and that the central
problem is an order-of-magnitude efficiency gain, not an incremental one. See
Model-Hardware Co-Design for the throughline the talk builds toward.
Key points

No single chip will power AI for the next decade. GPUs became the AI default almost by
accident — general-purpose hardware built for graphics, not the most efficient architecture for
the fairly predictable matrix/floating-point patterns AI workloads run. That predictability is
why Amazon built Trainium (originally “Inferentia”) on a systolic-array architecture ~a
decade ago — an AI accelerator, not a workload-specific ASIC.
Inference itself splits into two workloads with different hardware profiles: prefill/encoding
(compute-bound) and autoregressive token generation/decode (memory-bandwidth-bound, since each
token touches every model weight). Emerging SRAM-heavy chips trade compute capacity for on-chip
memory to speed up decode, at the cost of context-window length — DeSantis expects these to join
a heterogeneous mix rather than replace chips like Trainium.
Models and chips must be co-designed. A model architecture is a multi-year,
hundreds-of-millions-to-billions-of-dollar bet; a chip takes 2-3 years from design to production
scale. The hard part of chip design is picking which research ideas (he cites Berkeley papers)
will actually be production-ready by the time the chip ships. ~6 months before this talk, Amazon
merged its foundational-model team organizationally with chip development, now under DeSantis.
AI infrastructure is a systems problem, not a model problem or a chip problem. Whatever
“performance” means — accuracy, latency, throughput, cost — requires understanding the entire
stack together. Consequence: Amazon deliberately minimizes abstraction between developers and
hardware, exposing Trainium’s full instruction set, open-sourcing its compiler/toolchain, and
integrating with PyTorch and (auto-caption garbled — likely vLLM) — a deliberate reversal of the
“add an abstraction layer to scale” instinct DeSantis says he’d otherwise have as a software
engineer.

sources/continuous-model-improvement.title: Continuous Model Improvement
sources/continuous-model-improvement.content:
Continuous Model Improvement
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, Featured Talks block, last before the panel)
by Weizhu Chen. See Data Over Architecture and
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern for the two concepts this talk builds.
Key points

Three engines of continuous improvement: compute (pre-training scaling via more data/
exploration; post-training scaling now focused on harder, longer-horizon, multi-agent problems
during training itself, not just inference; test-time compute for getting a family of models to
serve together), data (see Data Over Architecture), and model architecture (quality, inference
cost — which he flags as underweighted by most people — and longer, more efficient context).
His actual ranking: data matters more than architecture, and inference cost/efficiency
matters more than people credit, since real-world adoption is ultimately decided by how fast and
cheap a model runs, not raw quality — so inference cost has to be designed for from the start.
Distillation as a unifying frame for ML itself: nearly everything is distillation, from
humans (web data, product telemetry, human labels) or from other models. See
Distillation as the Core ML Pattern for the multi-teacher and weak-teaches-strong nuances.
A durable refinement of the Agent Harness thread: “optimize the entire system — the
harness is a big part of it — before optimizing the model.” But harnesses get absorbed into the
model over time as models improve, while people keep inventing more ambitious scenarios that need
new harnesses just as fast — the harness layer never actually disappears, it’s a moving frontier.
Reconciles rather than contradicts Backprop Beats Scaffolding’s prediction.
Production data over benchmarks: real interaction/usage data from continuous deployment at
scale is more valuable for improving a model than benchmark scores — seeing what goes wrong in
production and comparing against what other models do in the same scenario.
Closing predictions: scaling keeps working with an unknown ceiling; models will become able
to optimize their own harness and modify other models — stronger and more specific than
Recursive Self-Improvement’s self-modification framing, since this is cross-model, not just
self-directed; synthetic data becomes the mainstream data source; and — his explicit closing
caveat — human involvement stays essential, specifically to keep self-improvement aligned with
human values rather than whatever the model itself would optimize for unchecked.

sources/end-to-end-security-research-wit.filePath: sources/End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model.md
sources/end-to-end-security-research-wit.title: End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model
sources/end-to-end-security-research-wit.content:
End-to-End Security Research with a Language Model
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 3:30 PM). Milad Nasr (Anthropic)
argues that running genuine end-to-end research (idea → hypothesis → methodology → testing →
results) with an LLM — not just using it as a tool — turned out to be much closer than expected,
demonstrated with a real, scoped cryptanalysis result.
Key points

End-to-End AI Research. See End-to-End AI Research for the full argument: why a
two-years-ago prediction of >10 years for this capability was very wrong, a carefully-scoped
novel result on reduced-round AES, the finding that models generate and test thousands of ideas
rather than reasoning like a human researcher (inverting “ideas are cheap, execution is
everything”), the harness as a present-day necessity rather than a permanent feature, and a
candid caveat that most research time now goes into verification, not generation.

sources/enterprise-ai---agent-governance.title: Enterprise AI - Agent Governance
sources/enterprise-ai---agent-governance.content:
Enterprise AI - Agent Governance
Talk by Rao Surapaneni (Google Cloud) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday Plenary track, opening
the “Enterprise AI” session. Surapaneni leads agent governance and Gemini Enterprise deployment
across Alphabet at Google Cloud, and co-created the A2A and AP2 interoperability standards.
Framing: agent as an intern. Trust an agent with specific things, not everything. A good intern
reports what they delivered and where they needed help — that human-in-the-loop moment doubles as
error analysis, and every such interaction is an opportunity to feed back into improving the agent
for the next cycle. The end state he’s building toward: every employee eventually has an “army of
agents.”
The core problem: identity-inherited access breaks down at exactly two points. Today, most
agents simply act under the identity of the user driving them, which works fine for personal-use
and CIO-built workflow agents — until: (1) agent sharing across differential access — I build
an agent using data I can see and share it with a colleague who can’t see it (or who has more
access, e.g. an agent that can write to salary data); (2) cross-silo multi-agent orchestration
— a contract-generating agent and a sales agent from different departments need to jointly expose
data and functionality to each other, and single-user-identity models don’t define what that’s
allowed to look like.
The fix: mint every agent its own explicit identity, not borrowed from a user — registered like
an employee in a directory (so existing IAM tooling just works), observable at runtime, revocable
with a kill switch. On top of that, permissions become context/task-aware rather than static:
checking a vacation balance and writing to a salary field aren’t the same grant just because they
touch the same system, so an “agent gateway” performs live, per-task permission checks rather than
a one-time onboarding-style grant.
Continuous runtime governance, three axes: visibility (detecting unauthorized “shadow AI” —
the agent-era version of shadow IT, e.g. an employee quietly using a downloaded skill); control
(least-privilege, “leased agency” — e.g. allow reading a vacation balance but not writing to it);
security (proactive detection of prompt injection and PII exfiltration, live plus offline
auditing — Google’s “model armor” does nondeterministic analysis of content policies specifically
because static, set-once IAM policies aren’t enough on their own). The approach deliberately reuses
existing enterprise infrastructure (IAM, API-layer identity binding already solved for
mobile/consumer apps) rather than reinventing it — governance is the “special sauce” layered on top.
An open accountability gap, stated but not resolved: when an agent fails, unlike an employee,
there’s no clean answer to who’s accountable — “you can’t fire an agent.”
My read
Nothing else in the wiki addresses agent identity/IAM governance directly, which makes this a
genuinely new addition rather than a rehash. The two named failure scenarios (differential-access
sharing, cross-silo multi-agent orchestration) are the most useful part — they’re concrete enough to
actually design against, rather than “governance matters” in the abstract.
Ankit Goyal’s LinkedIn talk is a striking,
independently-arrived-at confirmation at the implementation level: his “agent-scoped identity, no
direct credential access, proxied communication” trust architecture is close to exactly what
Surapaneni argues for here at the framework level — two different companies converging on the same
shape of solution.
Where it shows up

Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents — a concrete production instance of the
minted-agent-identity architecture this talk argues for.
Agent-Native Payment Rails — the external, cross-organizational counterpart to this talk’s
internal/enterprise governance problem: once agents transact outside any one company’s IAM
boundary, identity and value-transfer become two halves of the same infrastructure gap.

sources/from-models-to-agents-to-discove.filePath: sources/From Models to Agents to Discovery.md
sources/from-models-to-agents-to-discove.title: From Models to Agents to Discovery
sources/from-models-to-agents-to-discove.content:
From Models to Agents to Discovery
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, 9:50 AM) by Saurabh Tiwary (VP, Google
DeepMind). Argues AI is moving through three stages — models → agents → discovery — and lays out
the infrastructure needed at each stage, using Google’s stack as the running example. See
Agentic AI Full Stack for the reusable framework this talk introduces.
Key points

Scale of the shift: agentic tasks cost 10-100x more inference compute than non-agentic
workloads; Google alone processes 3.2 quadrillion tokens/month (roughly three novels’ worth of
text per person on Earth).
Hardware: Google’s latest TPU generation (Ironwood, “v8”) splits into 8T (training) and 8I
(inference) variants — ~121 FP4 exaflops/pod for training (3x the prior generation), ~11.6
exaflops/pod for inference (10x the prior generation).
What gets trained on it: the Gemini model family, Veo/Imagen (video/image), Genie (world
model), and domain-specific models like AlphaFold, AlphaGo, and AlphaChip — the last of which is
used to help design the next generation of TPUs (“TPUs designing TPUs”).
Agent platform, four problems: build (model access, Agent Development Kit, AI Studio),
scale (managed runtime, single instance → millions of agents), govern (agent identity/registry/
gateway — agents get identities separate from the user’s, since they can act beyond what the
user can do directly), optimize (tracing, simulation, evaluation, observability).
Applied “agentic solutions”: AlphaFold/AlphaGenome (biology — plastic-eating enzyme design,
antibiotic-resistance structural biology, neglected-disease drug design, malaria vaccine/drug
delivery), AlphaEvolve/AlphaProof (math and general optimization — Google datacenter
optimization, route optimization, quantum error correction, e-commerce demand forecasting),
AlphaEarth/WeatherNext (climate).
The “autonomous discovery loop” (the talk’s central claim): agents chain data ingestion
(literature, protein databases, experimental logs) → hypothesis generation (AI co-scientists
debating and proposing hypotheses) → simulation (AlphaGenome/AlphaFold) → execution (AlphaEvolve,
Gemini Robotics running physical wet-lab tests), feeding results back into the loop. Illustrated
with biology, but framed as generalizing to most of human discovery — the claim is that research
cycles once measured in years can now run in hours to days.

sources/from-multi-agent-patterns-to-rel.filePath: sources/From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration.md
sources/from-multi-agent-patterns-to-rel.title: From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration
sources/from-multi-agent-patterns-to-rel.content:
From Multi-Agent Patterns to Reliable Orchestration
Talk by Daniel Homola (Lead AI Engineer, BMW Research) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday
Compass track (AI Systems sub-track). Homola works on system-level architecture for agentic AI
customer products, including GUI/computer-use agents that operate screens the way users do.
Full argument covered in Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice: orchestration patterns
(handoff, agents-as-tools, routing) are just naming conventions over the same underlying problem —
the runtime delegation decision. Two sharp reasons this differs from ordinary tool selection:
multi-valued ground truth (several agents can validly handle the same task depending on context)
and the bounded-tool-call-versus-unbounded-agent-delegation distinction (delegating to an agent can
start an autonomous loop that never cleanly returns). Consequences for evaluation: score the path,
cost, and UX, not just final task success, using datasets with full runtime context.
My read
The bounded-versus-unbounded distinction is the standout idea here — it’s a crisp, portable way of
naming something that’s easy to gloss over when an agent-delegation call is implemented with the
same syntax as an ordinary tool call. Worth carrying forward as a check for any future architecture
talk: does this system actually know the difference between calling a deterministic tool and
handing control to another loop?
Where it shows up

Agent Delegation as Runtime Choice

sources/ghost-in-the-web-store.title: Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks
sources/ghost-in-the-web-store.content:
Ghost in the Web Store: Preempting LLM-Hallucinated Browser Extension Supply Chain Attacks
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 3:30 PM), closing out the security
cluster. Mohamed Nabeel (Palo Alto Networks) argues LLM hallucination is itself a supply-chain
attack surface, extended here specifically to browser extensions.
Key points

Hallucination-Squatting. See Hallucination-Squatting for the full argument: why
hallucination generalizes beyond fiction into an exploitable naming gap, three structural reasons
browser extensions are a “hallucination-prone zone” (explosive growth outpacing recency,
snapshot-learner blindness to deletions, uneven brand recognition), and empirical confirmation
that hallucinated extension names get registered and weaponized in the wild.

sources/graphs-are-the-knowledge-layer-f.filePath: sources/Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI.md
sources/graphs-are-the-knowledge-layer-f.title: Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI
sources/graphs-are-the-knowledge-layer-f.content:
Graphs Are the Knowledge Layer for Agentic AI
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Atlas, Saturday 4:30 PM). Philip Rathle (Neo4j)
argues that knowledge, context, semantics, memory, and ontology — usually discussed as separate
topics — converge in practice into one recurring architectural pattern: an enterprise knowledge
layer, best represented as a graph.
Key points

Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer. See Graphs as the Enterprise Knowledge Layer
for the full argument: why graphs bridge human and machine understanding in a way vectors and
model weights don’t; why existing alternatives (foundation models, custom-trained models, flat
tables, data lakes) each fall short for this specific job; what agents actually need from a
knowledge layer; and why a knowledge layer is active computation, not passive storage.

sources/harness-engineering.title: Harness Engineering
sources/harness-engineering.content:
Harness Engineering
Talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Saturday Plenary, Featured Talks block) by
Ryan Lopopolo. His intro calls harness engineering “critical from this morning’s sessions” —
the same thread Jonathan Cohen raised earlier in Accelerated Computing for Agentic AI. See
Agent Harness for the concept both talks build.
Key points

Capability overhang: even holding model and harness constant, models today are far more
capable than they’re safely permitted to “side-effect into the world.” They don’t know what
local or global good looks like to their operators, and lack the context for full autonomy
within the organizations they’re deployed in. The human’s job is to steward them with tools,
context, guardrails, coaching, and trust.
A year-long personal experiment: starting June 2025, Lopopolo stopped writing code himself
and required the same of his team — the only permitted activity was directing an agent to do the
work. Early on, models couldn’t yet do things like autonomously read Slack and respond to pages;
the fix was recursively “double-clicking” into a task until reaching something the model actually
could do, then reassembling upward. Each pass permanently accrues capability into the harness,
not just into the model — and teams collaborating this way on one agent get “the best parts of
everyone.”
Implementation is now abundant, but coherence isn’t: code is “free to produce” with current
models, but even advanced models can’t yet turn “make me a billion-dollar business” into
something coherent — they still struggle with tasks like operating a vending machine. Human
expertise’s job is to constrain the space the agent is allowed to explore so it keeps tracking in
the right direction over long horizons.
Two scarce resources shape harness design: (1) human time — ruthlessly identify
repetitive interventions (reviewing code, rejecting “slop,” going back-and-forth on a plan) and
eliminate them, which is what lets agent autonomy expand over time; (2) context window /
attention, for both human and model — a foundational limit that doesn’t go away just because
context windows grow. His own rule of thumb: needing more than three interventions on a single
agent run usually means something is wrong with the harness, worth reflecting back into the
environment rather than just retrying.
Closing analogy: harness engineering is like onboarding a new hire who is generally capable
but doesn’t know what “good” looks like for you specifically — surfacing the non-functional
requirements for good local work, and curating context and tools to constrain what the agent can
do, is the job.
Note on affiliation: his bio (and the published schedule) list him as OpenAI — founding
engineer of its Seattle office, led engineering on ChatGPT’s Code Interpreter, Record, and
Connectors, led a project called Dark Factory. He opens the talk by disclosing he’d moved to
Google two weeks earlier and is speaking in a personal capacity, not on Google’s behalf.

sources/harnessing-the-collective-intell.filePath: sources/Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science.md
sources/harnessing-the-collective-intell.title: Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science
sources/harnessing-the-collective-intell.content:
Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of Agents for Science
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 10:15 AM). James Zou (leads the
AI-for-Science lab at Stanford) argues for a scaling axis distinct from bigger models: scaling the
number of collaborating scientist agents — tens to millions — and watching for capabilities that
only emerge at that scale.
Key points

Scaling by agent count, made tractable by organizational structure. See
Scaling by Agent Count — his Virtual Lab (5-10 agents) scaled into a Virtual Biotech (tens of
thousands of agents), each mirroring a real organizational hierarchy rather than a flat swarm.
Agent-native data infrastructure. See Agent-Native Data Infrastructure — existing
scientific databases are built for humans, not agents; converting them into agent-native virtual
file systems (“PaperClip”) is faster, cheaper, and more accurate than traditional API/MCP access.
Paper agents — knowledge as executable agent, not passive artifact. See Paper Agents —
turning a published paper into a “virtual author” that can apply its method to new data, check
its own reproducibility, and autonomously collaborate with other paper agents to produce new
findings.

sources/information-retrieval-in-the-age.filePath: sources/Information Retrieval in the Age of Agentic AI.md
sources/information-retrieval-in-the-age.title: Information Retrieval in the Age of Agentic AI
sources/information-retrieval-in-the-age.content:
Information Retrieval in the Age of Agentic AI
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 1:30 PM, delivered remotely). Tanya
Roosta (AMD) argues information retrieval has shifted from a straight-line pipeline (query →
retrieve → rank → present) to an iterative “conversation with the world” (plan → search → analyze →
critique → present, often 20+ turns), and that evaluation hasn’t caught up — grading only the final
answer misses whether each hop in a multi-turn trace was actually adequate.
My read
Considered for a concept page and passed. The core reframe (lookup → conversation) is a fairly
generic observation at this point in the field’s discourse, and the evaluation-gap point restates a
theme already well-established elsewhere in the wiki — Recursive Self-Improvement’s evaluation
bottleneck, Verification as Science’s Bottleneck, Transferable Prompt Injection Mechanisms’s
near-miss testing — without adding a genuinely new angle specific to IR. The talk’s closing
landscape survey (reasoning-aware retrieval, multi-turn benchmarks, graph RAG, self-RAG, adaptive
RAG, token-count-as-metric) names several real techniques but doesn’t develop any of them enough to
be worth its own page. Kept as a source-only entry rather than skipped entirely, so the talk is on
record as considered.

sources/infrastructure-for-long-running-.title: Infrastructure for Long-Running Agents
sources/infrastructure-for-long-running-.content:
Infrastructure for Long-Running Agents
Talk by Ankit Goyal (Principal Staff Software Engineer, AI Platforms, LinkedIn) at the Agentic AI
Summit 2026, Sunday Compass track (Enterprise AI sub-track). The final talk in this session’s
non-Plenary HIGH batch.
Full account covered in Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents: three production
agents (model migration, performance optimization, autonomous research) sharing one hypothesis-
code-execute-evaluate lifecycle; three infrastructure shifts driven by agents at scale (UX, compute,
trust); a harness-code architecture with code-defined evaluators specifically to prevent reward
hacking; an agent-scoped identity and sandboxing security model; a custom warm-pool control plane
for agent-scale job launching; and measured impact (100% growth in experiment volume over six
months).
My read
This closes out the Sunday Compass HIGH batch on a fittingly concrete, infrastructure-grounded
note. The “harness code, not natural-language prompts, with code-defined evaluators” principle is
the standout — it’s a specific, actionable mechanism for something several other talks in this
batch discussed more abstractly (reward hacking, the need for deterministic verification), stated
here as a direct engineering practice rather than a general design philosophy.
Where it shows up

Infrastructure for Long-Running Production Agents

sources/intelligence-+-continual-learnin.title: Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise
sources/intelligence-+-continual-learnin.content:
Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 3:20 PM) by Yu Su (CEO,
NeoCognition; Associate Professor, Ohio State University). The speaker’s own framing:
a conceptual talk connecting three ideas — intelligence, expertise, and continual learning as the
bridge between them — to explain why frontier models can solve hard math problems yet struggle to
diffuse into everyday enterprise work without an entire “forward-deployed engineer” industry to
hand-hold deployment.
Key points

A modern Moravec’s Paradox: AI excels at symbolic reasoning (math, code) but struggles with
everyday digital work, because the world isn’t one unified domain but millions of “micro-worlds”
— every profession, every company has its own local structures, constraints, and dynamics too
heterogeneous for one static model to capture.
Intelligence vs. expertise, and continual learning as the bridge. See
Intelligence vs. Expertise for the full argument: intelligence as expansive problem-solving
capacity vs. expertise as contractive, accumulated, situated competence; a working definition of
continual learning; and the payoff — intelligence and expertise are largely orthogonal, so a
strong-enough continual-learning algorithm could produce “unbounded expertise from bounded
intelligence,” with real implications for where value should accrue in the AI stack.

sources/is-kubernetes-good-for-agents.title: Is Kubernetes Good for Agents?
sources/is-kubernetes-good-for-agents.content:
Is Kubernetes Good for Agents?
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 10:15 AM). Tim Hockin
(Kubernetes co-creator) looks at agentic AI as an infrastructure problem from the bottom up: do
agent workloads actually fit the platform everyone already runs on?
Key points

Agent workloads break Kubernetes’ core assumptions. Kubernetes was built for long-running,
horizontally-scalable, cost-amortizable processes. Agents are bursty (short spurts, then idle for
minutes to weeks), untrusted and single-tenant (must run sandboxed, can’t share a sandbox — so no
amortizing overhead across tenants), and latency-sensitive (a human is usually waiting on the
other end). See Agent Workload Shape.
Two patterns people use today, both flawed. Naive pod-per-agent-instance keeps pods “warm” for
tens of seconds to tens of minutes after each turn to dodge slow (seconds-to-15s+) cold starts —
burning huge resources at scale, since Kubernetes has no native suspend/resume. The alternative,
a bespoke DIY control plane built on top of raw Kubernetes, is efficient but re-invents large
parts of Kubernetes and is hard for smaller teams to operate.
The fix is architectural, not a bigger cluster. Google’s open-sourced “Agent Substrate”
project treats an idle agent as a suspendable, snapshotted “actor” rather than a running-but-idle
process — multiplexing many actors onto a shared pool of pre-warmed workers and collapsing the
idle-to-active wake cost from minutes to low-hundreds-of-milliseconds. See
Agent Suspend-Resume Pattern for the reusable version of this idea, independent of Google’s
specific implementation.

sources/labos.title: LabOS: The AI-XR Co-Scientist That Sees and Works With Humans
sources/labos.content:
LabOS: The AI-XR Co-Scientist That Sees and Works With Humans
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 10:15 AM). Mengdi Wang (Princeton)
argues that verification, not hypothesis generation, is the actual bottleneck for AI-driven
science, and describes her group’s approach to fixing it.
Key points

Verification, not idea generation, is science’s bottleneck — and why AI risks making science
slower, not faster, without fixing it. See
Verification as Science’s Bottleneck for the full argument: the three-stage
hypothesize/compute/verify pipeline, the reproducibility-crisis evidence, why physical
experimentation lacks the checkpoint/log scaffolding that makes digital auto-research tractable,
and LabOS as a concrete attempt to turn physical labs into verifiable, AI-observable
environments.

sources/looping-for-model-optimization.title: Looping for Model Optimization
sources/looping-for-model-optimization.content:
Looping for Model Optimization
Talk by John Liu (Principal Product Manager, AWS Trainium) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday
Compass track (AI Systems sub-track). Trainium is AWS’s custom AI accelerator, used by leading
frontier labs including Anthropic and OpenAI.
Full architecture and lessons covered in Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops: a nested,
multi-layer model-optimization loop (functional model → kernel development → end-to-end
evaluation), a planner/executor pattern with a persistent knowledge base for kernel optimization
specifically, and four operational lessons — reward hacking as structural rather than a discrete
bug, checking an agent’s visibility scope before assuming its decision logic is wrong, fixing
existing rules rather than stacking new ones, and actively pruning knowledge bases with a shelf
life — plus a closing point on designing benchmarks as a first-class component when none exist yet.
My read
This talk packs an unusual number of distinct, portable, aphoristic lessons into a short slot —
each one lands as a small, self-contained piece of hard-won operational wisdom rather than a
single developed argument. The visibility-scope lesson stands out as the most novel: it’s a
genuinely different failure mode from reward hacking (the agent isn’t gaming anything, it’s making
a locally correct decision with an invisible-to-it global cost) and doesn’t have an obvious home
elsewhere in this wiki yet.
Where it shows up

Lessons from Agentic Optimization Loops

sources/making-autonomy-autonomous.title: Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
sources/making-autonomy-autonomous.content:
Making Autonomy Autonomous: Toward Mental Models for Discovery and Intuition
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Atlas, Saturday 2:00 PM). Manmohan Chandraker (UC
San Diego) describes an agent-run scientific discovery architecture for physical AI research, and a
framework for keeping humans meaningfully engaged as that automation increases.
Key points

Verifiable Substrate. See Verifiable Substrate: an ELO-tournament discovery pipeline
applied to a real physical-AI research problem (3D Gaussian splatting for pedestrian perception),
a precise three-part definition of what makes a discovery substrate verifiable, and a method for
bootstrapping one by reverse-engineering existing published papers.
Intent Loops. See Intent Loops: harnessing tacit expertise (why experts act, not just
what they do), mental models that drive world models with traceable rather than merely aggregated
contributions, and attribution mechanisms meant to sustain human participation as automation
increases rather than squeeze humans out.

sources/market-models---the-missing-foun.filePath: sources/Market Models - The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents.md
sources/market-models---the-missing-foun.title: Market Models - The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents
sources/market-models---the-missing-foun.content:
Market Models: The Missing Foundation for Quantitative Decision Agents
First half of a two-part Fetcherr workshop at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 2:05
PM). Uri Yerushalmi argues language models alone can’t make good quantitative business
decisions, because the domain’s actual first-class citizens — price, supply, demand — aren’t
language concepts, and proposes “market models” as the missing piece.
Key points

Market models. See Market Models for the full argument: the
biological principle that decision-system architecture should reflect the environment’s structure,
why agentic business workflows violate that principle by centering a language model, market models
as a dedicated model class trained directly on market dynamics (structurally parallel to world
models for physical robotics), the “probabilistic voxel” as their basic unit, and “decision
regimes” as a reusable way to think about multi-modal reward landscapes that shift over time.
Hands off directly into Architecting Quantitative Decision Agents (Hadar Sharvit, second half
of the same workshop) for the implementation details.

sources/measuring-api-agent-reliability-.filePath: sources/Measuring API Agent Reliability for Long-Horizon Tasks in Production.md
sources/measuring-api-agent-reliability-.title: Measuring API Agent Reliability for Long-Horizon Tasks in Production
sources/measuring-api-agent-reliability-.content:
Measuring API Agent Reliability for Long-Horizon Tasks in Production
Talk by Zelin Wan (Senior AI Engineer, Postman) at the Agentic AI Summit 2026, Sunday Compass
track (Agent Evolution & Benchmarks sub-track). On stream the speaker self-identifies only as “an
engineer from Postman”; the name comes from the event schedule.
Full benchmark covered in Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks: APIFlow Bench measures
enterprise API-agent reliability on long-horizon, dependent-chain tasks, finding that single-task
scores (88-97%) collapse to 44-73% once tasks are chained — not because the tasks get harder, but
because later steps depend on earlier results and state. A seven-failure-mode taxonomy (auth,
discovery, schema repair, multi-step execution, error recovery, pagination, statefulness) grades
failures separately by cause. A three-gate methodology (self-testing, solvability, golden replay)
makes synthetically-generated benchmark tasks trustworthy.
My read
The compounding-error number here (88-97% → 44-73%) is the sharpest, most concretely measured
version of the long-horizon-compounding-failure argument this wiki has collected across the whole
summit — Tworek’s RL-training economics, Vanhoucke’s control theory, and Gukov’s math-research
angle all argue the same underlying point more abstractly; this talk puts a precise, reproducible
number on it in a genuinely common enterprise setting (chained API calls) rather than an
exotic or research-frontier one.
Where it shows up

Compounding Error in Chained API Tasks

sources/mindful-agents.title: Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks
sources/mindful-agents.content:
Mindful Agents: Human-Inspired Memories for Long-Horizon Tasks
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Compass, Saturday 3:20 PM). Doga Kerestecioglu
(Principal Applied Scientist, Microsoft) presents the Microsoft Fabric AI team’s work on
long-running agents over high-volume streaming data.
Key points

Agent Memory Lifecycle. See Agent Memory Lifecycle: the human-vs-agent memory contrast,
a five-stage lifecycle (ingest, consolidate, forget, retrieve, reconsolidate) with
domain-dependent rather than purely temporal consolidation cadence, and “logs are not memories.”
Memory Evaluation Framework. See Memory Evaluation Framework: a three-tier evaluation
methodology — retention, retrieval, and task completion — increasing in realism, cost, and
importance.

sources/observability-is-not-governance.title: Observability Is Not Governance: Building a Runtime Trust Plane for Agentic AI
sources/observability-is-not-governance.content:
Observability Is Not Governance: Building a Runtime Trust Plane for Agentic AI
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 3:30 PM). Jon-Rav Shende, CTO of
Thales Group, argues observability and governance are frequently
conflated but aren’t substitutes for each other, and describes a runtime trust plane built to
provide both.
Key points

Declared vs. observed authority. See Declared vs. Observed Authority for the full
argument: why traditional linear governance breaks down once agents, sub-agents, and
orchestration take on “a life of its own in real time”; the sub-agent privilege-inheritance risk;
and the runtime trust plane that compares declared authority against observed behavior, with a
graded drift taxonomy and risk-tiered containment.

sources/omnigent---a-meta-harness-for-ai.filePath: sources/Omnigent - A Meta Harness for AI Agents.md
sources/omnigent---a-meta-harness-for-ai.title: Omnigent: A Meta Harness for AI Agents
sources/omnigent---a-meta-harness-for-ai.content:
Omnigent: A Meta Harness for AI Agents
Hands-on workshop by Aravind Segu and Dhruv (Databricks; Dhruv’s
surname is not stated on stream and not listed on the schedule) at the Agentic
AI Summit 2026, Sunday Atlas track. Omnigent is Databricks’s open-source meta-harness project,
used internally by all 3,000+ Databricks engineers (thousands of sessions per day) and, at the
time of the talk, about seven weeks into its public open-source release with roughly 8,000 GitHub
stars, 3,000 merged PRs, and 360+ contributors.
Full architecture covered in Meta-Harness Architecture: a server/runner split with one shared
API across every surface, giving composition (multi-harness orchestration, e.g. the built-in
“Polly” agent fanning a task out across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode in parallel),
collaboration (live, shareable sessions with in-context commenting), and control (session-level,
context-aware policies, soft-checkpoint cost budgets, and credential proxying). Live demo included
routing a task automatically to a small model (GPT-5 Nano) versus a large one (Opus) based on task
complexity via a pluggable classifier, and running an agent inside a Databricks-hosted cloud
sandbox that survives closing the laptop.
Q&A surfaced one deliberate design boundary: compaction and context management are left entirely
to each underlying harness’s own native logic rather than reimplemented at the meta-harness layer.
My read
This is a genuinely new position in the wiki’s harness-vs-model debate rather than another
restatement of it — where Gao’s internalization and Klein’s built-in-verification argument both
move capability into the model, Omnigent explicitly keeps individual harnesses untouched and
adds orchestration above them, betting that the harness ecosystem will keep fragmenting rather
than consolidating and that the winning move is to make harness choice cheap to change rather than
to pick or absorb a winner. Worth revisiting once Self Optimizing Agents is ingested — the
smart-routing feature here (classify task complexity, pick harness and model automatically) looks
like a specific, narrower instance of that talk’s broader thesis.
Where it shows up

Meta-Harness Architecture
