sources/world-models-for-physical-ai-sim.title: World Models for Physical AI Simulation
sources/world-models-for-physical-ai-sim.content:
World Models for Physical AI Simulation
Sanja Fidler (University of Toronto; formerly VP of AI Research, NVIDIA — she announced leaving
NVIDIA the day before this talk, and presents NVIDIA work as a departing affiliate). Atlas stage,
Agentic AI Summit 2026.
Fidler frames physical AI — intelligence moving into robots, at the edge — as the next “breakpoint”
after the ChatGPT moment (2022) and the current agentic AI era, and argues that simulation is
foundational infrastructure for robotics: you cannot develop robotics without really good
simulation, because unlike LLM evaluation (sample, score, maybe involve a human), robot software has
to be validated in closed loop — deployed, acting, observed — and physical-robot time is bounded by
real time, while simulated time can scale across GPUs.
She traces three stages of simulation technology and gives a detailed architecture recipe for the
current, generative stage — see Simulation Evolution for Physical AI for the stage-by-stage
history and Interactive World Model Architecture for the technical recipe and speed trajectory.
A specific worked example: at NVIDIA, autonomous-driving software ran through two million simulated
rollouts per day on reconstruction-based (NeRF/Gaussian-splat) simulation before the generative
stage existed at all — an illustration of how much scale simulation-based development already
required, even in the “digital twin” era before generative world models.
Talk uses the same elephant-on-the-road generalization example as Vincent Vanhoucke’s
Trustworthy Agents in the Real World (World Models for Closed-Loop Agents) — independently,
from a different speaker and company, converging on the same test case for whether a world model
truly generalizes beyond its training distribution versus merely interpolating (e.g., rendering an
elephant-shaped truck instead of an elephant).
My read
This talk is best read as a pair with Bolei Zhou’s Scaling Sidewalk Autonomy with World Models:
both describe the same reconstruction-based simulation limitation (one environment per captured
video — a “digital twin”), just from different companies and robot domains (NVIDIA/autonomous
vehicles here, Coco Robotics/sidewalk delivery there), and propose different fixes — Zhou’s is
scene-graph variation from a single capture (Digital Twins vs. Digital Cousins); Fidler’s is
fully generative hallucination unconstrained by any single capture. Combined with Vanhoucke’s talk,
that’s three independent talks at the same summit converging on video-generation-based world models
as the near-term path forward for physical AI simulation.

sources/zero-ops---agents-operate,-human.title: Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern
sources/zero-ops---agents-operate,-human.content:
Zero Ops - Agents Operate, Humans Govern
Five-minute lightning talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Nexus, Saturday 1:30 PM).
Shamir Abdul Aziz (Microsoft) distills two years of building and running agents at Microsoft
into a compact set of durable principles.
Key points

Zero Ops. See Zero Ops for the full argument: removing operations from
humans rather than humans from operations, “models are not the moat,” outcome-based engineering
(humans reviewing validated outcomes rather than diffs), a refined crawl-walk-run-fly maturity
model, and the trust requirements enterprises need before deploying agents at scale.

sources/vllm.title: vLLM: Building Open and Efficient Inference for Agents
sources/vllm.content:
vLLM: Building Open and Efficient Inference for Agents
Featured talk at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 (Atlas, Saturday 4:30 PM). Woosuk Kwon
(co-creator of vLLM, the open-source inference engine started at UC Berkeley) argues the API layer
for using an LLM has barely changed for agents — everything that’s changed is underneath it, in
the inference-serving engine itself.
Key points

Agents stress inference infrastructure along three axes: large (trillion-parameter) models,
long context (up to a million tokens across hundreds of turns), and exploding, effectively
unbounded token demand.
No universal parallelism strategy, and why hardware has to diversify. See
Inference Parallelism and Hardware Diversity: the right model-parallelism configuration
depends on model architecture, cluster setup, and workload shape simultaneously, with no default
that wins; and token economics have flipped (a token’s value now exceeds its generation cost),
driving demand that outpaces GPU supply and forcing support for many hardware backends.
Dynamic KV-cache management for hybrid attention and long-lived sessions. See
Dynamic KV-Cache Management: hybrid attention architectures (mixing full and
linear/sliding-window attention) need dynamic rather than static GPU memory partitioning between
attention types, and long, intermittent agent sessions need idle KV cache offloaded to external
storage and restored rather than recomputed.
